en.aproximar:
From Latin ~approximāre~ (“to draw near to”), from ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) + ~proximāre~ (“to come near”), a verb built on ~proximus~ (“nearest”), the superlative of the adverb ~prope~ (“near”), itself usually traced to a Proto-Indo-European base *~pro-~ (“forward, in front”). Cognate with English ~approximate~ and ~proximity~, Italian ~approssimare~, and Portuguese ~aproximar~.

The double comparison inside the word is easy to miss: ~proximus~ is already a superlative (“nearest of all”), so ~aproximar~ means, literally, “to bring toward the nearest.” Older and legal Spanish kept a concrete spatial sense — moving one body toward another — while modern usage leans figurative: an estimate that is ~aproximado~ (“approximate”), or two people who grow closer (~aproximarse~). The same family gave Spanish ~próximo~ (“next, near”), ~proximidad~, ~aproximación~, and the adverb ~aproximadamente~.
en.apuntar:
From ~a-~ plus ~punto~ (“point, dot”), which descends from Latin ~punctum~ (“a prick, a puncture, a point”), the neuter past participle of ~pungere~ (“to prick, to pierce”). ~pungere~ goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~pewǵ-~ (“to prick, to punch”). It is cognate with Italian ~appuntare~ and French ~pointer~, and — through ~pungere~ and its participle — with English ~point~, ~puncture~, ~pungent~, and ~poignant~, all of them sharp in one way or another.

The core idea is making a point or mark, and ~apuntar~ fanned out from it into a startling spread of senses: to aim a weapon (to bring it to a point on a target), to point at something, to jot down (to set a point of ink on paper), and — in the theatre — to prompt an actor, which is why a prompter is an ~apuntador~. From the same ~punctum~ Spanish also drew ~punto~ (“point”), ~punta~ (“tip”), ~puntual~ (“punctual”), ~puntería~ (“aim”), ~apunte~ (“note”), and ~puntuar~ (“to punctuate”). The tiny prick of ~pungere~ thus points, notes, aims, and punctuates all at once.
en.archivar:
From ~archivo~ (“archive”), from Latin ~archīvum~ (also ~archīum~), from Ancient Greek ~ἀρχεῖον~ (~archeîon~, “public office, town hall”) — the building where a magistrate kept official records — from ~ἀρχή~ (~arkhḗ~, “beginning; rule, magistracy”). Cognate with Italian ~archiviare~ and French ~archiver~, and — through Greek — with English ~archive~.

The chain hides a small irony: to ~archivar~ a document is, etymologically, to lodge it in the ~ἀρχή~, the seat of power, so filing was once an act of governance, not of forgetting. Modern Spanish has bent the word the other way — ~archivar~ un asunto now often means to shelve it, to let it lie. The Greek ~ἀρχή~ carried two senses, “beginning” and “rule,” and Spanish harvested both: from the first came the ~arqui-~/~arce-~ prefix of ~arquitecto~ (“chief builder”) and ~arzobispo~ (“archbishop”); from a related stem, the ~-arca~ of ~monarca~ and ~jerarquía~. The noun ~archivo~ now also names a computer file.
en.argumentar:
From Latin ~argūmentārī~ (“to argue, adduce proof”), from ~argūmentum~ (“evidence, proof”), from ~arguere~ (“to make clear, prove, demonstrate”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂erǵ-~ (“bright, white; to shine”). Cognate with Italian ~argomentare~ and French ~argumenter~, and — through the same root — with English ~argue~ and ~argument~.

The root meant brightness, and Latin ~arguere~ began as “to make bright,” hence “to make clear, to prove” — so to ~argumentar~ is, at bottom, to bring a matter to light. The most vivid relative hides in plain sight: from the same *~h₂erǵ-~, “the shining metal,” Latin named silver ~argentum~ — which gave Spanish ~argén~ and, by way of the silver-freighted Río de la Plata, the country name ~Argentina~. Greek preserved the root in ~ἄργυρος~ (~árgyros~, “silver”). Spanish also keeps ~argumento~, ~argüir~, and the participle-noun ~arguyente~ from this bright, argumentative family.
en.armar:
From Latin ~armāre~ (“to arm, equip with weapons”), a denominal verb from ~arma~ (“weapons, tools, equipment”). ~arma~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~h₂er-~ (“to fit together, join”), via a form *~h₂(e)rmos~ (“that which is fitted”) — so weapons were, literally, the things fitted together, the gear. The root is richly attested: cognate with Ancient Greek ~ararískō~ (“to fit together”) and Sanskrit ~áram~ (“fittingly”). Within Latin it also produced ~ars~ (“skill, art”) and ~artus~ (“joint, limb”). The Romance verbs run parallel: Italian ~armare~, French ~armer~, Portuguese ~armar~.

The core image never left: to ~armar~ is to fit pieces together, and Spanish keeps that concrete sense vividly — one can ~armar~ a bookshelf, a tent, or an argument, not only an army. From the sense of fitting and joining, the vocabulary of skill and order also grew: the same root underlies ~arte~ (“art”), ~artículo~ (“article; joint”), ~armonía~ (Greek for “a fitting-together”) and ~arma~ itself. Colloquial idiom pushed the “assemble” sense toward chaos, too: ~armar~ un lío or ~armar~ un escándalo is to kick up a fuss — to assemble a mess. From ~armāre~ come directly ~armario~ (“wardrobe,” a place to store gear), ~armada~ (“fleet”) and ~armadura~ (“armor”).
en.arrancar:
The origin of ~arrancar~ is genuinely disputed, and the sources agree only that no single etymon is secure. By the account Corominas favored, it descends from an Old Spanish *~esrancar~, formed on Old Occitan ~ranc~ or Old French ~ranc~ (“row, rank of soldiers”) — the Germanic-derived word that also gave English ~rank~ — with the idea of tearing a fighter out of the line. A rival account derives it from Latin ~ēruncāre~ (“to weed out”), perhaps crossed with ~ērādīcāre~ (“to uproot”); Romanian ~arunca~ (“to throw”) and Sicilian ~arruncari~ are cited in its support. An older guess tracing it to a Gothic *~wrankjan~ (“to twist”) is rejected on phonetic grounds.

Whatever its source, the verb fixed on the image of wrenching something loose from where it sat rooted — pulling up a plant, yanking out a tooth, tearing off a strip. From that violent tug came its everyday modern senses: a car ~arranca~ when its engine is jolted into motion, and a sprinter ~arranca~ bursting from the line. The noun ~arranque~ names both an engine’s “ignition” and, figuratively, a sudden “fit” of temper or generosity — a surge that grips you as abruptly as a root torn from soil. Nearby forms include ~arrancada~ (“a sudden spurt, a lurch forward”) and ~arrancador~.
en.arrastrar:
Spanish ~arrastrar~ (“to drag, haul”) is a prefixed formation: ~a-~ + ~rastrar~ (from ~rastro~) + the suffix ~-ar~. ~rastro~ (“rake; trail, trace”) descends from Latin ~rastrum~ (“rake, hoe”), an instrument noun from ~rādere~ (“to scrape, scratch, shave”), from a Proto-Indo-European root reconstructed as *~reh₁d-~ (“to scrape, scratch”). English ~erase~ (from Latin ~ērādere~) belongs to the same verb, and Spanish keeps ~raer~ (“to scrape off”) and ~arrasar~ (“to raze, level”) beside it.

The image inside ~arrastrar~ is vivid once you see it: a rake — ~rastrum~ — is a tool dragged along the ground, so ~rastro~ came to mean both the rake and the trail it leaves, and the verb came to mean pulling something across the ground the way a rake is pulled. Madrid’s famous flea market, ~El Rastro~, is named for that same “trail” sense, reputedly the trace of blood dragged from a nearby slaughterhouse. From the same root Spanish keeps ~rastrear~ (“to track, trace”), ~rastrillo~ (“rake”) and the noun ~rastro~ itself.
en.arreglar:
Spanish ~arreglar~ is a prefixed derivative — ~a-~ plus ~regla~ (“rule, ruler”) — parallel to Late Latin ~regulāre~ (“to regulate”), from ~regula~ (“a straight rod, rule”), from ~regere~ (“to keep straight, guide, rule”). The root is Proto-Indo-European *~h₃reǵ-~ (“to straighten, direct”). It is one of the most productive roots in the family: through ~regula~ it gives English ~rule~ (via Old French) and ~regular~; through ~regere~ and ~rēx~ (“king”) it gives ~regent~, ~royal~, and ~correct~; and the Germanic branch of the same root gives English ~right~.

To ~arreglar~ something is to bring it back into line with the ~regla~ — the straight measuring rod — hence to set it right, put it in order, adjust, or repair it. Old Spanish also had the barer ~reglar~; the ~a-~ form won out for everyday “to fix.” The root’s Spanish harvest is large: ~regla~ (“rule, ruler”), ~reglamento~ (“regulation”), ~regular~, ~regir~ (“to govern”), ~rey~ (“king,” worn from ~rēx~), ~región~, ~recto~ (“straight”), ~corregir~ (“to correct”), and ~dirigir~ (“to direct”), all sharing the idea of the straight line.
en.arrojar:
~arrojar~ has no classical Latin ancestor of its own; the standard account, advanced by Menéndez Pidal and endorsed by Corominas, derives it from an unattested Vulgar Latin *~arrotulāre~ / *~rotulāre~ (“to send rolling”), from ~rotulus~ (“little wheel, roller”), the diminutive of ~rota~ (“wheel”). ~rota~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~Hret-~ (“to roll, run”), the root also behind German ~Rad~ (“wheel”) and, in Latin, ~rotāre~. So ~arrojar~ belongs, by this account, to the wheel-and-roll family that also gave Spanish ~rueda~, ~rodar~ and ~rótulo~.

If that etymology is right, ~arrojar~ began as something concrete and physical: to set a thing ~rotulāre~, rolling downhill, and hence to hurl or fling it. First recorded in the fourteenth century, it broadened from the literal throw to a wide arc of casting-out senses — to throw, to give off, to yield: a ledger ~arroja~ a balance, a report ~arroja~ results, and colloquially a queasy stomach ~arroja~ (“vomits”). From the same act Spanish drew ~arrojo~ (“boldness, daring” — the spirit of one who throws himself forward) and the adjective ~arrojado~ (“bold, rash”), where the old rolling stone has become a headlong courage.
en.articular:
From Latin ~articulāre~ (“to divide into joints; to utter distinctly”), from ~articulus~ (“small joint”), a diminutive of ~artus~ (“joint, limb”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂er-~ (“to join, fit together”). It is cognate with Italian ~articolare~ and French ~articuler~, and was borrowed into English as ~articulate~. The same root surfaces in Greek ~ἄρθρον~ (~árthron~, “joint,” whence the word arthritis) and in Latin ~ars~ (“skill, art”) — something well fitted together.

The metaphor runs from anatomy to speech: where bones meet at a joint, breath is likewise jointed into distinct sounds, so ~articular~ came to mean both to connect and to pronounce clearly. Spanish keeps both threads: ~articulación~ names a knuckle and a crisp enunciation alike; an ~artículo~ is a jointed “little member” of a text or a law; and ~arte~ preserves the older notion of fitting things aptly together. To articulate an argument is, at heart, to set its joints in the right order.
en.ascender:
From Latin ~ascendere~ (“to climb up, mount”), from ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) + ~scandere~ (“to climb”), from Proto-Indo-European *~skend-~ (“to climb, dart, leap”). Cognate with Italian ~ascendere~ and Portuguese ~ascender~; through the same root, with English ~ascend~, ~descend~ and ~scan~, and — more distantly — with Welsh ~esgyn~ (“to ascend”).

Latin ~scandere~ named physical climbing and, in verse, the “climbing” of metrical feet — the origin of English ~scan~. Prefixed with ~ad-~, it became “to climb toward,” hence to go up; Spanish kept both the literal sense of climbing a height and the figurative ones (to be promoted, to rise in rank). From the same Latin verb Spanish drew ~ascenso~ (“ascent, promotion”), ~ascensor~ (“elevator”), and ~ascendiente~/~ascendente~ (“ancestor; ascending”); the prefixes ~de-~ and ~trans-~ yielded ~descender~ and ~trascender~, and ~con-~ gave ~condescender~.
en.asegurar:
From ~a-~ plus ~seguro~ plus the verbal ending ~-ar~ — literally “to make secure.” ~seguro~ comes from Latin ~sēcūrus~ (“free from care, safe”), a compound of ~sē-~ (“without”) and ~cūra~ (“care, concern”). Cognate with French ~assurer~ and ~sûr~, and with English ~secure~ and ~sure~ — the latter two a famous doublet, ~secure~ borrowed straight from Latin and ~sure~ worn down through Old French.

So to assure or ensure is, at root, to remove someone’s cares. The Latin ~sēcūrus~ described a mind at peace, untroubled; from that inner calm the word drifted toward outward safety and reliability. Spanish keeps both threads in ~seguro~, which is at once “safe,” “sure,” and (as a noun) “insurance” — the contract that buys freedom from worry. Relatives include ~seguridad~ (“security”) and, from the same ~cūra~, the verb ~curar~ (“to cure, to care for”) and the noun ~cura~ (“cure,” and also “priest,” the one charged with the care of souls).
en.asesinar:
The verb ~asesinar~ was formed from the noun ~asesino~ (“assassin, murderer”), which came through Italian ~assassino~ and Medieval Latin ~assassīnus~ from Arabic ~ḥaššāšīn~, a name given to the Nizari Ismaili sect of Syria and Persia in the era of the Crusades. Cognate with French ~assassin~, English ~assassin~, and Portuguese ~assassinar~.

The traditional account, popularized by Marco Polo, reads ~ḥaššāšīn~ as “hashish-users,” from Arabic ~ḥašīš~ — the story being that the sect's members were drugged before their killings. That etymology is disputed: there is little evidence the Ismailis used hashish, and the label appears to have been a slur coined by rival Muslims; a competing account instead ties the name to their founder ~Ḥasan~ ibn al-Ṣabbāḥ, whose followers would be “Hasan's men.” Either way, the sect's reputation for targeted political killing is what fixed the word's meaning: through Italian it came to mean a hired killer, and Spanish ~asesinar~ is simply to murder — especially by treachery or for hire. Modern relatives: ~asesino~ and ~asesinato~ (“murder”).
en.asignar:
From Latin ~assignāre~ (“to mark out, allot, assign”), a compound of ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and ~signāre~ (“to mark”), from ~signum~ (“sign, mark, standard”). The deeper root is disputed: ~signum~ is traced either to Proto-Indo-European *~sek-~ (“to cut,” a mark cut in) or to *~sekʷ-~ (“to follow,” the standard a legion follows), and the sources do not settle which. From ~assignāre~ come Italian ~assegnare~, Portuguese ~assinar~, and French ~assigner~; from ~signum~ itself, English ~sign~.

To assign was originally to mark something out and set it apart for a purpose — a plot of land, a duty, a share. Spanish shows the usual split between a popular and a learned line from ~signum~: the inherited ~seña~ and ~señal~ beside the bookish ~signo~, ~signar~, and ~designar~. A charming descendant is ~asignatura~ — a school “subject,” literally something “assigned” to be studied — and ~insignia~, ~consigna~, and ~diseñar~ (“to design,” to mark out a plan) belong to the same clan. Whether the root first meant a cut or a thing-to-follow may stay unresolved, but either way ~asignar~ has always been about marking one thing off for another.
en.asistir:
From Latin ~assistere~ (“to stand by, take one’s place beside”), a compound of ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and ~sistere~ (“to cause to stand, to take a stand, to halt”). ~sistere~ is a reduplicated form built on ~stāre~ (“to stand”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~steh₂-~ (“to stand”) — the same root behind ~estar~. It gave Italian ~assistere~, French ~assister~, and English ~assist~; and through ~sistere~ it is cognate with English ~exist~, ~insist~, ~resist~, ~consist~, and ~persist~.

To “stand beside” someone is to be there both for support and as a witness, and ~asistir~ split along exactly that line. In Spanish (as in French ~assister~) it chiefly means “to attend, to be present”: one ~asiste a~ a class or a concert. But it also keeps the “stand-by-to-help” sense in ~asistir~ (“to assist”) and in ~asistencia~ (“assistance; attendance”) and ~asistente~ (“assistant”). English ~assist~, by contrast, narrowed to helping alone — a tidy false-friend trap. The ~sistere~ family stands tall across Spanish: ~existir~, ~insistir~, ~resistir~, ~consistir~, ~persistir~, ~desistir~, and ~subsistir~, every one of them, at root, a way of standing.
en.asociar:
From Latin ~associāre~ (“to join to, unite with”), a compound of ~ad-~ (“to, toward,” assimilated to ~as-~) and ~sociāre~ (“to join, ally”), the verb built on ~socius~ (“companion, ally, partner”). ~socius~ meant literally “a follower” and descends from Proto-Indo-European *~sekʷ-~ (“to follow”) — the same root that gave Latin ~sequī~ (“to follow”). The cognate web is wide: through ~sequī~ English took (by borrowing) ~sequence~, ~sequel~, ~second~ (“the following one”) and ~pursue~. The learned Romance descendants of the compound include Italian ~associare~, French ~associer~ and Portuguese ~associar~.

The logic is transparent: companions are those who follow together, and to associate is to make someone a ~socius~, a fellow-goer. From ~socius~ Spanish keeps ~socio~ (“partner, member”), ~social~, ~sociedad~ (“society”), ~asociación~ (“association”) and ~asociado~ (“associate”). The deeper root *~sekʷ-~, through ~sequī~ and its participle ~secūtus~, fanned out enormously: ~seguir~ (“to follow”), ~seguido~, ~secuencia~ (“sequence”), ~consecuencia~ (“consequence”), ~perseguir~ (“to pursue”), ~ejecutar~ (“to execute, follow through”) and even ~segundo~ (“second,” the following one). To associate ideas, then, is to let one “follow” another — companionship written into cognition itself.
en.aspirar:
From Latin ~aspīrāre~ (also ~adspīrāre~, “to breathe upon, breathe toward”), from ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) plus ~spīrāre~ (“to breathe”). Cognate with Italian ~aspirare~ and French ~aspirer~, and — through ~spīrāre~ — with English ~aspire~, ~respire~, and ~conspire~; the noun ~spīritus~ (“breath, spirit”) came down to Spanish as ~espíritu~.

The origin of ~spīrāre~ is uncertain: it has no secure cognates, and de Vaan judges it probably onomatopoeic, an imitation of the very sound of breathing; an older proposal tied it to Proto-Indo-European *~(s)peys-~ (“to blow”). ~Aspirar~ began as “to breathe toward” and, by way of the breath one draws in longing, took on the figurative “to aspire, yearn for.” Its concrete senses stayed close to the lungs — “to inhale,” “to aspirate” a consonant, and colloquially “to vacuum” (hence ~aspiradora~). The breathing family is large: ~respirar~, ~espirar~, ~suspirar~, ~inspirar~, ~conspirar~, ~expirar~, and ~aspiración~ all trace back to that single Latin breath.
en.asumir:
From Latin ~assūmere~ (“to take up, adopt, claim”), formed from ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and ~sūmere~ (“to take up”), itself ~sub-~ (“up from below”) plus ~emere~ (“to take, buy”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₁em-~ (“to take, distribute”). It is cognate with French ~assumer~, Italian ~assumere~, and Portuguese ~assumir~, and with the Latin-derived English ~assume~; through ~emere~ it is also kin to English ~example~ and ~exempt~.

In Latin ~emere~ first meant “to take” and only later specialized to “to buy” — a shift from grasping a thing to grasping it by purchase. Its compound ~sūmere~ kept the “take up” sense, and ~asumir~ today means to take something on: a duty, a role, a cost. The ~sūmere~ line gave Spanish ~consumir~, ~presumir~, and ~resumir~, while the older ~emere~ surfaces in ~ejemplo~ (from ~exemplum~, “a sample taken out”), ~redimir~, and ~eximir~. What unites them all is the plain, physical act of taking.
en.atacar:
From Italian ~attaccare~ (“to attach, to join,” and in ~attaccare battaglia~, “to join battle”), taken into Spanish in the sixteenth century as a military term. The Italian verb is generally linked to a Germanic word for a stake or post — Gothic *~stakka~, also the source of Spanish ~estaca~ — the idea being to fasten one thing to another; but the details of that descent are disputed. From the same Italian source come French ~attaquer~ and, as doublets, English ~attach~ and ~attack~.

The journey from a fence post to open warfare runs through the idea of fastening: to ~attaccare~ was to fix things together, and ~attaccare battaglia~ was to “knit” two armies into combat. Spanish borrowed only the martial sense, so ~atacar~ came to mean purely “to assault,” while the older “fasten” meaning stayed abroad in English ~attach~. If the stake origin holds, the native Spanish cousin is ~estaca~, and with it ~destacar~ (originally “to detach a body of troops,” now “to stand out”) and ~estacada~. It is a striking case of one Germanic post branching, through Italian, into fastening, detaching and attacking.
en.atender:
From Latin ~attendere~ (“to stretch toward, direct one’s mind to”), from ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and ~tendere~ (“to stretch”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ten-~ (“to stretch”). Cognate with Italian ~attendere~ and — with a telling shift of sense — French ~attendre~ (“to wait”) and Portuguese ~atender~; through ~tendere~ it is kin to English ~tend~ and ~tension~.

The Romans pictured attention as a physical reaching: to ~atender~ was to stretch the mind toward something. Spanish kept the engaged senses — to heed, to look after, to serve — so that in a shop a clerk ~atiende~ a customer, a false friend for English speakers who expect it to mean simply to be present. The same ~tendere~ left a homely trace: Spanish ~tienda~ (“shop,” earlier “tent”) began as a stretched-out awning of cloth. Related descendants include ~atención~ (“attention”), ~tender~ (“to spread, hang out”), ~extender~ (“to extend”), and ~tenso~ (“tense”).
en.atraer:
From Latin ~attrahere~ (“to draw toward”), a compound of ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and ~trahere~ (“to draw, drag, pull”); Spanish reshaped it on its own inherited ~traer~ (also from ~trahere~). The deeper origin of ~trahere~ is uncertain — De Vaan reconstructs a possibly non-Indo-European root *~trāgʰ-~, perhaps shared with Celtic, and a much-debated link to Proto-Germanic *~draganą~ (source of English ~draw~ and ~drag~). Romance cognates include French ~attraire~, Italian ~attrarre~, and Portuguese ~atrair~, while English ~attract~ comes from the Latin participle ~attractus~.

The metaphor is purely physical: to “draw something toward” you, whether by a magnet or by charm. From ~trahere~ Spanish inherited a large, productive family — ~traer~ (“to bring”), and the prefixed ~atraer~, ~contraer~, ~extraer~, ~distraer~, ~sustraer~, ~retraer~, and ~abstraer~. Alongside these run the learned ~-tract-~ nouns and adjectives: ~tractor~ (“one that pulls”), ~tracción~, ~atractivo~, ~contrato~, and ~retrato~ — a portrait being, quite literally, a face “drawn again.”
en.atrapar:
Either from ~a-~ + ~trapa~ (an old Spanish word for a snare), or taken from French ~attraper~ (“to catch in a trap”), from Old French ~trape~ (“trap”), ultimately from a West Germanic *~trappa~ (“snare”). The Germanic word belongs to a family meaning “to tread, step,” which surfaces in English ~trap~, German ~Treppe~ (“staircase”), and Middle Dutch ~trappe~. Its earliest written trace is the Late Latin ~trappa~ recorded in the Frankish Lex Salica. Cognates include Italian ~trappola~, Portuguese ~trapa~, and French ~trappe~.

The meaning moved from the concrete device — a pit or spring-snare that shuts on an animal — to seizing or catching anything, and then figuratively to “catching” a person in a lie or a promise. The link to treading recalls the hunter's trap triggered underfoot. From the same Germanic stock Spanish keeps ~trampa~ (“trap; cheat”), ~trampear~ (“to swindle”), ~trampolín~ (“springboard”), and ~atrapamoscas~ (“flytrap”).
en.atravesar:
Spanish ~atravesar~ is ~través~ with the prefix ~a-~, and ~través~ comes from Latin ~transversus~ (“turned across, lying crosswise”), the past participle of ~transvertere~, from ~trans~ (“across”) plus ~vertere~ (“to turn”). ~Vertere~ rests on Proto-Indo-European *~wert-~ (“to turn”), which also gave English ~-ward~ and, through Latin, ~verse~ and ~convert~. French built ~traverser~ from the same participle, the twin of English ~traverse~.

The image is bodily: to ~atravesar~ something is to move through it along the “turned-across” line — to cross, span, or pierce it. The stem ~través~ still means “aslant,” and the derivative ~travesía~ names a crossing or voyage. Most striking is ~travieso~: literally “lying crosswise,” it drifted from “wayward, contrary” to the affectionate modern “mischievous, naughty” said of a restless child. From the same ~vertere~ Spanish also draws ~verter~, ~convertir~, ~invertir~, ~verso~, ~universo~ and ~aniversario~.
en.atrever:
By the received account, from Latin ~attribuere~ (“to assign, attribute”) — specifically the reflexive ~attribuere sibi~, “to grant oneself (the power to do something)” — a compound of ~ad-~ (“to”) and ~tribuere~ (“to allot, assign”), from ~tribus~ (“tribe”), whose deeper origin is uncertain (one proposal analyzes it as ~tri-~, “three,” plus a form of “to be”). Cognate — through ~tribuere~ — with English ~tribute~, ~attribute~, ~contribute~ and ~tribe~.

The semantic path is neat: to grant oneself the capacity for a bold act is, in the end, to ~atreverse~ — to dare. The origin is not undisputed, however: struck by the Old Spanish variant ~estreverse~, Cuervo proposed instead a Germanic source, Old High German ~strëben~ (“to strive”), but that account has been rejected in favor of ~attribuere~. Spanish keeps the daring branch in ~atrevimiento~ (“audacity”) and ~atrevido~ (“bold, cheeky”), while the ~tribuere~ root also gave ~atribuir~, ~contribuir~, ~distribuir~, ~tributo~ and ~tribu~.
en.atribuir:
From Latin ~attribuere~ (“to assign, allot”), which is ~ad-~ (“to”) plus ~tribuere~ (“to allot, grant”), literally “to distribute among the tribes”. That verb rests on ~tribus~ (“tribe, a division of the Roman people”), whose own origin is unclear: by one traditional account it is built on ~trēs~ (“three”) — the three original tribes of early Rome — perhaps with an element from Proto-Indo-European *~bʰuH-~ (“to be, grow”), though this is contested, not settled. It is cognate with English ~attribute~ and ~tribute~.

The bookkeeping image never quite left: to ~atribuir~ is to assign a quality, cause, or credit to someone, as a share is allotted to a tribe. The Latin noun surfaces plainly as Spanish ~tribu~, and the verb radiated into a whole administrative vocabulary — ~tributo~ (“tribute, tax”), ~contribuir~, ~distribuir~, and ~retribuir~ (“to pay back, reward”) — each about apportioning something out to its recipients.
en.aumentar:
From Latin ~augmentāre~ (“to increase”), from ~augmentum~ (“growth, increase”), from ~augēre~ (“to increase, enlarge”), from Proto-Italic *~augeō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂ewg-~ (“to grow, increase”). Cognate with Italian ~aumentare~, French ~augmenter~, Portuguese ~aumentar~ and English ~augment~; through the root, with English ~eke~ and — via Germanic — ~wax~ (“to grow”).

The PIE root *~h₂ewg-~ was extraordinarily productive in Latin. Beyond ~aumentar~ it gave ~aumento~ and ~auge~ (“peak, height”); through ~auctor~ (“originator, one who makes grow”) came Spanish ~autor~; through ~augustus~ (“consecrated, majestic”), the month ~agosto~ and the name ~Augusto~; and through ~auxilium~ (“help, reinforcement”), ~auxilio~. Even the diviner’s ~augurio~ may belong to this family. To increase is, at bottom, to make something grow.
en.autorizar:
From Medieval Latin ~auctorizāre~ (“to give authority to”), from Latin ~auctor~ (“originator, promoter, author”), an agent-noun of ~augēre~ (“to increase, to make grow”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂ewg-~ (“to increase”). The growth-root is prolific: cognate with English ~augment~, ~auction~ (Latin ~auctiō~, “an increasing” of bids), and ~august~, and — through Germanic — with the archaic English ~eke~ (“to add to, to increase”).

An ~auctor~ was one who caused a thing to grow — who originated, backed, or vouched for it — so to ~autorizar~ is to lend one's authority to an act and let it stand. At the center of the Spanish family sit ~autor~ (“author”) and ~autoridad~ (“authority”), joined by ~aumentar~ (“to increase”), ~auge~ (“peak, boom,” a high point of growth), and ~augusto~ (“august, majestic”), the imperial epithet of ~Augusto~ (Augustus) that also named a month.
en.avanzar:
Spanish ~avanzar~ (“to advance”) goes back to Vulgar Latin *~abantiāre~, a verb built on Late Latin ~abante~ (“forward, in front”), itself the univerbation of ~ab~ (“from”) and ~ante~ (“before”). The ~ante~ half rests on Proto-Indo-European *~h₂énti~ (“in front, before”). It is cognate with French ~avancer~, Italian ~avanzare~ and Catalan ~avançar~ — and, through Old French, with English ~advance~. That English ~d~ is a historical mistake: scribes wrongly read the ~av-~ as if it held the prefix ~ad-~ and inserted a ~d~ that never belonged there. The war-word English ~vanguard~ (from French ~avant-garde~, “fore-guard”) comes of the same ~abante~.

The etymology is a picture of forward motion: to ~avanzar~ is to move “from the front,” to push the front line onward. In Spanish the verb serves every kind of progress — an army, a project, an argument, a clock all ~avanzan~. It kept, too, a quieter commercial sense of “to advance” money, to pay ahead. Its Spanish family marches in the same direction: ~avance~ (“advance, progress; a film trailer”), ~avanzado~ (“advanced”), ~avanzada~ (“outpost, vanguard”) and ~avanzadilla~ (“advance party”). And the ~ante~ at its heart is everywhere in Spanish — in ~antes~, ~anterior~, ~antaño~ and ~delante~ — the little Indo-European word for “in front” still doing its work.
en.avisar:
From Vulgar Latin *~advīsāre~ (“to advise, notify”), from ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) + the past participle ~vīsum~ of ~vidēre~ (“to see”), from Proto-Indo-European *~weyd-~ (“to see, to know”). It reached Spanish through Old French ~aviser~. Cognate with Italian ~avvisare~ and French ~aviser~, and — through French — with English ~advise~ and ~advice~.

The word grew from a Romance idiom, ~m’est vis~ (“it seems to me,” from Latin ~mihi est vīsum~): an ~aviso~ was first an opinion, a view laid before someone to see, and only then a warning or piece of notice. Spanish ~avisar~ thus means to put something before another’s eyes — to notify, alert, warn. The root *~weyd-~ is one of Indo-European’s most fertile: through Latin ~vidēre~ Spanish holds ~ver~, ~vista~, ~visión~, ~previsión~, and ~improvisar~; through Greek it stands behind ~idea~ and ~historia~; through Germanic, behind English ~wit~ and ~wise~.
en.ayudar:
From Latin ~adiūtāre~ (“to help, assist”), the frequentative of ~adiuvāre~, itself ~ad-~ (“toward”) plus ~iuvāre~ (“to help, please”), a verb of uncertain deeper origin. Old Spanish had ~aiudar~ before settling on ~ayudar~. It is cognate with Italian ~aiutare~, Portuguese ~ajudar~ and French ~aider~, and — borrowed through Old French — with English ~aid~ and the learned ~adjutant~.

The frequentative ~adiūtāre~ conveyed repeated or earnest helping, and it is this intensive form, not plain ~iuvāre~, that the Romance languages inherited. Because ~iuvāre~ has no secure Proto-Indo-European pedigree, prudence forbids attaching it to a root here. Within Latin it kept lively company: it was linked to ~iūcundus~ (“pleasant, agreeable”), the source of English ~jocund~. In Spanish the same stem gives ~ayuda~ (“help, aid”), ~ayudante~ (“assistant”) and the learned ~coadyuvar~ (“to contribute, cooperate”), which preserves the ~-iuv-~ that popular ~ayudar~ wore away.
en.añadir:
Spanish ~añadir~ comes, through Old Spanish ~eñadir~ (also ~añader~), from a Vulgar Latin *~innaddere~ or *~inaddere~ — Latin ~addere~ (“to add, put to”) reinforced with the prefix ~in-~. The doubled ~nn~ of the reconstructed form is what Spanish needed to yield the ~ñ~. ~addere~ is itself ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) plus ~dare~ (“to give”): literally “to give to, put to.” ~dare~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~deh₃-~ (“to give”), one of the most widespread roots there is — source of Latin ~dōnum~ (“gift”) and Spanish ~dar~, Greek ~dídōmi~ (“I give”), and, via Latin, English ~date~, ~donate~, and ~add~ — the last from ~addere~ itself, the very verb that ~añadir~ elaborates.

The quiet lesson of ~añadir~ is redundancy: Latin ~addere~ already meant “to add” (its ~ad-~ = “to”), yet Vulgar Latin piled a second directional prefix, ~in-~, on top — a doubling-up of “to it” that is exactly what adding feels like. The word’s ~ñ~ is a fossil of the assimilated ~in-~ + ~n~ cluster. Spanish also inherited ~addere~ by the learned road as ~aditar~ (“to add, annotate”) and the nouns ~adición~ (“addition,” including the arithmetic operation) and ~aditivo~ (“additive”). From the broader *~deh₃-~ root come ~dar~, ~dado~ (“die; given”), ~dádiva~ (“gift”), ~donar~, ~perdonar~, and ~dosis~ (from Greek ~dósis~, “a giving”).
en.bailar:
By the usual account, from Late Latin ~ballāre~ (“to dance”), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ~βαλλίζειν~ (ballízein, “to dance, jump about”); the Real Academia marks the descent as only probable (~quizá~). Corominas argues the Spanish word is not a direct heir but an adaptation of Old Occitan ~balar~, and he leaves the puzzling ~i~ of ~bailar~ unexplained — possibly a crossing with a homonym ~bailar~ (“to rock, sway”), from Latin ~bāiulāre~. So the deep origin is genuinely disputed. Cognate with Italian ~ballare~, French ~baller~, and Portuguese ~bailar~.

Whatever the exact path, the whole European family of dancing and dance-events flows from ~ballāre~: English ~ball~ (a formal dance) and ~ballet~ both trace to it, and even ~ballad~ began as a song to dance to. Spanish keeps a lively cluster — the noun ~baile~ (“dance”), ~bailarín~ (“dancer”), and ~bailable~ (“danceable”) — so that a modern ~baile~ still, distantly, jumps to a Greek beat.
en.bajar:
From Vulgar Latin *~bassiāre~ (“to lower”), from Late Latin ~bassus~ (“low, short, thick”). Old Spanish had ~baxar~, later reshaped to ~bajar~ as its old sh-sound hardened into the jota. Cognate with French ~baisser~ and Italian ~abbassare~; the same parent adjective surfaces in English ~base~ (“low, mean”) and the musical ~bass~ (“low in pitch”).

The engaging part is the disputed source of ~bassus~ itself. Classical Latin used the word only rarely, mainly as a personal name, and its origin is genuinely uncertain; the sources hedge. By competing accounts it was borrowed from Oscan, or from a Celtic word, or connected to Greek ~bathýs~ (“deep”) — none settled, so the adjective is best labeled “of uncertain origin.” Whatever its root, ~bassus~ flourished in Spanish, yielding ~bajo~ (“low; under”), ~bajada~ (“descent”), ~rebajar~ (“to lower, reduce”), ~abajo~ (“below”), and ~bajón~ (“slump”).
en.basar:
From the noun ~base~ (“base, foundation”) plus the verbal ending ~-ar~; ~basar~ is a denominal verb, coined rather than inherited. ~base~ comes from Latin ~basis~ (“base, pedestal”), borrowed from Ancient Greek ~βάσις~ (“a step, a stepping, base”), a noun built on the verb ~βαίνω~ (“to go, to step”). That verb descends from Proto-Indo-European *~gʷem-~ (“to go, come”) — the same root that, on the Germanic side, produced English ~come~. Romance preserved the Latin noun broadly: Italian ~base~, French ~base~, Portuguese ~base~.

Because ~basar~ was formed on the noun, its story is really the story of ~base~, which moved from the concrete “pedestal, that on which a thing stands” to the abstract “foundation, grounds”; the reflexive ~basarse~ means “to rest on, be grounded in.” A pleasant surprise: the modest Greek ~βαίνω~ (“to step”) also hides inside ~diabetes~ (Greek for “a passing through”) and ~acróbata~ (one who “walks” on the heights). Spanish relatives of ~base~ include ~básico~, ~basamento~, and the chemistry term ~base~.
en.bastar:
From Old Spanish ~bastar~, from Vulgar Latin *~bastāre~ (“to bear, carry a weight”), generally traced to Greek ~βαστάζειν~ (~bastázein~, “to lift, carry, bear a load”). It is cognate with Italian ~bastare~, Portuguese ~bastar~, and Catalan ~bastar~, all sharing the sense “to be enough.”

Medieval Spanish kept meanings much closer to the Greek: ~bastar~ could mean to endure, to hold out, to reach as far as, to last, or to bear a weight. From “to be able to sustain something” it slid to “to be sufficient,” the sense that prevailed — what suffices is what can carry the load. The same root feeds ~bastante~ (“enough, quite”), the exasperated interjection ¡~basta~! (“enough!”), and the family ~abasto~ and ~abastecer~ (“to supply”), from the idea of providing enough. So the modern accountant's “that will suffice” still carries, faintly, the Greek porter's burden.
en.beber:
From Latin ~bibere~ (“to drink”), from Proto-Italic *~pibō~ — a reduplicated present — from Proto-Indo-European *~píph₃eti~, from the root *~peh₃-~ (“to drink”). Cognate with Italian ~bere~, Portuguese ~beber~ and French ~boire~, and — through the same root — with Sanskrit ~píbati~ and the English Latinisms ~potable~ and ~potion~.

The root's initial ~p~ became ~b~ in Latin, most likely under the pull of the second ~b~ — an assimilation that leaves ~bibere~ looking nothing like its ~p~-initial cousins. Spanish carried it through Old Spanish ~bever~ to modern ~beber~. From the same verb come ~bebida~ (“drink”), ~bebedor~ (“drinker”) and ~biberón~ (“baby bottle,” by way of French), while the past participle ~bibĭtus~ (“having drunk”) yielded the adjective ~beodo~ (“drunk, tipsy”).
en.beneficiar:
~beneficiar~ is built on ~beneficio~ (“benefit”), from Latin ~beneficium~ (“a kindness, favor, service”), a compound of ~bene~ (“well”) and ~-ficium~, from ~facere~ (“to do, make”) — literally “a well-doing.” The adverb ~bene~ belongs to ~bonus~ (“good”), from Old Latin ~duenos~, of debated further origin; ~facere~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to put, do”), the root of English ~do~ and German ~tun~. Romance kept the verb: French ~bénéficier~, Italian ~beneficiare~, Portuguese ~beneficiar~.

In Latin a ~beneficium~ ranged from a personal good turn to an official grant of land or office — the feudal “benefice” that let a churchman live off an endowment. Spanish ~beneficiar~ thus spans “to benefit, do good to” and the technical “to work, process” (to ~beneficiar~ ore or a hide is to render it useful). The reflexive ~beneficiarse~ is “to profit from.” Kin include ~benéfico~, ~beneficencia~, ~benefactor~, and — from ~bene~ alone — ~bendecir~ and ~benévolo~.
en.bloquear:
One of the newer verbs in this set. Spanish ~bloquear~ comes from French ~bloquer~, derived from ~bloc~ (“a block, solid mass”), which French borrowed from Middle Dutch ~bloc~ (“trunk of a tree, log”), of Germanic origin (compare Frankish *~blok~), from Proto-Germanic *~blukką~ (“block, log”). Beyond that the trail grows faint: many trace it to Proto-Indo-European *~bʰl̥ǵ-~ (“thick plank, beam”), though the deep root is uncertain. It is cognate with English ~block~, German ~Block~ and Dutch ~blok~.

The image behind the word is concrete: a felled log or heavy block set down to obstruct a passage. From “to close off with blocks” the sense fanned out to block, blockade, jam, and — in modern finance and computing — to freeze an account or lock a screen. Spanish took it comparatively late, largely through French military and naval usage, alongside the noun ~bloqueo~ (“blockade”) and ~bloque~ (“block,” including a political ~bloque~ of nations). The reversible ~desbloquear~ (“to unblock, unlock”) is a purely modern coinage. It is a small Germanic word that grew up to run the world's networks.
en.borrar:
From ~borra~ (“coarse wool, flock”) plus the verbal ending; ~borra~ itself descends from Late Latin ~burra~ (“shaggy wool of little value”), a word of uncertain further origin. The shift from Latin ~u~ to Spanish ~o~ is regular (compare ~bucca~ → ~boca~). Cognate with Italian ~borra~ and French ~bourre~ (“stuffing, flock”); from that French word, through the coarse cloth ~burel~ that once covered writing tables, English drew ~bureau~ and hence ~bureaucracy~.

Why a word for cheap wool came to mean “erase” is charmingly literal, though not beyond doubt: the favored account is that a wad of ~borra~ was the cloth used to wipe chalk from a slate, so to ~borrar~ was to rub something out with wool; a rival account points instead to the sediment or dregs of ink. Either way, the modern family is tidy — ~borrador~ means both “eraser” and “rough draft,” ~borrón~ is a blot or crossing-out, and ~borroso~ means “blurred, smudged.”
en.brindar:
Unlike its Latinate neighbors, ~brindar~ is a Germanic import. It derives from the noun ~brindis~ (“a toast”), which Spanish borrowed in the sixteenth century from the German toasting phrase ~bring dir’s~ — a running-together of ~(ich) bring dir’s~, “I bring it to you.” The verb behind it is German ~bringen~ (“to bring”), cognate with English ~bring~, both from Proto-Germanic *~bringaną~. The little words matter too: ~dir~ is “to you” (dative, cognate with English ~thee~) and the clitic ~’s~ is ~es~ (“it”). Italian ~brindare~ and Portuguese ~brindar~ borrowed the same festive word from Spanish.

The story behind the word is vivid and, unusually, well documented: when the Landsknechte — German mercenaries in the service of Charles V — sacked Rome in 1527, they are said to have raised their cups crying ~bring dir’s~, offering the drink to a companion. Spanish soldiers carried the custom and the cry home, and by the early 1600s ~brindar~ and ~brindis~ were common enough that Covarrubias recorded them in his 1611 Tesoro de la lengua castellana. The meaning then broadened gracefully: from “to drink someone’s health” to “to offer, to provide” in general — today one can ~brindar~ apoyo (“offer support”) or ~brindar~ una oportunidad (“provide an opportunity”), a generosity still audible in that original “I bring it to you.”
en.buscar:
Inherited from Old Spanish ~buscar~, but of genuinely uncertain origin — Corominas and the DLE alike label it « de origen incierto ». Several hypotheses compete, none settled. By one account it is tied to ~bosque~ (“forest”), the earliest sense being to beat the woods for game; by another it descends from a Celtic *~boudi~ (“gain, victory”), compared with Old Irish ~búaid~ and Welsh ~budd~. It shares its mystery with cognate Portuguese ~buscar~ and Italian ~buscare~ (“to scrounge, wangle”).

Whatever its source, ~buscar~ had by the medieval period already generalized to “to look for, seek,” and it remains one of the plainest, most frequent verbs in the language. The hunting-in-the-woods story is memorable but rests on the unproven ~bosque~ link, so it is best told as one guess among several rather than as fact. The verb is productive in its own right: it yields ~búsqueda~ and ~busca~ (“search”), ~buscador~ (“search engine; seeker”), ~rebuscar~ (“to search thoroughly”), and the old noun ~buscón~ (“petty crook”), immortalized in Quevedo's picaresque novel ~El Buscón~.
en.caber:
From Old Spanish ~caber~, from Latin ~capere~ (“to take, seize, hold, contain”), from Proto-Italic *~kapiō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~kap-~ (“to grasp, seize”). Cognate with Portuguese ~caber~ and — through the same Latin verb — with the borrowings ~capaz~ and ~captura~; English has ~capture~ and ~capable~ from ~capere~, and, from the same PIE root, the native ~heave~.

The meaning shifted from grasping to spatial room: Latin ~capere~ meant “to take” or “to hold, contain,” and Spanish narrowed the “contain” side to “to fit, have room for” — a box ~cabe~ on the shelf, five people ~caben~ in the car. The irregular present ~quepo~ (“I fit”) preserves Latin ~capiō~ under metathesis, and the preterite ~cupe~ reflects a Vulgar Latin perfect *~capuī~. From ~capere~ Spanish also drew ~capaz~, ~cabida~ (“capacity”), ~caudal~, and the shared-root ~recibir~ and ~concebir~.
en.caer:
From Latin ~cadere~ (“to fall”), from Proto-Italic *~kadō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~ḱad-~ (“to fall”). The intervocalic ~-d-~ dropped away, giving Old Spanish ~caer~. Cognate with Italian ~cadere~, Portuguese ~cair~ and the now-archaic French ~choir~.

Latin’s ~cāsus~ (“a falling”), the past participle of ~cadere~, became a metaphor for whatever “befalls,” hence Spanish ~caso~ (“case, chance”) and ~casualidad~ (“coincidence”), and grammatical “case.” The setting sun falls: ~ocaso~ (“sunset, decline”) and ~occidente~ (“the West”) come from ~occidere~ (“to fall down, to set”). English borrowed the same verb widely — ~cadence~, ~accident~, ~occasion~, ~decay~ and ~cascade~. Other Spanish descendants: ~caída~, ~decaer~, ~recaer~ and ~cadencia~.
en.calcular:
From Latin ~calculāre~ (“to compute, reckon”), from ~calculus~ (“a pebble”), the diminutive of ~calx~ (genitive ~calcis~, “limestone, small stone”), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ~khálix~ (“small pebble, gravel”). The ultimate origin is unknown — Beekes finds no convincing etymology for the Greek word. Cognate with Italian ~calcolare~, French ~calculer~ and Portuguese ~calcular~.

The homely detail is that a ~calculus~ was a counting-pebble: Romans “placed pebbles” (~ponere calculōs~) on a reckoning board to add and subtract, so to ~calcular~ is, at root, to push stones around. From ~calx~ English also drew ~chalk~ and ~calcium~, and the medical ~calculus~ is still a “little stone” in the body. Spanish keeps ~cálculo~, ~calculadora~ and ~recalcular~.
en.calificar:
~calificar~ comes from Medieval Latin ~quālificāre~ (“to endow with a quality”), a compound of Latin ~quālis~ (“of what kind”) and ~facere~ (“to make, do”) — literally “to make of a certain kind.” ~quālis~ traces to the Proto-Indo-European interrogative-relative stem *~kʷo-~ (source also of ~qué~ and ~cuál~), while ~facere~ goes back to *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to put, place, do”), the root behind English ~do~ and ~deed~ and German ~tun~. The same coinage spread as Italian ~qualificare~, French ~qualifier~, and English ~qualify~.

The scholastic Latin verb meant “to attribute a quality to,” a technical sense still alive in “to qualify” a statement with reservations. Spanish specialized it toward judgment and assessment: a teacher ~califica~ (“grades”) an exam and gives it a ~calificación~ (“grade, rating”). The neutral “assign a quality” lingers when we ~calificar~ a remark as rude or brilliant. Kin from the ~facere~ half include ~fácil~, ~hacer~, ~facción~, and countless ~-ificar~ verbs; from the ~quālis~ half come ~cualidad~ and ~cualitativo~.
en.cambiar:
From Late Latin ~cambiāre~ (“to exchange, barter”), a term of Gaulish (Celtic) origin, traced to a Gaulish ~cambion~ and a Celtic *~kambos~ (“curved, crooked”), reflecting Proto-Indo-European *~(s)kamb-~ (“to bend, curve”). It is cognate with Italian ~cambiare~, Portuguese ~cambiar~ and French ~changer~, and — through Old French — with English ~change~.

The verb began as commercial jargon: ~cambiāre~ first surfaces in Apuleius, and the noun ~cambium~ (“exchange”) appears only later, in medieval Latin banking. The tie to the Celtic root is engaging but wants care: by one account the sense moved from the physical “to bend, turn” of *~kambos~ to the abstract “to give one thing and turn it into another,” yet this semantic bridge is a proposal, not a documented step. What is secure is the family the verb seeded in Spanish: ~cambio~ (“change, small coin”), ~intercambiar~, ~recambio~ (“spare part”) and, borrowed back through Catalan and Occitan, ~canje~ (“exchange, swap”).
en.caminar:
From ~camino~ (“road, path”) plus the verbal suffix ~-ar~; ~camino~ descends through Old Spanish from Vulgar Latin ~camminus~, a word Latin borrowed from Gaulish (Celtic), ultimately from Proto-Celtic *~kanxsman-~ (“step, pace”), an action-noun built on *~kengeti~ (“to step”). Being Celtic rather than Latin, it is cognate not with a Latin verb but with Welsh ~cam~ (“step”). The Romance family kept it everywhere: French ~chemin~ and ~cheminer~, Italian ~cammino~ and ~camminare~, Portuguese ~caminho~ and ~caminhar~.

The Celtic loan spread precisely because road-building and road-travel were where Gaulish vocabulary left its deepest mark on Latin; ~camminus~ eventually displaced native Latin words for “road” across much of the West. The verb ~caminar~ simply means “to walk” or “to travel a road,” and Spanish elaborated the family richly: ~caminante~ (“traveler, wayfarer”), ~caminata~ (“a long walk, hike”), ~encaminar~ (“to set on the right path, direct”), and the pilgrim’s ~Camino~ de Santiago. The English ~camino~, now used for that pilgrimage route, is a direct borrowing of the Spanish noun.
en.cancelar:
From Latin ~cancellāre~ (“to cross out, cancel”), literally “to mark with a lattice of crossing lines,” from ~cancellī~ (“a lattice, grating, crossbars”). ~cancellī~ is a diminutive form related to ~cancer~ / ~carcer~ (“an enclosure, lattice, prison”). Cognate with English ~cancel~, and — surprisingly — with ~chancel~ and ~chancellor~, discussed below.

A Roman clerk voided a document by drawing a grid of crossing lines over it — a little lattice, ~cancellī~ — so ~cancellāre~ meant “to lattice through,” i.e. to strike out. The same word for a lattice screen took a different route: the ~cancellī~ that railed off part of a church gave English ~chancel~ (the screened-off area near the altar), and the official who stood at that lattice barrier became the ~cancellārius~ — English ~chancellor~ and Spanish ~canciller~. From the lattice sense Spanish also keeps ~cancel~ (“a screen, storm door”) and ~cancela~ (“a wrought-iron gate”), while the “strike out” sense lives on in ~cancelación~ (“cancellation”).
en.cansar:
By Corominas’s account, Spanish ~cansar~ came from Latin ~campsāre~ (“to round a headland, tack, turn aside from a course”), a nautical term the Romans had taken from Greek ~κάμπτειν~ (“to bend”), aorist ~κάμψαι~. The Latin verb is scantily attested, which is why the derivation, though standard, is drawn from the Greek. Portuguese ~cansar~ is the direct cognate.

The path of meaning is the memorable part: from “to double a cape, change course” the verb slid to “to abandon the course one is on,” then to “to give up an effort,” and at last to “to grow weary” — so a word for tiredness set out as a sailor rounding a headland. The reflexive ~cansarse~ is “to tire oneself.” Spanish built more on the stem: ~cansancio~ (“weariness”), ~cansado~ (“tired”) and, with the reversing prefix ~des-~, ~descansar~ — literally “to un-tire,” that is, “to rest.”
en.cantar:
From Latin ~cantāre~ (“to sing”), the frequentative of ~canere~ (“to sing”), from Proto-Indo-European *~keh₂n-~ (“to sing”). It passed unchanged in shape to Portuguese ~cantar~ and Italian ~cantare~, and became French ~chanter~; through the same root it is cognate with English ~chant~ and ~accent~, and even with English ~hen~ (originally “the singing bird”) and German ~Hahn~ (“rooster”).

~Cantāre~ began as an intensive of ~canere~ — not just to sing but to sing repeatedly — and it so thoroughly displaced the plain verb that every Romance language sings with the frequentative. The root *~keh₂n-~ radiated widely in Spanish: ~canto~, ~cántico~, ~cantante~, ~encantar~ (“to enchant,” literally to sing a spell over someone) and, borrowed back from French, ~chantaje~ (“blackmail”).
en.capacitar:
A learned formation from ~capaz~ (“capable”) plus the verb-forming ~-itar~. ~capaz~ descends from Latin ~capāx~ (“able to hold much, roomy”), from ~capere~ (“to take, hold, grasp”), from Proto-Indo-European *~keh₂p-~ (“to grasp, seize”). Cognate through that root with English ~heave~ (Old English ~hebban~) and, through Latin ~capere~, with English ~capable~ and ~capacity~.

~capāx~ meant literally “holding a lot” — a roomy vessel — so ~capaz~ first described capacity, then a person “able to hold” a task, i.e. competent. ~capacitar~, built on that, means to make someone capable: to train, qualify, or empower. Latin ~capere~ was extraordinarily fertile in Spanish, which changed its vowel and kept the plain verb as ~caber~ (“to fit”); the same root yields ~captar~, ~capturar~, ~recibir~ (from ~recipere~), ~concebir~ (from ~concipere~), and ~ocupar~. So ~capacitar~ and ~caber~ — “to enable” and “to fit” — are cousins under one Latin verb of holding.
en.captar:
From Latin ~captāre~ (“to try to seize, catch at”), a frequentative of ~capere~ (“to take, seize”), formed with the iterative suffix ~-tāre~. The verb goes back to Proto-Italic *~kapiō~ and to the Proto-Indo-European root *~kap-~ (“to grasp, seize”). Cognate with Italian ~captare~ and French ~capter~, and — through the same root — with English ~have~ and ~heave~ and German ~haben~.

Spanish inherited ~captāre~ twice over. Its popular, orally worn-down form became Old Spanish ~catar~ (“to look at, examine”), which survives in ~acatar~ (“to obey”) and in ~catar~ (“to taste”); ~captar~ is the later, learned re-borrowing that preserved the Latin cluster. Its senses radiate out from “seizing”: to capture a signal or an image, to grasp an idea, to win over an audience, even to collect rainwater. From the wider ~capere~ family Spanish also drew ~captura~, ~cautivo~, ~capaz~, ~caber~ (“to fit”), and ~recibir~ (“to receive”).
en.capturar:
From Latin ~captūra~ (“a catching, seizure”), a noun from ~captus~, the past participle of ~capere~ (“to take, seize”), from Proto-Indo-European *~keh₂p-~ (“to grasp, seize”). Cognate with Italian ~catturare~ and French ~capturer~, and — through the same root — with English ~capture~, ~captive~, and even ~have~ and German ~haben~, which descend from the same grasping root through Germanic.

Latin ~captūra~ named the act of catching game or fish; Spanish kept that concrete, hunterly edge, and ~capturar~ still suggests seizing a live, resisting thing — a fugitive, an animal, a piece on a chessboard. It is a learned re-formation: the same ~capere~ had already come down through popular speech, worn smooth, as ~caber~ (“to fit”) and, via the frequentative ~captāre~, as ~catar~ (“to taste, examine”) and ~cazar~ (“to hunt”). The prolific root *~keh₂p-~ also gave Spanish ~cautivo~, ~capaz~, ~caza~, ~recibir~, ~concebir~, and ~aceptar~.
en.caracterizar:
Spanish ~caracterizar~ is formed from ~carácter~ plus the verb-forming suffix ~-izar~. ~carácter~ comes from Latin ~character~, a borrowing from Ancient Greek ~kharaktḗr~ (“an engraving tool; the mark it stamps; a distinctive imprint”), from the verb ~kharássō~ (“to scratch, to engrave, to sharpen”). The Greek noun first named the stamp on a coin or the brand cut into a surface, then the distinctive mark it left, and finally a person's stamped-in nature. Spanish ~caracterizar~ is a learned formation. It is cognate with Italian ~caratterizzare~, French ~caractériser~, Portuguese ~caracterizar~, and English ~characterize~.

The metaphor buried in ~caracterizar~ is the engraver's: to characterize something is, at root, to press a distinguishing mark into it, to say what stamp it bears. Spanish uses it in two live senses — to describe the defining traits of a thing (“what characterizes this region”) and, in the theatre, to make oneself up and dress for a role, to ~caracterizar~ a character on stage. The Greek ~kharássō~ (“to engrave”) sits behind the whole family: Spanish ~carácter~, ~característica~, ~caracterización~, and the typographic sense of ~carácter~ as a written sign — the “characters” of an alphabet, still literally little marks stamped onto a page.
en.carecer:
~Carecer~ comes from Latin ~carēscere~, an inchoative in ~-scere~ built on ~carēre~ (“to lack, be without”). The deeper origin is disputed: one proposal derives ~carēre~ from Proto-Italic *~kazēō~ and a Proto-Indo-European root *~ḱes-~ (“to cut,” hence “to be cut off from”), but de Vaan rejects it as semantically strained, and the ultimate root remains uncertain. It is cognate with Portuguese ~carecer~ and French ~carence~, and it survives in English ~caret~.

The inchoative ~-sc-~ gave ~carēre~ a “coming-to” nuance: ~carecer~ is not just to lack but to fall into lacking. The most charming descendant is the proofreader’s mark ~caret~ (^), which is simply Latin ~caret~, “it is lacking” — the third-person present of the same verb, flagging a spot where a word has been left out. Spanish keeps the plainer relatives ~carente~ (“lacking”) and ~carencia~ (“shortage, deficiency”). De Vaan even wonders whether ~caries~ (“decay”) belongs here too, though that link, like the root, is far from settled.
en.cargar:
From Vulgar Latin *~carricāre~ (“to load a wagon”), a verb built on Latin ~carrus~ (“wheeled vehicle, wagon”). ~carrus~ was itself borrowed from Gaulish ~carros~, a Celtic word, and traces to the Proto-Indo-European root *~ḱers-~ (“to run”), the same root behind Latin ~currere~ (“to run”). In its passage to Spanish the double consonant softened, the ~-i-~ dropped, and the second ~c~ voiced to ~g~, giving ~cargar~, already attested in the twelfth-century Poem of the Cid. It is cognate with Italian ~caricare~, French ~charger~, Portuguese ~carregar~, and English ~charge~ and ~cargo~.

The image at the root is concrete: to pile a load onto a ~carrus~, a Gaulish cart — so ~cargar~ began as a teamster's word for loading a wagon and then generalized to loading of every kind: a ship, a rifle, a battery, a debt, an emotional weight. English shows how far the ~carrus~ family traveled — “car,” “carriage,” “career,” “cargo,” and “charge” in its electrical sense all descend from the same Celtic-Latin cart. In Spanish the family is large: ~carga~, ~carro~, ~cargo~, ~cargamento~, ~descargar~, ~encargar~, ~acarrear~, and ~ferrocarril~.
en.casar:
Spanish did not inherit its everyday verb for marrying from Latin's marriage vocabulary; it built one at home. ~casar~ comes from the noun ~casa~ (“house”) plus the verb-forming suffix ~-ar~ — literally “to set up house” or “to become a member of the household.” The noun descends from Latin ~casa~ (“hut, cottage, cabin”), a humble word of uncertain further origin. The same household-based verb arose across Ibero-Romance: Portuguese ~casar~ and Catalan ~casar~ likewise mean “to marry.”

Where Latin framed marriage with ~mātrimōnium~ and stately legal phrases, Iberian Romance reframed it as founding a house — a domestic fact as much as a rite. That image survives in the reflexive ~casarse~ (“to get married”) and in ~casamiento~ (“wedding”), and echoes in ~casero~ (“homely; landlord”) and the diminutive ~casilla~ (“box on a form, cubbyhole”). Beware a look-alike: the legal ~casar~ (“to quash a judgment”) is a wholly separate verb, from Latin ~cassāre~ (“to annul”), from ~cassus~ (“empty, void”); the two merely fell together in spelling. From the same ~casa~ also come ~caserío~ (“hamlet”) and, borrowed worldwide, ~casino~.
en.causar:
From Latin ~causāre~ (“to cause, to give as a reason”), a verb built on the noun ~causa~ (“cause, reason, legal case”). It is cognate with Italian ~causare~, French ~causer~ and Portuguese ~causar~, and with English ~cause~, taken through Old French. The ancestry of ~causa~ beyond Latin is genuinely uncertain: it goes back to Old Latin ~caussa~, but no secure Proto-Indo-European source is agreed, and some scholars have proposed a non-Indo-European — possibly Etruscan — origin.

In Roman usage ~causa~ leaned heavily toward the courtroom — a “case, suit, legal matter” — and Spanish still keeps that legal sense alongside the ordinary one, so a ~causa~ can be either a cause or a criminal case. The noun's most startling descendant, though, is utterly ordinary: in Vulgar Latin ~causa~ (“matter, affair”) weakened all the way to “thing,” giving Spanish ~cosa~, French ~chose~ and Italian ~cosa~. From the same Latin stem come ~acusar~, ~excusar~, ~recusar~ and ~causante~.
en.ceder:
From Latin ~cēdere~ (“to go, withdraw, give way”), traced to Proto-Italic *~kesd-o-~ (“to go away”) and the Proto-Indo-European root *~ked-~ (“to go, yield”). Spanish ~ceder~ is cognate with Italian ~cedere~ and French ~céder~, and — through the same verb — with English ~cede~; its frequentative ~cessāre~ (“to hold back, leave off”) gave both Spanish ~cesar~ and English ~cease~.

The core sense “to go, move off” narrowed to “to give up one’s place, yield” — what one does by stepping back. Latin loved compounding ~cēdere~ with prefixes, and Spanish inherited the whole set: ~conceder~, ~acceder~, ~preceder~, ~suceder~ (“to follow; to happen”), ~exceder~, ~proceder~ and ~retroceder~. From the past participle ~cessus~ came a matching crowd of nouns — ~cesión~, ~proceso~, ~acceso~, ~exceso~ — and ~antecessor~ (“one who goes before”), which through French reached English as ~ancestor~.
en.celebrar:
From Latin ~celebrāre~ (“to frequent, throng, honor, solemnize”), from ~celeber~ (“much-frequented, crowded, populous; famous”). Cognate with Italian ~celebrare~, French ~célébrer~, Portuguese ~celebrar~ and English ~celebrate~. The deeper origin of ~celeber~ is uncertain; it has been linked to ~celer~ (“swift”), but that connection is unproven and the sources leave the root undetermined, so it is best treated as disputed.

The core image is a crowd: a ~celeber~ place was one thronged with people, and ~celebrāre~ first meant “to fill, to frequent in numbers,” then “to honor with a gathering,” and finally “to solemnize.” A festival is still, etymologically, a well-attended event. The same family gave Spanish ~célebre~ (“famous”), ~celebridad~ and ~celebración~. The oft-repeated claim that ~celeber~ comes from ~celer~ “swift” is appealing but not established — by most accounts the origin remains unknown.
en.centrar:
From Spanish ~centro~ (“center”), from Latin ~centrum~ (“center of a circle; the fixed point of a compass”), itself a borrowing of Ancient Greek ~κέντρον~ (~kéntron~, “sharp point, goad, the stationary leg of a compass”), from the verb ~κεντέω~ (~kentéō~, “to prick, goad”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ḱent-~ (“to prick”). Cognate with Italian ~centrare~, French ~centrer~ and Portuguese ~centrar~; English ~center~ descends from the same Greek word.

The Greek noun first named the sharp point of a goad and then the fixed pivot around which a compass sweeps a circle — the geometric sense Latin took over. From that idea of a central point Spanish built the verb ~centrar~, “to place at the center,” whose senses branched into balancing, aligning and, reflexively, focusing: ~centrarse en~ means “to concentrate on.” The same root seeded a broad family in Spanish, among them ~centro~, ~céntrico~, ~concentrar~, ~excéntrico~ and ~centímetro~.
en.cerrar:
Spanish ~cerrar~ comes from Late Latin ~serāre~ (“to bolt, lock, close”), a verb derived from the noun ~sera~ (“a bolt, bar, or lock for a door”). The classical form ~serāre~ appears already in Varro and Tibullus (~serāre forēs~, “to bolt the doors”). Two changes reshaped it in the mouths of speakers. First, the ~-r-~ doubled to ~-rr-~ through confusion with ~serra~ (“saw”) and ~serrāre~ (“to saw”) — an entirely different word — so a Vulgar Latin *~serrāre~ arose, still living as Italian ~serrare~, French ~serrer~ (“to tighten, squeeze”), and Portuguese ~cerrar~. English ~serried~ (as in “serried ranks”) is borrowed from the French. Second, the initial ~s-~ became ~c-~ in Castilian — a shift Corominas attributes to the pull of the near-synonym ~cercar~ (“to enclose”).

So the word’s history hides a small comedy of errors: a verb for locking a door got tangled with the unrelated verb for sawing wood, borrowing its double ~r~, and then swapped its opening consonant under the influence of a synonym. The s-to-c shift is Corominas’s proposal, not a certainty, and is best held as the favored account rather than settled fact. Meaning stayed stable — to shut, close, seal — and Spanish grew a rich brood: ~cerradura~ (“lock”), ~cerrojo~ (“bolt”), ~cierre~ (“closure, zipper”), ~encerrar~ (“to lock up, enclose”), ~cerrado~ (“closed; dense; unintelligible”), and ~cerca~ (“fence,” and the adverb “near”). Beware the false friend: Spanish ~cerrar~ (“to close”) and ~serrar~ (“to saw,” from that same ~serra~) are separate verbs that merely sound alike.
en.certificar:
From Late Latin ~certificāre~ (“to make certain, attest”), a compound of Latin ~certus~ (“sure, settled”) and the combining form ~-ficāre~, from ~facere~ (“to make, do”). ~certus~ is the past participle of ~cernere~ (“to sift, separate, distinguish, decide”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~krey-~ (“to sift, discriminate”). It is cognate with French ~certifier~, Italian ~certificare~, and English ~certify~ and ~certain~.

The underlying image is agricultural: to be ~certus~ is to have been “sifted” — passed through a sieve until the matter is settled, just as grain is separated from chaff. The same root surfaces in the Greek cognate ~κρίνω~ (~krínō~, “to separate, judge”), which gave English ~crisis~ and ~critic~, and in Latin ~cribrum~ (“sieve”) and ~crīmen~ (“verdict, charge”). Spanish keeps a wide family from ~cernere~: ~cierto~ (“certain”), ~certeza~ and ~certidumbre~ (“certainty”), ~discernir~ (“to discern”), ~cerner~ (“to sift”), and — through ~crīmen~ — ~crimen~. To ~certificar~ is thus, at root, to sift a matter until it is sure.
en.cesar:
From Latin ~cessāre~ (“to hold back, leave off, be idle”), a frequentative of ~cēdere~ (“to go, withdraw, yield”), whose past participle ~cessus~ furnished the frequentative stem. The root is Proto-Indo-European *~ked-~ (“to go, yield”). Spanish ~cesar~ is cognate with French ~cesser~ and — by way of Old French — English ~cease~; and, through ~cēdere~ directly, with English ~cede~ and ~cession~.

A frequentative names a repeated or drawn-out action, so ~cessāre~ was “to keep withdrawing, go slack,” which slid easily into “to stop, cease.” Spanish inherited a whole family from ~cēdere~: ~ceder~, ~conceder~, ~exceder~, ~proceder~, ~suceder~ and ~acceder~, plus the nouns ~suceso~ and ~proceso~. A tempting false friend to disarm: the name ~César~ (Caesar) is unrelated. Its origin is genuinely uncertain, and the old story linking it to ~caedere~ (“to cut,” from a supposed birth “cut” from the womb) is a folk etymology the sources treat with doubt. When something ceases, it yields and steps aside — no emperor required.
en.circular:
From Latin ~circulāre~ (“to form or move in a circle”), from ~circulus~ (“little ring, circle”), the diminutive of ~circus~ (“ring, circle, circular arena”). ~Circus~ was borrowed from Ancient Greek ~kírkos~ (“ring,” and also the name of a circling hawk), and both go back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~(s)ker-~ (“to turn, bend”) — the same root that, through its Germanic branch, produced English ~ring~. Latin ~circus~ also lives on directly as English ~circus~ and ~circle~.

To ~circulāre~ was to go round in a ring, and the verb kept that turning motion: Spanish ~circular~ means “to circulate, move around” — of blood, of money, of traffic, of rumours — and, as an adjective, simply “circular, round.” When William Harvey described the blood’s ~circulación~ around the body in 1628, he was drawing on exactly this image of a closed ring. The diminutive lineage is rich in Spanish: ~círculo~ (“circle”), ~circo~ (“circus”), ~circuito~ (“circuit”), and — worn down through Vulgar Latin — ~cercar~ (“to encircle, fence in”) and even ~cerca~ (“near,” from Latin ~circā~, “around”).
en.citar:
From Latin ~citāre~ (“to summon, call forth, set in motion”), a frequentative of ~ciēre~ (“to move, rouse, stir”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ḱey-~ (“to set in motion”). Cognate with French ~citer~, Italian ~citare~, and — as learned borrowings — English ~cite~ and ~excite~.

The frequentative ~citāre~ meant to summon repeatedly or insistently, and that legal-sounding “call before a court” underlies the modern “quote an authority.” It also explains a happy Spanish ambiguity: ~cita~ means at once a “quotation,” an “appointment,” and a “romantic date” — all of them a calling-together at an agreed time. Kin from the same root abound: ~incitar~ (“to incite”), ~excitar~ (“to excite”), ~recitar~ (“to recite”), ~solicitar~ (“to request”), and vividly ~resucitar~ (“to resuscitate”), literally to stir back to life.
en.clasificar:
A learned compound coined from Latin ~classis~ (“a division, class, fleet”) plus the combining form ~-ficāre~, from ~facere~ (“to make”) — literally “to make into classes.” ~Classis~ came from Proto-Italic *~klāssis~, from Proto-Indo-European *~kelh₁-~ (“to call, shout out”), and so is kin to Latin ~calāre~ (“to call”), ~clāmāre~ (“to shout”) and ~clārus~ (“clear”), and to Ancient Greek ~kaléō~ (“I call”). Cognate formations include Italian ~classificare~, French ~classifier~ and Portuguese ~classificar~.

The startling turn is that a ~classis~ began as a military summons: by De Vaan's account the sense ran from a “calling out” of citizens to arms, to the ~classis~ or body of soldiers so called, to the property classes into which Servius Tullius sorted Roman citizens, and finally to any “class” or category. ~Clasificar~ therefore means to sort things into ranks first drawn up by a herald's cry. Related Spanish words are ~clase~, ~clásico~ and ~clasificación~.
en.cobrar:
From Old Spanish ~cobrar~, an aphetic (head-clipped) form of ~recobrar~ (“to recover, get back”), from Latin ~recuperāre~ (“to regain, recover”), related to ~recipere~ (“to take back, receive”). Some scholars instead posit a Vulgar Latin *~cuperāre~, a back-formation drawn out of ~recuperāre~, which would make ~cobrar~ old rather than merely clipped — the point is debated. Whatever the route, Latin ~recuperāre~ also survives as the learned Spanish doublet ~recuperar~, and gave Italian ~ricoverare~, French ~recouvrer~ and English ~recover~ and ~recuperate~.

The starting sense was “to get back what was lost,” and Spanish ~recobrar~ and ~recuperar~ still carry it. The clipped ~cobrar~, though, drifted toward money: its dominant modern meaning is “to charge, to collect payment, to get paid.” It keeps older senses too — a hunter ~cobra~ (retrieves) downed game, and a feeling can ~cobrar fuerza~, “gather strength.” The family includes ~cobro~ (“collection, charge”), ~cobranza~, ~cobrador~, ~recobrar~ and ~recuperar~.
en.cocinar:
Spanish ~cocinar~ was built from the noun ~cocina~ (“kitchen”) plus the verb-forming suffix ~-ar~. ~cocina~ descends from Latin ~coquīna~ (“kitchen”), a nominalization tied to ~coquere~ (“to cook”), from Proto-Italic *~kʷekʷō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~pekʷ-~ (“to cook, ripen”). The same root produced Italian ~cucinare~, French ~cuisiner~ and Portuguese ~cozinhar~, and — through the Latin verb directly — Spanish ~cocer~ (“to boil, cook”). English ~cook~, borrowed early from Latin ~coquus~ (“cook”), belongs to the same family.

The meaning has stayed remarkably steady: to prepare food, especially with heat. The surprising twist is phonetic. In Latin the initial p of *~pekʷ-~ assimilated to the following labiovelar, turning the root into ~coquere~ — which is why the Romance words for cooking begin with a hard c/k rather than the p the root would lead you to expect. From the same source Spanish also keeps ~cocinero~ (“cook”), ~cocido~ (“stew,” literally “cooked”) and ~bizcocho~ (“sponge cake, biscuit”), from ~bis~ (“twice”) + ~coctus~ (“cooked”) — literally something baked twice.
en.coger:
From Old Spanish ~coger~ (first attested around 1140), from Latin ~colligere~ (“to gather, collect”), a compound of ~com-~ (“together”) and ~legere~ (“to gather, pick, read”). ~legere~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~leǵ-~ (“to gather, collect”), the root that also gave Ancient Greek ~légō~ (“to gather, to say”) and hence ~lógos~. Sister forms of ~colligere~ include Italian ~cogliere~, French ~cueillir~, Portuguese ~colher~, and Catalan ~collir~.

The journey from “to gather up” to plain “to grasp, take, catch” was gradual, and Spanish generalized ~coger~ into one of its handiest everyday verbs — coger el autobús, coger un objeto, coger fruta. But the meaning kept drifting regionally: across much of the Americas (Argentina, Mexico, and beyond) ~coger~ acquired a vulgar sexual sense, so speakers there favor ~agarrar~ or ~tomar~ for the neutral idea. From the same ~legere~ root Spanish also holds ~colegir~ (“to infer,” to gather a conclusion), ~recoger~, ~escoger~, ~coleccionar~, and the learned ~colección~ — a whole cluster around the image of gathering things together.
en.coincidir:
From Medieval Latin ~coincidere~ (“to fall together, occupy the same place”), a learned compound of ~co-~ (“together”) and ~incidere~ (“to fall upon, into”), itself ~in-~ (“on, into”) plus ~cadere~ (“to fall”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ḱad-~ (“to fall”). English carries the borrowings ~coincide~, ~incident~, ~accident~ and ~cadence~.

Unlike the inherited verbs, ~coincidir~ was assembled by scholars — first for geometry, where two figures “coincide” by falling exactly onto each other — and only later widened to the everyday “to agree, to happen at once.” The parent ~cadere~ left Spanish an enormous progeny: the plain ~caer~ (“to fall”), ~caso~ (“case,” a “falling-out” of events), ~casualidad~ (“chance”), ~decaer~, ~ocaso~ (“sunset, decline”), ~incidente~, ~accidente~ and even ~cadáver~ — the Latin ~cadāver~, literally “the fallen one.” To coincide, then, is for two things to fall onto the very same point.
en.colaborar:
From Latin ~collaborare~ (“to labor together”), a compound of ~com-~ (“together, with”) and ~laborare~ (“to work, to toil”), which derives from the noun ~labor~ (“work, effort, hardship”). Spanish took it as a learned borrowing rather than by unbroken oral descent. It is cognate with English ~collaborate~, Italian ~collaborare~, French ~collaborer~, and Portuguese ~colaborar~, all reflecting the same late-Latin formation.

In classical Latin ~laborare~ carried a note of toil and hardship, not just activity; the prefix ~com-~ added the sense of shared effort toward a common end. That cooperative meaning stayed remarkably stable, though the twentieth century gave ~colaborar~ a darker political shading in the sense of aiding an occupying enemy. From the same root Spanish keeps ~labor~, ~laborable~, ~laboratorio~, ~laborioso~ and ~elaborar~, all turning on the old idea of work.
en.colgar:
From Latin ~collocāre~ (“to place, set, arrange”), an emphatic ~com-~ prefixed to ~locāre~ (“to put in place”), from ~locus~ (“place”). Spoken Latin carried ~collocāre~ into Romance twice over: the inherited, sound-worn form became Spanish ~colgar~, while a later learned borrowing of the same word gave the doublet ~colocar~ (“to place, position”). French took its own descendant as ~coucher~ (“to lay down, put to bed”), and English borrowed that as the noun ~couch~; Portuguese has ~colgar~ beside ~colocar~.

Where Latin ~collocāre~ meant to set a thing anywhere, Spanish ~colgar~ specialized upward — to place something so it dangles from a hook or nail, that is, to hang it. The learned twin ~colocar~ meanwhile kept the neutral “to place,” so the two verbs split the labor between them. Modern relatives cluster around the base ~locus~: ~local~, ~localizar~, ~lugar~ (“place,” worn down from ~locālis~), and, back in the ~colgar~ branch, ~descolgar~ (“to take down, unhook”) and ~colgadura~ (“hanging, drapery”).
en.colocar:
From Latin ~collocāre~ (“to place together, to arrange, to set in order”), a compound of ~com-~ (“together, with”) and ~locāre~ (“to place”), from ~locus~ (“place”). ~locāre~ and ~locus~ go back, through Old Latin ~stlocus~, to an uncertain earlier form, but the family is unmistakable in Romance: Italian ~collocare~, Portuguese ~colocar~, and — by inheritance rather than borrowing — French ~coucher~ (“to lay down, to put to bed”) and English ~locate~ and ~couch~ all spring from the same Latin verb.

Spanish inherited ~collocāre~ twice over. The popular, orally transmitted line — its pretonic vowel lost and its consonants worn smooth — yielded ~colgar~ (“to hang”), while a later learned borrowing taken straight from the books gave ~colocar~ (“to place, to position”). The two form an etymological doublet: a single Latin word that entered Spanish by two different roads. From ~locus~ the language also draws ~local~, ~localizar~, and ~lugar~ (the fully popularized reflex of ~locālis~). And from the French ~coucher~ branch came the borrowed ~colcha~ (“bedspread”) and ~colchón~ (“mattress”) — so that a sleeper's mattress and the tidy verb ~colocar~ are, at a great distance, the very same word.
en.combatir:
From Vulgar Latin *~combattere~, an intensive ~com-~ (“with, together”) prefixed to Late Latin ~battuere~ (“to beat, strike”). That base looks foreign to Latin — genuine Latin words rarely begin with b — and is widely thought borrowed from Gaulish (compare Welsh ~bathu~, “to strike, to coin”), perhaps going back to Proto-Indo-European *~bʰau-~ (“to strike”); this Celtic route is probable but not certain. It is cognate with French ~combattre~ and English ~combat~ and ~battle~.

The soldierly sense was there from the beginning: to ~combatir~ is to “beat against” an enemy. The plain descendant of ~battuere~ is Spanish ~batir~ (“to beat, whisk, pound”), and the same base spread widely into ~batalla~, ~combate~, ~debatir~ (originally “to thrash out”), and ~abatir~ (“to knock down, to dishearten”).
en.combinar:
From Late Latin ~combīnāre~ (“to join two by two”), from ~com-~ (“together”) plus ~bīnī~ (“two at a time, in pairs”), a distributive of ~bis~ (“twice”) that traces back to ~duo~ (“two”) and ultimately to Proto-Indo-European *~dwóh₁~ (“two”). English borrowed the same verb as ~combine~, and the ~bīnī~ element survives in ~binary~.

The word's whole logic is pairing: to combine is to set things two by two until they hold together. Late Latin coined ~combīnāre~ precisely to name that yoking of pairs, and Spanish kept the sense intact in ~combinación~ (“combination”), which can mean a chemical union, a subway connection, or a woman's slip. The numeral core shows up wherever “two-ness” is at stake — in ~binario~, ~combinado~ and the mathematics of ~combinatoria~. Far older, that same *~dwóh₁~ underlies Spanish ~dos~, ~doble~ and ~dúo~, making combine and its cousins a distant echo of the plain word for two.
en.comentar:
From Latin ~commentārī~ (“to consider thoroughly, study, discuss”), a deponent verb linked to ~comminīscī~ (“to devise, contrive, think up”), formed with ~com-~ (“together, thoroughly”) on the root of ~meminī~ (“to remember”) and ~mēns~ (“mind”), from Proto-Indo-European *~men-~ (“to think”). ~Comentar~ therefore shares its deepest root with ~mencionar~. It is cognate with Italian ~commentare~, French ~commenter~, Portuguese ~comentar~ and English ~comment~, and — through *~men-~ — with English ~mind~ and ~mental~.

The literal sense is “to have thoroughly in mind” — to turn something over in thought — and from that came the ideas of studying a text and remarking on it. The Latin noun ~commentārius~ meant a notebook or memorandum, a set of things thought over; Julius Caesar titled his war memoirs ~Commentāriī~, and the English “commentary” descends straight from it. Modern Spanish keeps the reflective streak: to ~comentar~ is to offer one's considered remark, and the ~comentario~ can range from a scholarly gloss to a passing aside. Related through *~men-~ are ~mente~, ~memoria~, ~mencionar~ and ~mentar~.
en.comenzar:
From Vulgar Latin *~cominitiāre~, a compound of intensive ~com-~ and ~initiāre~ (“to begin, initiate”), the verb of ~initium~ (“a beginning”). ~initium~ comes from ~inīre~ (“to go in, enter”), from ~in-~ (“in”) plus ~īre~ (“to go”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₁ey-~ (“to go”). Cognate with French ~commencer~, Italian ~cominciare~, Portuguese ~começar~, and Catalan ~començar~; English ~commence~ was borrowed from the Old French form.

The literal core is quietly logical: to begin is to “go into” a thing — ~inīre~ — and ~initium~ named the threshold, the point of entry. Late Latin stacked an intensifying ~com-~ onto ~initiāre~ to make the everyday “start,” and that doubled form, not classical ~incipere~, is what the western Romance languages inherited.
