The same verb also means “to be under way” — an illness that ~cursa~ with fever runs its course — and, in officialese, “to dispatch” a document, sending it on its way. From *~ḱers-~ Spanish keeps a crowded family: ~correr~, ~curso~, ~carrera~ (“race; career”), ~corriente~, ~ocurrir~, ~discurso~, ~concurso~, ~socorro~ (“help,” literally a running-to-aid), and ~carro~.
en.dar:
Spanish ~dar~ descends straight from Latin ~dare~ (“to give”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~deh₃-~ (“to give”) — one of the most stable meanings in the whole family. The same root shines through Latin ~dōnum~ (“gift”), Greek ~dídōmi~ (“I give”), and Sanskrit ~dádāti~. Italian ~dare~ and Portuguese ~dar~ kept the plain verb, but French abandoned it for ~donner~ (from ~dōnāre~, “to make a gift”), leaving Spanish among the languages that still simply “give” with ~dare~.

For so short a verb, ~dar~ carries an enormous idiomatic load in Spanish, while its root branches out into a whole family of giving. The language has ~dádiva~ (“gift”), ~don~ (“gift, talent”) and ~donar~ (“to donate”), and, through the Latin participle, ~dado~ (“given; a die”) and ~dato~ (“fact, datum”). Even English ~date~ and ~data~, borrowed from the same Latin participle ~datum~ (“given”), belong to this quietly generous root.
en.dañar:
From Latin ~damnāre~ (“to condemn, to fine, to inflict loss on”), from the noun ~damnum~ (“loss, damage, a penalty”), from Proto-Italic *~dapno-~ and Proto-Indo-European *~dh₂pnom~ (“expense, what is paid out”). Most etymologists tie this to the root *~deh₂p-~ and to Latin ~daps~ (“a sacrificial feast”), the shared idea being ritual expenditure — a loss given up — though the exact PIE reconstruction is debated. Cognate, through Old French, with English ~damn~ and ~damage~, and with the learned ~condemn~ and ~indemnity~.

Latin ~damnum~ was first the legal “loss” or “fine” a court imposed, and ~damnāre~ meant to sentence someone to such a loss. Popular Spanish narrowed the verb to plain physical harm — to ~dañar~ is to injure or spoil — while the courtroom sense went to the learned doublet ~condenar~ (“to condemn”). From the noun come ~daño~ (“harm, damage”) and ~dañino~ (“harmful”), and the loss-averting ~indemne~ (“unharmed”) — one who has been kept free of ~damnum~.
en.debatir:
From Old French ~debatre~ (“to fight, contend”), which joins ~de-~ (“down, completely”) to ~batre~ (“to beat”), from Latin ~battuere~ (“to beat, strike”). The deeper origin of ~battuere~ is genuinely disputed: rare in literary Latin yet common in speech, it is often taken as a loan from Gaulish (compare Welsh ~bathu~, “to beat, coin money”) and traced to Proto-Indo-European *~bʰedʰh₂-~ (“to stab, dig”), while other scholars judge it simply onomatopoeic — the sources do not settle it. Spanish ~debatir~ is cognate with French ~débattre~ and English ~debate~, ~battle~ and ~batter~.

The sense moved from literal blows to verbal ones: “to beat down” an opponent became “to argue, contend, discuss.” The ~battuere~ family is large in Spanish: ~batir~ (“to beat”), ~combatir~, ~abatir~, ~batalla~ and ~batería~. The memorable thread is that a debate is etymologically a fight — parties still “trade blows” and “hammer out” a question — and the very same root supplies the ~batería~ that powers a phone, named from the notion of guns “beating” a target. The pen may be mightier than the sword, but ~debatir~ never forgot the sword.
en.deber:
Spanish ~deber~ comes from Latin ~dēbēre~ (“to owe”), which began as a contraction of ~dē-~ (“from, away”) plus ~habēre~ (“to have”): to owe was “to have something from someone else,” held but not truly one's own. So ~deber~ is, at root, a compound of ~haber~. Its Romance siblings share it: French ~devoir~, Italian ~dovere~, Portuguese ~dever~. English ~debt~ and ~due~ come from the same Latin verb, borrowed through French, so they are cousins rather than natives.

From “owe,” ~deber~ grew a second, modal life: to owe an action is to be obliged to do it, so ~deber~ came to mean “must, ought” — ~debo irme~ (“I must go”). The noun ~deber~ means “duty,” and ~deberes~ are a schoolchild's “homework,” obligations owed. The financial thread survives in ~débito~ (“debit”), ~deuda~ (“debt”), and ~debido~ (“due, owed”) — the whole family circling the idea of something held that must be given back.
en.decidir:
From Latin ~dēcīdere~ (“to cut off, to determine”), from ~dē-~ (“off, away”) plus ~caedere~ (“to cut, to strike down”), from Proto-Indo-European *~kh₂eyd-~ (“to strike, to cut”). Cognate with French ~décider~, Italian ~decidere~, and English ~decide~ and ~decision~.

The metaphor is a blade: to decide is to cut off deliberation, severing every alternative but the chosen one — the mental equivalent of slicing through a knot. ~caedere~ was a violent, physical verb, and it left a bloody trail across Latin: it is the ~-cide~ of ~homicida~ (“murderer”) and ~suicidio~, literally acts of cutting down. Gentler siblings survive in Spanish too: from ~praecīdere~ (“to cut in front”) came ~preciso~ and ~precisar~ (“precise,” cut to exact measure), and from ~concīdere~ came ~conciso~ (“concise,” cut short). Every ~decisión~, then, is a small cut.
en.decir:
Spanish ~decir~ comes, through Old Spanish ~dezir~, from Latin ~dīcere~ (“to say, to tell”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~deyḱ-~ (“to show, to point out”) — saying imagined first as pointing something out. That root of showing gave, on the Germanic side, English ~teach~ and ~token~, and in Greek ~deíknymi~ (“I show”). The Romance reflexes stayed close: Italian ~dire~, French ~dire~, Portuguese ~dizer~.

The step from “point out” to “speak” is the whole story of the word, and the pointing sense lingers in its relatives. Spanish keeps the past participle ~dicho~ (“said; a saying”) and builds ~contradecir~ (“to contradict”) and ~bendecir~ (“to bless,” literally “to say well”). From the same root come ~dictar~ (“to dictate”) and ~dictado~, the legal ~edicto~ (“edict”), and ~índice~ (“index, forefinger”) — the very finger that points.
en.declarar:
From Latin ~dēclārāre~ (“to make clear, reveal, announce”), formed from an intensive ~dē-~ and ~clārāre~ (“to make clear, brighten”), a verb from the adjective ~clārus~ (“clear, bright, loud”). ~Clārus~ traces to Proto-Indo-European *~kelh₁-~ (“to shout, call out”), by way of *~kl̥h₁rós~ (“loud”). Spanish ~declarar~ is cognate with Italian ~dichiarare~, French ~déclarer~, Portuguese ~declarar~ and English ~declare~ and ~clear~; through *~kelh₁-~ it is kin to Latin ~clāmāre~ (“to shout”) and even to German ~hell~ (“bright”).

Here is the memorable twist: ~clārus~ began as a word for sound, “loud, ringing,” and only later crossed over to light and sight, “bright, clear” — the ancient mind treating the spreading of a shout and the spreading of light as one image. ~Dēclārāre~ rode that shift, moving from making a thing audibly plain to making it visibly clear, and finally to the modern “to declare,” to state openly. From ~clārus~ Spanish drew ~claro~ (“clear”), ~aclarar~ (“to clarify”), ~clarear~, ~claridad~ and ~clarín~ (“bugle”); and from the same root *~kelh₁-~, through ~clāmāre~, came ~clamar~ and the everyday ~llamar~ (“to call”).
en.decorar:
From Latin ~decorāre~ (“to adorn, embellish”), from ~decus~, ~decoris~ (“ornament, grace, honor”), related to ~decēre~ (“to be fitting, become”), from Proto-Indo-European *~deḱ-~ (“to take, accept; be fitting”). Cognate through that root with English ~decent~ and ~decorum~, and — more distantly — with ~dignity~ (from ~dignus~) and the ~docēre~ family (~doctor~, ~doctrine~).

The core idea of *~deḱ-~ is fittingness — what is accepted as becoming or graceful — so ~decus~ was “that which becomes one,” an ornament or honor, and ~decorāre~ was to add such grace. Spanish keeps ~decoración~, ~decorado~ (“stage set”), ~decoro~ (“decorum, propriety”), and ~decente~. A curious footnote: the Spanish ~decorar~ that means “to learn by heart” is a different word, from the phrase ~de coro~ (“by heart”) built on Latin ~cor~ (“heart,” once thought the seat of memory) — an accidental twin of the ornamental ~decorar~, not a descendant of ~decus~.
en.dedicar:
From Latin ~dedicāre~ (“to consecrate, to dedicate, to proclaim”), from ~de-~ (“completely, down”) + ~dicāre~ (“to proclaim solemnly, to consecrate”). ~dicāre~ is a first-conjugation relative of ~dīcere~ (“to say”), and both go back to Proto-Indo-European *~deyḱ-~ (“to show, to point out”). That root surfaces in Ancient Greek ~deíknumi~ (“I show”), German ~zeigen~ (“to show”), and English ~teach~ and ~token~. Spanish took the learned ~dedicar~ from Latin. Cognate with Italian ~dedicare~, French ~dédier~, and Portuguese ~dedicar~.

The root idea is pointing: to ~dicāre~ was to point something out with words, to proclaim it — and to ~dedicāre~ was to point it out entirely, to set it apart by solemn declaration, as a temple was dedicated to a god. Modern ~dedicar~ keeps that sense of setting time or effort apart for a purpose. The pointing root *~deyḱ-~ is astonishingly productive in Spanish: ~decir~, ~índice~ (“the pointing finger”), ~dedo~ (“finger”), ~juez~ and ~juzgar~ (“to point out the law,” ~ius~ + ~dicere~), ~predecir~, and ~dictar~.
en.defender:
From Latin ~dēfendere~ (“to ward off, protect”), from ~dē-~ (“away, off”) and a bound root ~-fendere~ (“to strike, push”), from Proto-Indo-European *~gʷʰen-~ (“to strike, kill”). The same root gave ~offendere~ (“to strike against”). Cognate with Italian ~difendere~, French ~défendre~, and — as borrowings — English ~defend~, ~fend~, and ~offend~.

Curiously, ~-fendere~ never stood on its own in Latin: no simple verb “to strike” is attested, only the compounds ~dēfendere~ (to strike the enemy away) and ~offendere~ (to strike against — hence to give offense). French pushed ~défendre~ in a legal direction, so it means both to defend and to forbid, while Spanish ~defender~ held to protection. Descendants in Spanish include ~defensa~ (“defense”), ~defensor~ (“defender”), ~ofender~ (“to offend”), and ~ofensa~ (“offense”).
en.definir:
From Latin ~dēfīnīre~ (“to set bounds to, limit, define”), formed from the prefix ~dē-~ (“off, completely”) and ~fīnīre~ (“to limit, bring to an end”), itself built on the noun ~fīnis~ (“boundary, border, end”). The deeper origin of ~fīnis~ is uncertain: one proposal links it to ~fīgere~ (“to fix, fasten, drive in”), as if a boundary were a stake fixed in the ground, but that connection is disputed and far from secure. Spanish ~definir~ is a learned borrowing, cognate with Italian ~definire~, French ~définir~ and Portuguese ~definir~; and because ~fīnīre~ passed through Old French, English ~finish~ belongs to the same family.

In Latin ~dēfīnīre~ meant to mark out the limits of a thing, whether a field or an idea; from drawing those edges came the abstract sense of saying precisely what something is — the modern “to define.” The noun ~fīnis~ was extraordinarily productive in Spanish, yielding the everyday ~fin~ (“end”), together with ~final~, ~finalizar~, ~confín~, ~finito~, ~infinito~ and, of course, ~definición~. The legal ~finiquito~ (“final settlement”) and the verb ~afinar~ (“to tune, refine”) descend from the same source, all preserving the core idea of bringing something to its edge or its end.
en.dejar:
From Old Spanish ~dexar~ (also ~lexar~), from Latin ~laxāre~ (“to loosen, slacken, let go”), the denominative verb of ~laxus~ (“loose, slack”), from Proto-Indo-European *~(s)leg-~ (“to be slack”). Cognate with Portuguese ~deixar~, French ~laisser~, and Italian ~lasciare~, all of which kept the original ~l-~; through the same Latin verb English acquired ~relax~, ~release~, and ~lease~, and through the same PIE root the native English ~slack~.

Latin ~laxāre~ first meant to slacken a rope or relax the limbs; in Ibero-Romance the sense drifted to “let go,” then “leave behind, allow.” The startling feature of the Spanish form is its initial ~d-~: by one commonly cited account, the expected ~l-~ shifted to ~d-~ under the pull of ~dar~ (“to give”), a neighbor in both meaning and grammar — a swap that sets ~dejar~ apart from its ~l-~-keeping cousins. First documented around 1140, it later spread from “leave” into “stop” and “let.” The same Latin verb seeded the learned Spanish ~laxo~, ~laxante~, and ~relajar~ (a bookish doublet of ~dejar~), plus ~dejadez~ (“lassitude, neglect”).
en.demandar:
From Latin ~dēmandāre~ (“to entrust, to commit to one's charge”), from ~dē-~ (here intensive) plus ~mandāre~ (“to order, to entrust”). ~mandāre~ is traditionally analyzed as ~manus~ (“hand”) plus ~dare~ (“to give”) — literally “to give into someone's hand” — from Proto-Indo-European *~man-~ (“hand”) and *~deh₃-~ (“to give”). Cognate with French ~demander~, Italian ~domandare~ and Portuguese ~demandar~; English ~demand~ arrived through Old French.

Latin ~dēmandāre~ meant “to entrust, to put in another's charge.” Across Romance the sense slid toward simple asking — French ~demander~ still means merely “to ask” — but Spanish ~demandar~ kept a firmer edge, “to demand,” and took on the courtroom sense “to sue, to file suit.” From the same ~mandāre~ come ~mandar~, ~mandato~, ~mandamiento~, ~comandar~, ~recomendar~ and ~encomendar~, while the older ~manus~ survives plainly in ~mano~. The image beneath all of them is a thing placed, quite literally, into a waiting hand.
en.demostrar:
Spanish ~demostrar~ comes from Latin ~dēmōnstrāre~ (“to point out, indicate, prove”), a compound of ~dē-~ (“fully, from”) and ~mōnstrāre~ (“to show, point out”). ~mōnstrāre~ is a denominal verb from ~mōnstrum~ — originally “a divine omen, a portent” — which in turn derives from ~monēre~ (“to warn, advise, remind”). ~monēre~ reflects Proto-Indo-European *~men-~ (“to think”), the vast root behind Latin ~mēns~ (“mind”) and English ~mind~, ~mental~, and ~mean~. English took ~demonstrate~, ~monster~, ~monstrance~, and ~monitor~ from this branch. Italian ~dimostrare~, French ~montrer~ / ~démontrer~, and Portuguese ~demonstrar~ are the Romance parallels of ~demostrar~.

The buried surprise is ~mōnstrum~: a monster was first not a beast but a sign — something shown by the gods as a warning, from ~monēre~ (“to warn”). A ~mōnstrum~ was a portent that pointed to something, and ~mōnstrāre~ meant to point it out; ~dēmōnstrāre~ intensified this into showing thoroughly, and thence proving. Spanish split the inheritance: popular ~mostrar~ evolved by regular sound change, while learned ~demostrar~ was reborrowed closer to the Latin. From the same ~monēre~ / *~men-~ family Spanish keeps ~mostrar~, ~muestra~ (“sample, sign”), ~monstruo~, ~amonestar~ (“to admonish”), ~mente~, and ~mención~.
en.denominar:
From Latin ~dēnōmināre~ (“to name, designate”), formed from ~de-~ (here intensive) and ~nōmināre~ (“to name”), from ~nōmen~ (“name”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₁nómn̥~ (“name”). It is cognate with French ~dénommer~, Italian ~denominare~, and Portuguese ~denominar~, and with the Latin-derived English ~denominate~. Straight from *~h₁nómn̥~ come English ~name~, German ~Name~, and Greek ~ónoma~.

Latin ~nōmen~ left Spanish two lines: the patrimonial ~nombre~ (“name”) and the learned ~nominar~ and ~denominar~ (“to name, designate”). A quiet gem sits in arithmetic: the ~denominador~ of a fraction is literally what “names” its parts — in three-fifths, the fifths are the name and the count. The same family gave ~nómina~ (“payroll,” once simply a list of names), ~nomenclatura~, ~denominación~ (as in the wine label ~denominación de origen~), ~renombre~ (“renown”), and the grammatical ~pronombre~ (“pronoun”).
en.denunciar:
From Latin ~dēnūntiāre~ (“to announce officially, give notice, proclaim, threaten”), from ~dē-~ (“down, fully”) plus ~nūntiāre~ (“to announce”), a verb built on ~nūntius~ (“messenger, message”). The origin of ~nūntius~ is uncertain: it is usually traced to Proto-Indo-European *~newH-~ (“to shout, cry”), with possible cognates in Sanskrit ~návate~ (“cries, sounds”) and Old Irish ~núall~ (“a loud cry”), while an older derivation from ~novus~ (“new”) is now rejected. Cognate with Italian ~denunciare~, French ~dénoncer~ and Portuguese ~denunciar~, and with English ~denounce~.

In Latin the word was formal and legal — to serve official notice, lodge a public declaration, even proclaim war. Spanish ~denunciar~ preserved that accusatory edge: to report a crime to the authorities or to condemn a wrong in public, a sense the noun ~denuncia~ carries in everyday legal Spanish. The ~nūntius~ family branched widely: ~anunciar~ (“to announce”), ~pronunciar~ (“to pronounce”), ~renunciar~ (“to renounce”) and ~nuncio~, the papal envoy who is, etymologically, simply a “messenger.”
en.depender:
From Latin ~dependēre~ (“to hang from, to hang down”), a compound of ~dē-~ (“down from”) and ~pendēre~ (“to hang, to be suspended”). ~pendēre~ traces to the Proto-Indo-European root *~(s)pend-~ (“to pull, to stretch, to spin”). The verb is thoroughly Romance — Italian ~dipendere~, French ~dépendre~, Portuguese ~depender~ — and through the same Latin root it matches English ~depend~, ~pendant~, ~pending~, and ~suspend~.

The metaphor is beautifully literal: to ~depender~ is to “hang from” something, exactly as a ~pendiente~ (“earring, pendant”) hangs from an ear. What hangs from a support is held up by it and cannot stand alone — so “hanging from” became “being contingent upon,” relying on. The same ~pendēre~ family gave Spanish ~pender~, ~pendiente~, ~suspender~, ~depender~, and ~independiente~. And here is the surprise: the frequentative ~pēnsāre~ (“to weigh carefully”), from the same root, split into two Spanish verbs — ~pesar~ (“to weigh”) and ~pensar~ (“to think”) — because to weigh an idea in the mind is to think it over. So ~depender~, ~pesar~, and ~pensar~ all hang, in the end, from the same thread.
en.depositar:
From Latin ~dēpositāre~ (“to lay down, deposit”), a frequentative built on ~dēpositum~ (“something laid down, a deposit”), the neuter past participle of ~dēpōnere~ (“to put down, lay aside”), from ~dē-~ (“down, away”) + ~pōnere~ (“to put, place”), itself a contraction of ~pō-~ + ~sinere~ (“to let, set down”). Cognate with English ~deposit~ and ~depose~, Italian ~depositare~, and French ~déposer~.

The idea under ~depositar~ is entrusting something by setting it down in a safe place — which is why one word covers laying sediment, placing money in a bank, and reposing trust in a person. Latin ~dēpōnere~ was likewise the verb for laying down an office and for giving sworn testimony, a legal echo still heard in ~deposición~ (“deposition”) and ~deponer~ (“to depose, testify”). The prolific ~pōnere~ seeded a vast Spanish family: ~poner~, ~poste~, ~posición~, ~depósito~, ~componer~, ~exponer~, and ~posar~.
en.derivar:
From Latin ~dērīvāre~ (“to lead or draw off [water]”), from ~dē-~ (“from, away”) + ~rīvus~ (“brook, stream, channel”). ~rīvus~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~h₃reyH-~ (“to flow”). Cognate with Italian ~derivare~ and French ~dériver~, and — through ~rīvus~ — with English ~derive~ and ~rival~.

The literal image is hydraulic: to ~derivar~ water is to lead it away from its main channel into a side one — exactly what an irrigation engineer does. From that physical sense grew the abstract one still dominant today: one thing “flows from” another, so a word, a right, or a conclusion is ~derivado~ (“derived”) from its source. The most charming relative is ~rival~: in Latin a ~rīvālis~ was literally someone who shared the same ~rīvus~ — a neighbor drawing water from the same stream — and since people who share a water source tend to quarrel over it, the word came to mean “competitor.” Spanish kept the whole watery family: ~río~ (“river,” straight from ~rīvus~), ~riachuelo~ (“little stream”), ~derivación~ (“derivation”), and ~deriva~ (“drift,” as in a boat going adrift).
en.derrotar:
Spanish ~derrotar~ (“to defeat”) belongs to the family of ~derrota~, originally “route, course,” which came through an old verb ~derromper~ (“to break through”) from Latin ~rupta~, the feminine past participle of ~rumpere~ (“to break”), from a Proto-Indo-European root *~rewp-~ (“to break, snatch”). The same ~rupta~ gave French ~route~ and, borrowed, English ~route~, ~rout~ and ~rupture~; the Italian cognate is ~rotta~.

The word ~rupta~ named a road “broken” open through obstacles, and from it ~derrota~ came to mean a ship’s or traveller’s course. The martial sense — a “defeat,” a breaking of the ranks — is late: Corominas finds no example of ~derrotar~ meaning “to defeat” before 1683 and judges it a borrowing shaped by French ~déroute~ (“rout”), from Old French ~desroter~; that Gallicism is the favored account rather than a settled fact. From the same root Spanish keeps ~romper~, ~ruptura~, ~corromper~ and the nautical ~derrotero~.
en.desaparecer:
From ~des-~ (a privative prefix, from Latin ~dis-~, “apart, reversal”) prefixed to ~aparecer~ (“to appear”), which comes from Latin ~appārēscere~, an inchoative (“to begin to be visible”) built on ~appārēre~ (“to appear, come into view”), from ~ad-~ (“to”) plus ~pārēre~ (“to come forth, be visible, obey”). The further origin of ~pārēre~ is uncertain. Cognate with Italian ~apparire~ (and ~sparire~), French ~apparaître~ (and ~disparaître~) and Portuguese ~desaparecer~, and with English ~appear~ and ~apparent~.

The ~-ēscere~ inflection is telling: ~aparecer~ is not merely “to be visible” but “to come into visibility,” an entering; ~des-~ then reverses the motion into “to pass out of sight, vanish.” The same ~pārēre~ underlies ~parecer~ (“to seem, to appear-to-be”) — appearing and seeming from one Latin verb — and feeds a wide family: ~aparición~ (“apparition”), ~aparente~ (“apparent”), ~transparente~ (“transparent”) and ~comparecer~ (“to appear in court”).
en.desarrollar:
A Spanish formation from ~des-~ (a prefix of reversal) and ~arrollar~ (“to roll up”), which is ~a-~ plus ~rollo~ (“a roll, scroll”). ~rollo~ descends from Latin ~rotulus~ (“little wheel, roll”), the diminutive of ~rota~ (“wheel”), from Proto-Indo-European *~Hret-~ (“to run, to roll”). The wheel-root has far-flung cognates: German ~Rad~ (“wheel”), Sanskrit ~rátha~ (“chariot”), and Old Irish ~roth~ (“wheel”); ~rotulus~ itself gave English ~roll~ and ~role~ through French ~rôle~.

The image is vivid and exact: to develop is literally to un-roll — ~des-~ + ~arrollar~ — as one opens a rolled scroll to reveal what is written inside. Growth, in this metaphor, is a scroll unspooling. English ~develop~ carries the very same picture by a different route (Old French ~desveloper~, “to unwrap”), so the two languages independently imagine progress as undoing a wrapping. From the same wheel-root Spanish keeps ~rollo~, ~arrollar~, ~rueda~ (“wheel,” straight from ~rota~), ~rótula~ (“kneecap”), and the borrowed ~rotación~ and ~control~ (via the roll-counter of French ~contre-rôle~).
en.descansar:
Spanish ~descansar~ is ~des-~ (“un-, reversal”) prefixed to ~cansar~ (“to tire”), so it means literally to un-tire — to rest. The verb ~cansar~ is the puzzle. The standard account, argued by Corominas, derives it from Latin ~campsāre~ (“to bend, turn, to double a cape”), a nautical borrowing of Ancient Greek ~kámptein~ (“to bend, curve”). The Romance reflexes are thin outside Ibero-Romance; Portuguese shares ~cansar~ and ~descansar~.

The semantic path is the memorable part, and it is Corominas’s reconstruction rather than a documented certainty: ~campsāre~ meant to swerve from a straight course — to double a headland, to turn aside — and from “turning aside, giving up the course” it drifted to “giving up, flagging,” hence “to tire.” Prefix ~des-~ and you reverse the flagging: ~descansar~, to recover, to rest. From the same ~cansar~ Spanish built ~cansancio~ (“tiredness”), ~descanso~ (“rest, break”), ~incansable~ (“tireless”), and ~cansino~ (“weary, plodding”).
en.descargar:
A compound of the prefix ~des-~ (“un-, reversal,” from Latin ~dis-~) and ~cargar~ (“to load”), from Vulgar Latin ~carricāre~ (“to load a wagon”), a verb built on Latin ~carrus~ (“wheeled wagon, cart”). ~Carrus~ was a Gaulish loan, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *~ḱers-~ (“to run”). Cognate with French ~charger~, Italian ~caricare~ and Portuguese ~carregar~; through ~carrus~ it is related to English ~charge~, ~cargo~ and ~car~.

At bottom ~descargar~ means to take the load off a cart — to ~cargar~ was to pile goods onto a ~carrus~, and ~des-~ reverses it. From that concrete image the word fanned out: to unload a ship, to fire (“discharge”) a weapon, to vent one's anger, to relieve an electric ~carga~ — and, in our century, to ~descargar~ a file from the internet, so that the newest sense of the word still rides on a Roman ox-cart. The family is large in Spanish: ~carga~, ~cargo~, ~cargamento~, ~carguero~, ~descarga~, ~recargar~, ~sobrecargar~ and ~encargar~, this last meaning “to entrust,” literally to load a task onto someone.
en.descartar:
From ~des-~ (“un-, away”) + ~carta~ (“card; letter”), from Latin ~charta~ (“sheet of papyrus, paper”), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ~khártēs~ (“leaf of papyrus”). Parallel formations run through Romance: Italian ~scartare~, Portuguese ~descartar~, and — built on the same ~card~ — English ~discard~.

~Descartar~ began at the card table: to ~descartar~ was to throw away unwanted playing cards (~cartas~), and only later did it broaden to discarding, ruling out, or setting aside anything at all (~descartar una posibilidad~). The Greek ~khártēs~ behind it also gave, through Latin ~charta~, a large Spanish family: ~carta~ (“letter, card”), ~cartel~ (“poster”), ~cartón~ (“cardboard”), ~cartera~ (“wallet”) and ~carpeta~ (“folder”) — and, through French, English ~chart~ and ~charter~. Fittingly, the surname of the philosopher ~Descartes~ happens to read as ~des~ + ~cartes~, though it in fact derives from a place-name, not from discarding at all.
en.descender:
From Latin ~dēscendere~ (“to climb down, to go down”), from ~dē-~ (“down from”) plus ~scandere~ (“to climb”), from Proto-Indo-European *~skend-~ (“to climb, to leap”). Cognate with French ~descendre~, Italian ~scendere~ and Portuguese ~descer~, and — through the same root — with English ~ascend~ and ~scan~.

The core verb ~scandere~ meant to climb, and Latin built a matched pair on it: ~ascendere~ to climb up, ~dēscendere~ to climb down. The same root gave ~scāla~ (“ladder, staircase”), whence Spanish ~escala~ and ~escalera~. A stranger descendant is ~scan~: to “scan” a line of verse was originally to mark its metrical feet by beating them out, as if climbing step by step through the rhythm. In Spanish the family includes ~descenso~, ~descendencia~, ~descendiente~ and ~ascender~.
en.desconocer:
A Spanish formation: ~des-~ (a negating and reversing prefix, from Latin ~dis-~) prefixed to ~conocer~ (“to know”). ~Conocer~ descends through Old Spanish ~conoscer~ from Latin ~cognoscere~ (“to get to know”), a compound of ~com-~ (intensive) and ~gnoscere~ / ~noscere~ (“to know”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ǵneh₃-~ (“to know”). Through that root it is cognate with English ~know~ and ~can~, and with the heirs of ~cognoscere~: Italian ~conoscere~ and French ~connaître~.

The prefix ~des-~ negates, so ~desconocer~ literally means “to not know,” but Spanish sharpened it into two everyday senses: to be unaware of or unacquainted with something, and, more pointedly, to refuse to recognize — to disown a signature, a debt, or a person one no longer acknowledges. The PIE root *~ǵneh₃-~ is one of the most fertile in the language, behind ~conocer~, ~conocimiento~, ~reconocer~, ~noticia~ and the learned ~cognición~.
en.describir:
From Latin ~dēscrībere~ (“to write down, copy off, sketch, describe”), a compound of the prefix ~dē-~ (“down, off”) and ~scrībere~ (“to write”). ~scrībere~ originally meant “to scratch, incise” — writing was cutting marks into a surface — and descends from Proto-Indo-European *~(s)kreybʰ-~ (“to scratch, tear, cut”), an extension of *~(s)ker-~ (“to cut”). A striking cognate survives in Ancient Greek ~skáriphos~ (“a scratching, outline, sketch”). Note the false friend: German ~schreiben~ (“to write”) looks cognate but was actually borrowed from the Latin verb, and English ~write~ comes from a different root entirely. The learned Romance descendants include Italian ~descrivere~, French ~décrire~ and Portuguese ~descrever~.

The metaphor of scratching stayed alive across the whole family. To describe is, etymologically, to “write down” the shape of a thing — to sketch it in words. From ~scrībere~ Spanish inherited ~escribir~ (“to write”) and built a dense thicket of compounds — ~describir~, ~inscribir~, ~prescribir~, ~suscribir~, ~transcribir~ — plus nouns like ~escritura~ (“writing, deed”), ~escritor~ (“writer”) and ~escritorio~ (“desk”). From the past participle ~scrīptus~ came ~escrito~ (“written; a writing”) and ~inscripción~ (“inscription”). English drew a matching crop of borrowings from the same Latin verb — ~scribe~, ~script~, ~scripture~, ~describe~ — all still carrying, faintly, the old sense of a stylus scoring a line.
en.descubrir:
From ~des-~ (a reversative prefix, from Latin ~dis-~) plus ~cubrir~ (“to cover”), which comes from Latin ~cooperīre~ (“to cover completely”), a compound of ~co-~ (intensive) and ~operīre~ (“to cover, close”). ~Operīre~ derives from Proto-Italic *~opweriō~ and the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₂wer-~ (“to cover, shut”). The formation matches Old French ~descovrir~, whence English ~discover~; compare Italian ~scoprire~ and Portuguese ~descobrir~.

The morphology is beautifully transparent: to ~descubrir~ is literally to un-cover, to take the lid off — and Spanish uses it both for physically uncovering and for the mental act of discovery, exactly as English ~discover~ pairs with ~cover~. Columbus’s ~descubrimiento~ of America is the same word as lifting a cloth. From the ~cubrir~ family come ~cubierta~, ~cobertura~, ~encubrir~ and ~recubrir~, while the reversative ~des-~ productively negates hundreds of Spanish verbs.
en.desear:
From Latin ~dēsīderāre~ (“to long for, miss, feel the want of”), traditionally analyzed as ~dē-~ + ~sīdus~ (stem ~sīder-~, “star, constellation”), and inherited by Old Spanish as ~desear~. Cognate with Italian ~desiderare~ and Portuguese ~desejar~, and — through the noun ~dēsīderium~ — with English ~desire~ (via Old French).

The star etymology is the classic account, pairing ~dēsīderāre~ with ~cōnsīderāre~ (“to observe the stars closely”): to desire would be to note a star’s absence, to long for what is no longer in sight. But this is disputed — some scholars reject the ~sīdus~ connection outright and derive the verb from a root meaning “stretch, survey,” so the celestial story, charming as it is, should be taken as one proposal, not settled fact. Secure descendants include ~deseo~, ~deseable~ and ~desiderátum~; from ~sīdus~ itself come ~sideral~ and ~considerar~.
en.desempeñar:
A Romance formation: the prefix ~des-~ (“un-, reversal,” from Latin ~dis-~) added to ~empeñar~ (“to pledge, pawn”), which comes from ~empeño~ and ultimately from the old noun ~peño~ (plural ~peños~, “a pledge”), from Latin ~pignus~ (“pledge, security, pawn”). The deeper source of ~pignus~ is uncertain; it is sometimes connected to ~pangere~ (“to fix, fasten”). Cognate formations appear in Portuguese ~empenhar~ and Italian ~impegnare~.

The literal sense came first: to ~desempeñar~ something was to redeem it — to undo a pledge and reclaim a pawned object. From there it turned figurative — to free oneself from an obligation, to make good on one's word — and finally to the modern “to discharge, carry out”: one ~desempeña~ a role, a post, or a duty. The noun ~desempeño~ now means “performance” in every sense, from a job review to an actor's delivery. From the same ~pignus~ Spanish also keeps ~empeño~ (“determination, resolve”) and, as a doublet through the Latin plural ~pignora~, the everyday word ~prenda~ (“a garment; a token of love”) — all of them, at root, something handed over as a guarantee.
en.designar:
From Latin ~dēsignāre~ (“to mark out, point out”), a compound of ~dē-~ (“off, out”) and ~signāre~ (“to mark”), from ~signum~ (“sign, mark, token”). The origin of ~signum~ is debated: it goes back to Proto-Italic *~seknom~ and, beyond that, to either Proto-Indo-European *~sek-~ (“to cut”) or *~sekʷ-~ (“to follow”). Spanish ~designar~ is a learned doublet of the inherited, popular ~diseñar~ (“to design, sketch”). English has ~designate~ and ~design~ from the same verb, French ~désigner~, and Italian ~designare~.

The core image is marking something out — and from “marking” the verb reached “to point to” and then “to appoint or name to a post,” the modern sense. ~signum~ seeded an unusually rich Spanish family: ~signo~, ~señal~, ~seña~, ~señalar~, ~asignar~, ~consignar~, ~insignia~, and the doublet pair ~designar~/~diseñar~. The prettiest surprise is ~enseñar~ (“to teach”), from Late Latin ~īnsignāre~ (“to mark in, imprint”) — teaching imagined as pressing a sign into the mind.
en.despedir:
From Latin ~expetere~ (“to demand, long for, strive after”), from ~ex-~ (“out”) + ~petere~ (“to seek, ask, aim at”), from Proto-Indo-European *~peth₂-~ (“to fly, rush”). Vulgar Latin doubled the prefix into *~deexpetere~ (~de-~ + ~expetere~), which Spanish reduced to ~despedir~; the simple ~petere~ gave Spanish ~pedir~ (“to ask”). Cognate with Portuguese ~despedir~.

The semantic path is striking. From ~petere~'s idea of “rushing toward” a thing — the same root that, through *~peth₂-~, gave ~penna~ (“feather”) and Greek ~pterón~ (“wing”) — ~expetere~ meant to reach out for something forcefully, and Spanish ~despedir~ turned the aim outward: to send off, dismiss, emit. So one ~despide~ a departing friend (a farewell, ~despedida~), ~despide~ a worker (a firing), and a lamp ~despide~ light. From ~petere~'s family Spanish also drew ~petición~, ~competir~, ~apetito~ and ~ímpetu~; English relatives include ~petition~, ~appetite~ and ~compete~.
en.despertar:
From Old Spanish ~espertar~, from Vulgar Latin *~expertāre~, from Latin ~experrēctus~ (“awakened”), the past participle of ~expergīscī~ (“to wake up, to rouse oneself”). The deeper make-up of that Latin verb is debated: it is often analyzed as ~ex-~ (“out”) plus ~per-~ plus a base tied to ~regere~ (“to direct”), but the reconstruction is uncertain and best left open. Cognate with Portuguese and Catalan ~despertar~.

The everyday Spanish form shows a prefix swap. Latin ~ex-~ gave Old Spanish ~espertar~, but the initial syllable was later reshaped to ~des-~, yielding modern ~despertar~ — a change of dress, not of sense, since the verb has meant “to wake” throughout. From it come the adjective ~despierto~ (“awake, alert”) and ~despertador~, the “awakener” that is the alarm clock. The tangled Latin ancestry is a caution worth stating plainly: the meaning “to wake” is secure, while the precise Indo-European root beneath ~expergīscī~ remains, honestly, unsettled.
en.desplazar:
A relative newcomer, ~desplazar~ was formed on the model of (or borrowed from) French ~déplacer~ — ~dé-~ (“away”) plus ~place~ — and built in Spanish from ~des-~ and ~plaza~ (“square, open space”). ~Plaza~ comes from Vulgar Latin *~plattea~, from Latin ~platea~ (“broad street, courtyard”), itself from Ancient Greek ~plateîa~ (“broad [way]”), the feminine of ~platýs~ (“broad, flat”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~pleth₂-~ (“to spread out, be flat”). The same ~platea~ surfaces as Italian ~piazza~, French ~place~, and — through Old French — English ~place~.

The Greek ancestor ~platýs~ means simply “flat, broad,” so a ~plaza~ was at heart a “broad place” — and Spanish ~desplazar~ literally means to move something out of its place: to displace, shift, oust. The reflexive ~desplazarse~ became the ordinary way to say “to get around, to travel from place to place,” and the noun ~desplazamiento~ means “displacement, movement” (including a ship’s tonnage). Through the same PIE root of flatness, ~platýs~ is a distant relative of the Germanic-derived English ~flat~; nearer to home, Spanish keeps ~plaza~, ~plano~, ~plancha~, and ~plato~.
en.desplegar:
From Latin ~displicāre~ (“to unfold, unroll”), from ~dis-~ (“apart”) plus ~plicāre~ (“to fold”), from Proto-Indo-European *~plek-~ (“to plait, fold”). Cognate with French ~déployer~ and Portuguese ~despregar~; through the same Latin verb English received the doublets ~display~ and ~deploy~.

~plicāre~ meant literally “to fold,” so ~displicāre~ was “to unfold” — to open out what had been folded up. From spreading cloth or a scroll the sense widened to spreading troops across a field (military deployment) and, figuratively, to unfolding one's energy or skill. The same root *~plek-~ gave a broad Spanish family: ~plegar~ (“to fold”), ~plegaria~ (“prayer,” once a folded petition), ~pliegue~ (“fold, crease”), and — through compounds of ~plicāre~ — ~aplicar~, ~replicar~, ~complicar~, and ~emplear~ (from ~implicāre~).
en.desprender:
From ~des-~ (“un-, apart,” Latin ~dis-~) plus ~prender~ (“to grasp, fasten, seize”), from Latin ~pre(he)ndere~ (“to grasp, take hold of”). That verb is ~prae-~ (“before”) plus an old ~-hendere~ (“to seize”), from Proto-Indo-European *~gʰend-~ (“to seize, take”). Cognate through that root with English ~get~ and ~forget~, and through Latin with French ~prendre~ and English ~prehensile~ and ~apprehend~.

If ~prender~ is to catch or fasten, ~desprender~ is its undoing — to unfasten, detach, or let loose, and reflexively ~desprenderse~ (“to come away; to part with; to follow, be inferred”). Latin ~pre(he)ndere~ seeded an unusually large Spanish clan: ~prender~, ~prenda~ (“a garment; a pledge,” something grasped as security), ~presa~ (“prey; a dam”), ~prisión~ (“prison,” a seizing), and the ~-prender~ / ~-prehender~ compounds ~aprender~ (“to learn,” to grasp mentally), ~comprender~, ~emprender~, and ~sorprender~. Even ~prensa~ (“press; the press”) belongs here — all of them, at root, acts of taking hold.
en.destacar:
A comparatively late loan: Spanish took ~destacar~ from French ~détacher~ (“to detach”), from Old French ~destachier~, the negative counterpart of ~atachier~ (“to attach”). French itself leaned on Italian ~staccare~ / ~distaccare~ (“to separate”), the antonym of ~attaccare~ (“to attach, join battle”). At the base lies a Germanic (Frankish) *~stakka~ (“stake, post”), the same source that gave Spanish ~estaca~ (“stake”). It entered Spanish dictionaries around 1705, cognate with English ~detach~.

The oldest sense was military: to ~destacar~ was to detach a body of troops from the main force. From “separate a part from the whole” grew the figurative “stand out, be conspicuous” — that which is set apart draws the eye. The very pair survives elsewhere in Spanish: ~atacar~ (“to attack”), taken from the ~attaccare~ side of the same Italian opposition, once meant “to join, engage.” Modern relatives include ~destacamento~ (“military detachment”), ~destacado~ (“prominent, outstanding”) and the shared ~estaca~.
en.destinar:
From Latin ~dēstināre~ (“to make fast, fix, determine, resolve”), a compound of the intensive prefix ~dē-~ and a verbal stem *~stanāre~ built on ~stāre~ (“to stand”). That stem descends from Proto-Indo-European *~steh₂-~ (“to stand, stand firm”) — the very root behind Spanish ~estar~. So to “destine” something was, at root, to make it stand fixed. The root’s cognates are everywhere: English ~stand~ and ~stay~, German ~stehen~, Greek ~hístēmi~ (“to make stand”). The learned Romance descendants include Italian ~destinare~, French ~destiner~ and Portuguese ~destinar~.

The image is of fixing something firmly in place — and from there the meaning slid toward fixing a purpose or endpoint. To ~destinar~ is to set something aside for a fixed use or send it toward a fixed goal; the past participle gave the noun ~destino~ (“destination; destiny, fate” — the fixed end toward which one stands bound). The same root *~steh₂-~ seeded an enormous Spanish family: ~estar~, ~estación~, ~estable~, ~estatua~, ~constante~, ~obstinado~ (“obstinate,” standing firm against) and ~destino~ itself. Curiously, ~obstinarse~ (“to be obstinate”) shares the exact ~-stinare~ stem — to stand fixed, but in stubbornness rather than fate.
en.destruir:
From Latin ~dēstruere~ (“to tear down, demolish”), from ~dē-~ (“down, un-”) and ~struere~ (“to pile up, build”), from Proto-Indo-European *~strew-~ (“to spread, strew”). Through Old Spanish ~destruir~ it is cognate with Italian ~distruggere~ and French ~détruire~, and — via the same ~struere~ — with English ~structure~, ~construct~ and, borrowed through Old French ~destruire~, ~destroy~.

Where ~struere~ meant to build by heaping things up, the prefix ~dē-~ reversed it: to unbuild, to pull a pile apart. The PIE root *~strew-~ (“to spread”) also underlies English ~strew~ and ~street~ (a “strewn,” paved way). In Spanish the same family gives ~construir~, ~instruir~, ~estructura~ and ~destrucción~.
en.detallar:
A borrowing from French ~détailler~ (“to cut up, sell at retail”), formed from ~dé-~ plus ~tailler~ (“to cut”), from Vulgar Latin *~tāliāre~ (“to cut, split”), from Latin ~tālea~ (“a cutting, rod, twig”). Spanish took the noun ~detalle~ from French ~détail~ at the same time. The French verb ~tailler~ also gave English ~tailor~ (one who cuts cloth) and ~entail~, while ~detail~ itself entered English from the same French source; Italian has the parallel ~dettagliare~.

The image at the root is concrete: ~tālea~ was a twig or slip cut for grafting, so “to detail” is literally to reduce a whole into small cut pieces — the retailer’s sense of selling in fractions and the descriptive sense of itemizing point by point are the same metaphor. Modern ~detallar~ means “to specify, itemize,” and ~detalle~ ranges from “a detail” to “a thoughtful gesture.” A ~detallista~ is both a retailer and a person attentive to little things. The native Spanish reflex of *~tāliāre~ survives separately as ~tajar~ (“to slice”) and the noun ~tajo~ (“a cut, gash”), the popular doublet of the learned, French-clothed ~detallar~.
en.detectar:
From Latin ~dētēctus~, the past participle of ~dētegere~ (“to uncover, lay bare”), formed from ~dē-~ (“off, away”) plus ~tegere~ (“to cover”), from Proto-Indo-European *~(s)teg-~ (“to cover”). Through that root it is cognate with English ~thatch~ and ~toga~ (a garment that “covers”), and with Portuguese ~detectar~ and French ~détecter~, the shared learned borrowing the Romance languages took from the same Latin stem.

To detect was, at heart, to un-cover — to strip away whatever conceals. Latin ~tegere~ founded a broad family: the roofing tile ~tēgula~ descended to Spanish ~teja~ and, with it, ~tejado~ and ~techo~ (“roof”), the very things that cover a house. The learned prefixed verbs surface in ~proteger~ (“to protect,” literally to cover in front of) and in the anatomical ~tegumento~ (“integument, covering skin”). ~Detectar~ itself entered Spanish late, as a technical term, keeping the crisp Latin logic that to detect a thing is to pull the cover off it.
en.detener:
From ~de-~ (“away, down”) joined to ~tener~, which comes from Latin ~tenēre~ (“to hold, keep”); the Latin verb rests on Proto-Indo-European *~ten-~ (“to stretch”), holding being understood as keeping something taut. It is cognate with Italian ~tenere~, French ~tenir~ and Portuguese ~ter~, and — through the same root — with English ~tenant~, ~tenure~ and ~contain~.

Latin ~dētinēre~ meant “to hold back, keep back,” and Spanish ~detener~ inherited exactly that: to stop something in its course, and by a natural step to arrest — which is why a person taken into custody is a ~detenido~. The reflexive ~detenerse~ softened to “to pause, to linger over.” The “hold” family is one of Spanish's densest — ~tener~, ~contener~, ~mantener~, ~obtener~, ~sostener~ and ~retener~ — while the underlying “stretch” sense surfaces in relatives like ~tenso~ and ~tienda~, a “tent” of stretched cloth.
en.determinar:
Spanish ~determinar~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~dētermināre~ (“to set bounds, mark off”), a compound of ~dē-~ (here intensive) and ~termināre~ (“to limit”), a verb on the noun ~terminus~ (“boundary, limit”). ~terminus~ descends from Proto-Italic *~termnos~ and Proto-Indo-European *~térmn̥~ (“boundary marker”), cognate with Ancient Greek ~τέρμα~ (térma, “goal, turning-post”) and ~τέρμων~ (térmōn, “border”). English took the same Latin word as ~determine~; ~term~ and ~terminal~ share the root.

The metaphor at the heart of the verb is spatial: to ~determinar~ is to draw a line around something, and by fixing its edges to fix what it is — hence the senses “to establish,” “to decide,” and “to cause.” The boundary was no small matter to the Romans: ~Terminus~ was a god, the deity of boundary stones, whose markers were sacred and whose festival, the ~Terminalia~, was kept each February. From the same root Spanish inherited ~término~ (“term, end”), ~terminar~ (“to finish”), ~terminal~, ~exterminar~, ~interminable~, and ~determinación~. To determine something, then, is to give it a ~terminus~ — an end that defines its beginning.
en.devolver:
From Latin ~dēvolvere~ (“to roll down, roll off”), a compound of ~dē-~ (“down, away, back”) and ~volvere~ (“to roll, turn, wind”). ~volvere~ comes from Proto-Italic *~welwō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~welH-~ (“to turn, to wind, to roll”) — the same root behind English ~wallow~ and Ancient Greek ~helíssō~ (“to turn round”) and ~hélix~. From ~dēvolvere~ descend Spanish ~devolver~ and Portuguese ~devolver~; from plain ~volvere~, Italian ~volgere~.

Latin ~dēvolvere~ was purely physical — to send something rolling downhill — but Spanish spun the “back” sense of ~dē-~ into the abstract idea of returning, giving back, sending back. A wonderful relative is ~volumen~: a Roman ~volūmen~ was a papyrus scroll, a thing literally rolled up, and only later did it come to mean a book’s bulk or a “volume” of sound. The ~volvere~ family is large in Spanish — ~volver~, ~revolver~, ~envolver~, ~volcar~, ~voluble~, ~revuelta~ — and even the pistol name ~revólver~ came into Spanish from English, where it was coined, at bottom, from the same rolling root.
en.diagnosticar:
A modern verb formed on the noun ~diagnóstico~ (“diagnosis”), from Greek ~diagnōstikós~ (“able to distinguish”), from ~diagignṓskein~ (“to distinguish, discern”): ~diá~ (“apart, through”) + ~gignṓskein~ (“to know, recognize”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ǵneh₃-~ (“to know”). The root is one of the great international ones: it gave Latin ~gnōscere~/~nōscere~ (whence Spanish ~conocer~), Greek ~gnôsis~, and, in Germanic, English ~know~ and ~can~.

In Greek medicine ~diágnōsis~ already meant “a distinguishing, a telling apart,” exactly a physician’s task; Spanish ~diagnosticar~ carries that literal sense — to know one condition apart from another. The word is now used well beyond medicine, of engines and economies alike. From the same PIE root *~ǵneh₃-~ Spanish holds a large family: ~conocer~, ~noción~, ~pronóstico~, ~ignorar~, ~reconocer~ and ~gnóstico~, all turning on knowing and recognizing.
en.dibujar:
By the usual account, from Old French ~deboissier~ (also ~desboissier~, “to carve or work in wood; to depict”), a derivative of ~bois~ (“wood,” from Frankish *~busk~). The origin is disputed: the sense is clear, but the sound-changes leading to Old Spanish ~debuxar~ and then modern ~dibujar~ are irregular, so etymologists mark the wood-carving etymon as probable rather than certain. Portuguese ~debuxar~ and Catalan ~dibuixar~ show the same descent; Italian, by contrast, uses ~disegnare~, from Latin ~designare~, an unrelated root.

If the etymology holds, the meaning traveled from cutting a figure into wood, through “to sketch or depict,” to plain “to draw” with pen or pencil — the wooden material fell away and left only the line. It is a nice irony that French itself abandoned ~deboissier~ and now says ~dessiner~ (also from ~designare~), so Spanish preserves, in ~dibujar~, a French verb the French no longer use. From it Spanish forms ~dibujo~ (“drawing”) and ~dibujante~ (“draughtsman”).
en.dictar:
~dictar~ comes from Latin ~dictāre~ (“to say over and over, dictate, compose”), the frequentative of ~dīcere~ (“to say, tell”). ~dīcere~ derives from Proto-Italic *~deikō~, from the Proto-Indo-European root *~deyḱ-~ (“to show, point out”) — the same root, with meaning shifted from showing to saying, that gave Ancient Greek ~deíknumi~ (“I show”), English ~teach~ and ~token~, and German ~zeigen~ (“to show”). From ~dictāre~ directly come Italian ~dettare~, French ~dicter~, and English ~dictate~.

The frequentative force of ~dictāre~ — “to say again and again” — fits both senses Spanish keeps: to ~dictar~ a letter (speaking so another writes it down) and to ~dictar~ a law or sentence (pronouncing it with authority). A ~dictador~ was originally a Roman magistrate granted emergency power to “pronounce”; only later did the word darken. The same ~dīcere~ underlies a huge family: ~decir~, ~dicho~, ~contradecir~, ~predecir~, ~dictamen~, ~diccionario~, and ~índice~.
en.diferenciar:
Spanish ~diferenciar~ is drawn from ~diferencia~, from Latin ~differentia~, a noun on ~differēns~, the present participle of ~differre~ (“to carry apart, to differ”), from ~dis-~ (“apart”) and ~ferre~ (“to carry, to bear”). ~Ferre~ continues Proto-Indo-European *~bʰer-~ (“to carry, to bear”), one of the most widely attested of all Indo-European verbs — cognate with Greek ~phérein~, with English ~bear~, and, through Latin, with ~transfer~ and ~refer~.

Latin ~differre~ carried two senses at once: literally “to bear in different directions,” hence “to scatter, to postpone,” and figuratively “to be unlike.” Spanish parcelled them out — ~diferir~ keeps “to defer” and “to differ,” while ~diferenciar~ specializes as “to distinguish, to tell apart.” The ~ferre~ family is vast: ~referir~, ~transferir~, ~conferir~, ~preferir~ and ~fértil~, plus ~ofrecer~ and its noun ~oferta~. The ancient root *~bʰer-~ is so basic that a form of it survives in nearly every branch of the family, from Sanskrit to Slavic to Germanic.
en.difundir:
From Latin ~diffundere~ (“to pour out, spread abroad”), a compound of ~dis-~ (“apart, in different directions”) and ~fundere~ (“to pour, melt”), from Proto-Italic *~fundō~ and the Proto-Indo-European root *~ǵʰewd-~ (“to pour”). That root is unusually well-travelled: through Latin it also surfaces in English ~confound~ and ~refund~, and its Germanic branch gave English ~found~ (in the metal-casting sense) and ~gush~. Sister descendants of the same verb include French ~diffuser~ and Portuguese ~difundir~.

The image is liquid: to ~diffundere~ was to pour something out so it ran in every direction, scattering and spreading. Latin quickly applied it to non-liquids — light, warmth, rumour — that radiate outward from a source, and Spanish ~difundir~ inherited exactly this: to spread, disseminate, broadcast (news, ideas, a radio signal). The past participle ~diffūsus~ gave the adjective ~difuso~ (“diffuse, hazy”) and the noun ~difusión~ (“broadcasting, diffusion”). From the same ~fundere~ Spanish also drew ~fundir~ (“to melt, cast”), ~fundición~ (“foundry, smelting”), ~confundir~, and ~infundir~.
en.dirigir:
Spanish ~dirigir~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~dīrigere~ (“to set straight, guide, direct”), a compound of ~dis-~ (“apart, asunder”) and ~regere~ (“to keep straight, rule, guide”). ~regere~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~h₃reǵ-~ (“to straighten, direct, rule”), one of the most productive of all roots, cognate with Latin ~rēx~ (“king”), Sanskrit ~rājan~ (“king”), German ~recht~ (“right”), and English ~right~ itself. French ~diriger~ and Italian ~dirigere~ are the Romance parallels.

The literal image is a straight line: to ~dirigir~ is to make something go straight toward a target — hence “to aim,” “to guide,” “to address (a letter),” and “to conduct or manage” an orchestra, a company, a film. Its popularly inherited cousin ~aderezar~ (“to season, to garnish, to set right”), worn smooth by ordinary transmission from the same Latin stock, stands beside the bookish, near-intact ~dirigir~. From ~regere~ and its root Spanish drew a rich harvest: ~regir~ (“to govern”), ~dirección~, ~director~, ~corregir~ (“to correct,” literally “to set right again”), ~erigir~, ~recto~ (“straight”), ~regla~ (“rule”), ~región~, and — presiding over them all — ~rey~ (“king”).
en.discutir:
From Latin ~discutere~ (“to shake apart, dash to pieces”), a compound of ~dis-~ (“apart”) and ~quatere~ (“to shake, strike”), from Proto-Indo-European *~kʷeh₁t-~ (“to shake”). Cognate through ~quatere~ with English ~quash~ and, via the participle ~quassus~, with ~concussion~ and ~percussion~. The Latin verb itself descends into Italian ~discutere~, French ~discuter~, and Portuguese ~discutir~.

The literal Latin sense was violent: ~discutere~ meant to strike something so hard it flew to pieces. Roman writers then stretched it metaphorically: to “shatter” a question was to break it open and examine every fragment, and from that courtroom-and-lecture-hall usage came the modern “to discuss, debate.” Spanish kept both the reasoned sense and the heat, so ~discutir~ today spans calm “to discuss” and sharp “to argue.” From the same ~quatere~ came a very physical Spanish verb, ~sacudir~ (“to shake”), out of Latin ~succutere~, plus ~percutir~, ~repercutir~, and the noun ~discusión~.
en.diseñar:
A Renaissance borrowing from Italian ~disegnare~ (“to draw, to design”), which itself continues Latin ~dēsignāre~ (“to mark out, trace, designate”), a compound of ~dē-~ (“out, down”) and ~signāre~ (“to mark”), from the noun ~signum~ (“sign, mark”). It is cognate with French ~dessiner~ and English ~design~, and — from the same Latin verb by a learned path — with Spanish's own ~designar~.

Here lies a neat doublet. Latin ~dēsignāre~ reached Spanish twice: once directly from Latin as the learned ~designar~ (“to appoint, designate”), and once through Italian, where ~disegnare~ had narrowed to the artist's act of “drawing, laying out a design” — that borrowing became ~diseñar~, with the noun ~diseño~. So a single Latin verb split into “to designate” and “to design.” The base ~signum~ radiates through Spanish in ~signo~, ~señal~, ~seña~, ~insignia~ and even ~enseñar~ (“to teach”), literally to “mark out” something for a learner.
en.disfrutar:
Spanish ~disfrutar~ was formed within Spanish itself from the prefix ~dis-~ and ~fruto~ (“fruit, produce”), with the verbal ending ~-ar~. ~fruto~ comes from Latin ~frūctus~ (“fruit, produce, profit”), the past participle of the deponent verb ~fruī~ (“to enjoy, have the use of”). That verb goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~bʰruHg-~ (“to make use of, enjoy”). The root surfaces widely: Latin ~frūx~ (“crop, fruit”) gave ~frūgālis~, source of English ~frugal~; and through the Germanic branch it yielded English ~brook~ (the verb “to tolerate, put up with,” originally “to make use of, enjoy”) and German ~brauchen~ (“to need, use”). French ~fruit~ and Portuguese ~fruto~ / ~desfrutar~ are close Romance kin.

The metaphor is agricultural: to ~disfrutar~ something was first to draw the fruits or profit from it — to reap the yield of an estate — and only afterward to enjoy it in the modern sense of taking pleasure. Old legal Spanish kept the concrete meaning of usufruct, the right to gather another’s produce, and the doublet ~usufructo~ still names it in law. Today ~disfrutar de la vida~ (“to enjoy life”) has fully abstracted the harvest into pleasure. From the same ~fruto~ family Spanish holds ~fruta~, ~fructífero~ (“fruitful”), ~usufructo~, and ~frugal~; the learned ~fruición~ (“keen enjoyment”) comes straight from ~fruī~’s participle ~fruitus~.
en.disminuir:
From Latin ~dēminuere~ (“to lessen, to make smaller”), from ~dē-~ (here intensive, “completely”) and ~minuere~ (“to make small, to diminish”), a verb from ~minus~ (“less”). All of this rests on the Proto-Indo-European root *~mey-~ (“small, few”). The Spanish form was reshaped under the influence of the prefix ~dis-~, giving ~disminuir~; it is attested from the early fifteenth century. It is cognate with Italian ~diminuire~, French ~diminuer~, Portuguese ~diminuir~, and English ~diminish~, and — through ~minus~ — with English ~minus~, ~minor~, and ~minute~.

The root *~mey-~ is the great Indo-European word for smallness, and the Latin verb ~minuere~ meant to make something less — to chip away at a quantity. Spanish ~disminuir~ carries exactly that: to reduce, to lessen, to make or grow smaller in number, size, or intensity. A curious point of morphology is the prefix swap — Latin's ~dē-~ was replaced by ~dis-~ in the Spanish outcome — so the standard word today wears a prefix its Latin ancestor did not. From the same ~minus~ / *~mey-~ family Spanish drew a crowd of words: ~menos~, ~menor~, ~mínimo~, ~minuto~, ~menudo~, ~menguar~, ~ministro~, and ~disminución~.
en.disparar:
From Latin ~disparāre~ (“to separate, set apart”), a compound of ~dis-~ (“apart”) and ~parāre~ (“to prepare, make ready”), whose root is the Proto-Indo-European *~per-~ (“to produce, procure”) that also underlies ~parere~ (“to give birth”). Spanish ~disparar~ keeps company with Portuguese ~disparar~ and Italian ~sparare~ (“to shoot”); through ~parāre~ it is kin to Spanish ~parar~ and, in English, to ~prepare~ and ~repair~.

The leap from “separate” to “fire a weapon” runs through the crossbow. A loaded bow was a thing made ready — ~parado~, prepared — held under tension; to ~disparar~ it was to “un-ready” it, releasing the string so the bolt flew. From that release the modern senses of firing, shooting and bolting away all grew. The same verb produced a delightful side-branch: ~disparate~ (“nonsense, an absurdity”), literally something loosed off at random, out of all order. Sharing the ancestral ~parāre~ are ~preparar~, ~separar~, ~reparar~ and the noun ~aparato~.
en.disponer:
Spanish ~disponer~ continues Latin ~dispōnere~ (“to arrange, set in order, distribute”), a compound of ~dis-~ (“apart, in different directions”) and ~pōnere~ (“to place, put”). ~pōnere~ is itself contracted from an older ~po-~ (a by-form of the prefix meaning “away”) plus ~sinere~ (“to let, leave”), so its literal weight is “to set down, put in place.” The Romance cognates are exact — Italian ~disporre~, French ~disposer~, Portuguese ~dispor~ — and English ~dispose~ arrived through Old French.

The prefix ~dis-~ paints the picture: to ~disponer~ is to place things about, each in its own spot — hence “to arrange” and, from having things arranged and ready, “to have at one’s disposal.” The reflexive ~disponerse a~ means to get ready to do something. ~pōnere~ is one of the great Latin verb-factories, and Spanish reflects it everywhere: ~poner~ (“to put”), ~componer~, ~exponer~, ~proponer~, ~suponer~, ~posición~, ~puesto~, and the derived noun ~disposición~ (“arrangement, disposal, willingness”). The adjective ~disponible~ (“available”) carries the same idea — something set out and ready to hand.
en.disputar:
From Latin ~disputāre~ (“to weigh, examine, argue”), a compound of ~dis-~ (“apart, in different directions”) and ~putāre~ (“to reckon, to think” — earlier “to prune, clean”). ~Putāre~ is generally traced to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning “to cut, strike,” though its deeper history is debated. The Latin verb descends into Italian ~disputare~, French ~disputer~, and Portuguese ~disputar~, and English borrowed it as ~dispute~.

The buried metaphor in ~putāre~ is a gardener’s. It first meant to prune a vine — cutting away the dead wood so a clean reckoning of the plant remained — and from there “to settle an account, to reckon, to think.” Prefix it with ~dis-~ and you get accounts reckoned from opposing sides, hence “to argue.” Spanish ~disputar~ ranges from formal “to debate” to competitive “to contend for” a title or a match. The same ~putāre~ seeded a whole thicket of words: ~computar~ and its popular doublet ~contar~ (“to count; to tell”), ~amputar~ (literally “to prune away”), ~imputar~, ~reputar~, and ~diputado~ (“deputy” — one reckoned to stand for others).
en.distinguir:
From Latin ~distinguere~ (“to separate, to mark off, to distinguish”), from ~dis-~ (“apart”) plus ~stinguere~. The traditional account reads ~stinguere~ as “to prick,” from Proto-Indo-European *~steyg-~ (“to be pointed, to prick”) — so distinguishing is “separating by pricking or marking.” Cognate on that reading with English ~sting~ and ~stick~, and with Greek ~stízō~ (“to tattoo, to prick”), source of ~stigma~. Spanish shares it with English ~distinguish~ and ~distinct~.

Here the vivid image is also the disputed one, and it should be flagged: the “separate by pricking” story — punctuation once pricked into parchment — is attractive but not certain. De Vaan instead derives this ~stinguere~ from a root meaning “to push, to thrust,” which would make ~distinguere~ literally “to push apart” and neatly separate it from ~extinguir~ (“to quench”), long grouped with it. Either way the Spanish sense settled on “to tell apart, to discern.” The family includes ~distinto~, ~distinción~ and ~distintivo~, plus the ~steyg-~ relatives ~instigar~, ~estímulo~ and ~estigma~.
en.distribuir:
From Latin ~distribuere~ (“to divide, deal out”), from ~dis-~ (“apart, individually”) + ~tribuere~ (“to allot, assign”), itself from ~tribus~ (“tribe, division of the people”). The origin of ~tribus~ is uncertain: it is often connected to ~trēs~ (“three”), as if an original threefold partition of the Roman people, but the derivation is disputed. Cognate with Italian ~distribuire~, French ~distribuer~ and Portuguese ~distribuir~.

To ~tribuere~ was to allot something “to the tribes,” so distribution began as an act of civic division. English took the whole cluster from the same ~tribuere~: ~tribute~ (what is paid out), ~attribute~, ~contribute~ and ~distribute~. Spanish keeps ~tribu~, ~tributo~, ~atribuir~, ~contribuir~ and ~retribuir~.
en.divertir:
From Latin ~dīvertere~ (“to turn aside, go separate ways”), from ~dī-~ (a form of ~dis-~, “apart”) plus ~vertere~ (“to turn”), from Proto-Indo-European *~wert-~ (“to turn, rotate”). Cognate with Italian ~divertire~, French ~divertir~, Portuguese ~divertir~, and English ~divert~ and ~diversion~; the root also gives English ~-ward~ and German ~werden~ (“to become”).

English and Spanish took the same “turning aside” in different directions. English ~divert~ stayed close to the literal — to turn something off its course. Spanish ~divertir~ turned inward and pleasant: to turn the mind aside from its cares, hence “to amuse, entertain.” From the shared ~vertere~ Spanish keeps a great wheeling family: ~verter~ (“to pour”), ~verso~ (“verse,” a turning of the line), ~versión~, ~convertir~, ~adverso~, ~universo~ (“turned into one”), and ~aniversario~ (“a turning of the year”).
en.dividir:
From Latin ~dīvidere~ (“to force apart, to divide”), from ~dis-~ (“apart”) and a distinct verbal root *~-videre~ (“to separate”) — not, despite appearances, the ~vidēre~ that means “to see.” The separating root goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~h₁weydʰ-~ (“to divide”), the very root that also produced Latin ~vidua~ and thus, through Germanic, English ~widow~ — a person “separated” from a spouse. Cognates include English ~divide~ and French ~diviser~.

The image beneath ~dīvidere~ is forcible separation, and Spanish keeps that edge in ~dividir~. Its most philosophical descendant is ~individuo~ (“individual”), from Latin ~indīviduus~ (“undivided, indivisible”) — the individual being, literally, that which cannot be split further. From the same source come ~división~, ~dividendo~, ~divisor~, and ~divisa~ (a “device” or emblem, and later a “currency”), all turning on the idea of a whole parcelled into shares.
en.doler:
From Latin ~dolēre~ (“to feel pain; to grieve”), from Proto-Italic *~doleō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~delh₁-~ (“to split, to cut”) — the meaning presumably moving from “be cut/split” to “hurt,” a bridge that is inferred rather than documented. The Latin verb was also linked to ~dolāre~ (“to hew, chop”). Cognates: Italian ~dolere~, Portuguese ~doer~ and Old French ~douloir~.

~Dolēre~ covered both bodily pain and grief, and Spanish ~doler~ keeps both — a tooth ~duele~, and one may ~dolerse~ (“to grieve, regret”). The noun ~dolor~ yielded ~doloroso~, ~dolencia~, ~doliente~, ~condolencia~ and ~indolente~ (literally “feeling no pain”); and ~duelo~ in the sense “mourning” descends from ~dolēre~ — distinct from its homonym ~duelo~ (“duel”), which comes from Latin ~duellum~. If the *~delh₁-~ etymology holds, ~doler~ is a distant kin of words for cutting and splitting — an apt image for pain.
en.dominar:
From Latin ~domināri~ (“to be lord, to rule”), from ~dominus~ (“lord, master”), literally “the man of the house,” from ~domus~ (“house, home”), from Proto-Indo-European *~dem-~ (“to build; household”), beside the noun *~dṓm~ (“house”). From ~dominus~ Spanish inherited ~dueño~ (“owner”) and the titles ~don~ and ~doña~; Portuguese has ~dono~ and Italian ~donno~. English carries the learned ~dominate~ and ~dominion~, and — startlingly — ~danger~, through Vulgar Latin *~dominiārium~ (“a lord’s power”).

The whole word rests on the Roman house: the ~dominus~ was the master of the ~domus~, and his power, ~dominium~, spread outward from the household to the estate, the province, the world. The most charming descendant is ~domingo~ (“Sunday”), from ~diēs dominica~, “the Lord’s day” — because ~dominus~ became a title for God. Around it cluster ~dominio~, ~dominante~, ~dominical~, ~domicilio~, and ~doméstico~, along with the courteous ~don~ and ~doña~ — every one of them still, at heart, about who runs the house.
en.dorar:
From Latin ~deaurāre~ (“to gild, cover with gold”), from ~de-~ (here intensive) plus a verb on ~aurum~ (“gold”). Latin ~aurum~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~auzom~ and to the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₂ews-~ (“to shine, to dawn”) — the same root behind ~aurōra~ (“dawn”) and, in the Germanic branch, behind English ~east~ and ~Easter~, the direction and festival of the rising light. Cognate on the Romance side with Italian ~oro~ and French ~or~.

Gold was named for its glow, and so ~dorar~ first meant to sheathe a thing in gold leaf; only later did cooks borrow it for browning food to a golden crust. The Spanish idiom ~dorar~ la píldora (“to gild the pill,” to sweeten bad news) keeps the older, literal sense alive. From ~aurum~ Spanish also draws ~oro~ itself, ~dorado~ (“golden, gilded”), ~orfebre~ (“goldsmith”), and ~oropel~ (“tinsel, showy glitter”) — a whole vocabulary of shine radiating from one word for the dawn.
en.dormir:
From Latin ~dormīre~ (“to sleep”), from Proto-Italic *~dormiō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~drem-~ (“to sleep”). The Romance sisters kept it almost untouched: Italian ~dormire~, French ~dormir~, Portuguese ~dormir~. Outside Latin the root surfaces in Ancient Greek ~darthánō~ (“to sleep”), Sanskrit ~drāti~ (“he sleeps”), and Old Church Slavonic ~drěmati~ (“to doze”).

Latin already had the frequentative ~dormītāre~ (“to be drowsy, keep nodding off”), and from ~dormīre~ Spanish grew a rich bedtime vocabulary: ~dormitorio~ (“bedroom, dormitory”), ~durmiente~ (“sleeping” — as in ~La Bella Durmiente~, “Sleeping Beauty”), ~adormecer~ (“to lull to sleep, numb”), and ~dormitar~ (“to doze”). Notice the stem-vowel play Spanish keeps from the Latin conjugation: the ~o~ of ~dormir~ becomes ~ue~ when stressed (“duermo”) and ~u~ elsewhere (“durmió”), a living trace of how the verb was accented.
en.dotar:
From Latin ~dōtāre~ (“to endow, to provide with a dowry”), from ~dōs~ (genitive ~dōtis~, “dowry, gift”), a noun built on ~dāre~ (“to give”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~deh₃-~ (“to give”). It is cognate with French ~doter~ and, through the same root, with English ~donate~ and even ~dose~ (via Greek ~dósis~, “a giving, a portion”).

A dowry is “what is given” with a bride, and Spanish keeps that concrete sense in ~dote~ while ~dotar~ broadened to “to endow” in general — to furnish a school with books, or nature with a gift. The root *~deh₃-~ is one of the great givers of the lexicon: from it Spanish also has ~dar~, ~donar~, ~dádiva~ (“a gift”), ~dosis~, and — through Greek — ~anécdota~, literally “things not given out”, i.e. unpublished.
en.dudar:
From Old Spanish ~dubdar~, from Latin ~dubitāre~ (“to waver, to hesitate, to doubt”), a frequentative tied to ~dubius~ (“wavering, doubtful”), which goes back to ~duo~ (“two”), from Proto-Indo-European *~dwóh₁~ (“two”). To doubt is to be “of two minds.” Cognate with Italian ~dubitare~, French ~douter~ and Portuguese ~duvidar~; through ~duo~ it is kin to Spanish ~dos~ and to English ~two~, and English ~doubt~ is itself a borrowing of the same Latin verb by way of French.

At the heart of ~dudar~ lies the number two: to doubt is to hover between two possibilities, unable to come down on either side. Old Spanish still wrote the Latin ~b~ as ~dubdar~, which the language later smoothed away — just as ~dubda~ became ~duda~ and ~cibdad~ became ~ciudad~. English kept the opposite habit: the silent ~b~ in ~doubt~ was put back by Renaissance scholars to advertise its descent from ~dubitāre~, a fossil of the very letter Spanish threw out. From ~dubius~ Spanish also has ~duda~, ~dudoso~, ~indudable~ and the learned ~dubitativo~, and from ~duo~, the numeral ~dos~ and ~doble~.
en.durar:
From Latin ~dūrāre~ (“to last, harden”), from ~dūrus~ (“hard”), and from Proto-Italic *~dūros~. The deeper root is debated: by one account ~dūrus~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~dweh₂-~ (“long, far”) — making it kin to Ancient Greek ~dērós~ (“long-lasting”) and Sanskrit ~dūrá~ (“distant”) — while another derives it from *~deru-~ (“firm, solid”), the source of English ~tree~ and ~true~. Cognate with Italian ~durare~, French ~durer~ and Portuguese ~durar~.

Latin ~dūrāre~ meant both “to harden” and “to hold out, last,” and Spanish kept the durative sense while physical hardness stayed with the adjective ~duro~. English borrowed the same family as ~durable~, ~during~ (originally “while something lasts”) and ~endure~. From the same Latin stock Spanish also draws ~duración~, ~durante~, ~endurecer~ and ~perdurar~.
en.echar:
From Latin ~iactāre~ (“to throw repeatedly, to toss about”), the frequentative of ~iacere~ (“to throw, to cast”). The root reaches back to the Proto-Indo-European *~(H)yeh₁-~ (“to throw, to let go”). ~iactāre~ also produced Italian ~gettare~ and French ~jeter~, and through French it seeded English ~jet~, ~jetsam~, and ~jettison~; the participial stem ~-ject-~ of ~iacere~ underlies English ~eject~, ~inject~, ~project~, and ~reject~.

Few Spanish verbs travel further from their spelling: ~iactāre~ lost its ~j~-sound and its ~-ct-~ cluster to become ~echar~, one of the language’s most protean verbs — to throw, pour, put, emit, sprout, or dismiss. It anchors countless idioms: ~echar de menos~ (“to miss”), ~echar a correr~ (“to break into a run”), ~echar una mano~ (“to lend a hand”). The learned ~-ject-~ stem re-entered Spanish in ~sujeto~, ~objeto~, ~proyecto~, ~inyectar~, and ~trayecto~. And the stative twin of ~iacere~ — Latin ~iacēre~ (“to lie down”) — gave Spanish ~yacer~, so that the verb for throwing and the verb for lying at rest are, in the end, cousins.
en.editar:
A learned borrowing from Latin ~editus~, past participle of ~ēdere~ (“to put forth, to give out, to publish”), a compound of ~ē-~ / ~ex-~ (“out”) and ~dare~ (“to give”), and so from Proto-Indo-European *~deh₃-~ (“to give”). Spanish took the word in through French ~éditer~; English ~edit~ and ~edition~ share the same Latin source.

There is a neat trap here: Latin had two verbs spelled ~ēdere~. One, from ~dare~, meant “to give out, to bring forth, to publish”; the other, ~edere~ (“to eat”), came instead from Proto-Indo-European *~h₁ed-~ — the root of English ~eat~. Only the first gave ~editar~, which in Spanish first meant “to publish” (a book, a journal) and later, under English pressure, also “to edit.” Kin from the same “give” root include ~edición~, ~editor~, ~editorial~ and the everyday ~dar~, ~dato~ and ~donar~.
en.educar:
Spanish ~educar~ comes from Latin ~ēducāre~ (“to rear, bring up, train”), a first-conjugation verb built on ~ex-~ (“out”) and the family of ~dūcere~ (“to lead”) — the same base as the noun ~dux~ (“leader, guide”). Beneath it lie Proto-Italic *~doukō~ and the Proto-Indo-European root *~dewk-~ (“to pull, lead”). Through that root ~educar~ is kin to English ~duke~, ~conduct~ and ~educe~, to Spanish ~conducir~ and ~aducir~, and to Italian ~educare~ and French ~éduquer~. Latin kept two closely related verbs apart: ~ēducāre~, “to rear a child,” and the third-conjugation ~ēdūcere~, “to lead or draw out.”

In Rome ~ēducāre~ meant the daily work of raising and feeding a child, and only by extension the shaping of mind and character; from that rearing sense Spanish inherited today’s ~educar~. A popular idea holds that education is a “leading out” of the potential already within a pupil — a lovely image, but etymologically loose: it borrows the meaning of the sister verb ~ēdūcere~ (“to lead out”) and reads it into ~ēducāre~, whose own core sense was simply “to nourish and rear.” The shared root *~dewk-~ seeded a broad Spanish family: ~conducir~, ~producir~, ~reducir~, ~seducir~, ~traducir~ and the noun ~duque~ (“duke”), all turning on the idea of leading, drawing or guiding.
en.efectuar:
From Medieval Latin ~effectuāre~ (“to bring about, to carry out”), built on Latin ~effectus~, participle of ~efficere~ (“to accomplish, to bring to pass”), from ~ex-~ (“out, thoroughly”) + ~facere~ (“to do, to make”). ~facere~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to put, to place, to set”). Cognate with Italian ~effettuare~ and French ~effectuer~, and — through ~facere~ — with English ~effect~, ~effectuate~, and ~fact~.

The chain packs the meaning tightly: ~ex-~ (“out”) intensifies ~facere~ (“to make”), so ~efficere~ is to “make something come out” — to accomplish it fully — and its result-noun ~effectus~ is the “thing brought out,” the effect. ~efectuar~ therefore means to carry a plan through to its result, a shade more formal than hacer. The root *~dʰeh₁-~ is one of the most productive in Indo-European, underlying not only the huge Latin ~facere~ family but Greek ~títhēmi~ (“I place”) and English ~do~ and ~deed~. Spanish descendants of ~facere~ are everywhere: ~hacer~ (“to do, to make”), ~hecho~ (“fact, deed”), ~efecto~ (“effect”), ~eficaz~ (“effective”), ~defecto~, ~perfecto~, and ~fábrica~ (“factory”).
en.ejecutar:
From Latin ~exsequī~ / ~exsequor~ (“to follow out, carry through, pursue to the end”), from ~ex-~ (“out, thoroughly”) plus ~sequī~ (“to follow”), from Proto-Indo-European *~sekʷ-~ (“to follow”). Spanish ~ejecutar~ was formed on the participial stem ~exsecūtus~ (later ~exēcūtus~). The root ~sequī~ is one of the most prolific in the Romance languages, giving Spanish ~seguir~, Italian ~seguire~ and French ~suivre~; through it English gained ~sequence~, ~consequence~, ~prosecute~ and ~execute~ itself, and Ancient Greek ~ἕπομαι~ (~hépomai~, “to follow”) shows the same root outside Latin.

The evolution runs from “to follow through” to “to accomplish, carry out,” and Spanish ~ejecutar~ inherited the full spread: to execute a plan, to perform a piece of music (~ejecutar una sonata~), to run a computer program, and — chillingly — to put a condemned person to death. That grim sense arose because a sentence, once pronounced, was “followed out” upon the body of the offender. From the same participle come ~ejecución~, ~ejecutivo~ (“executive”) and ~ejecutor~; from the wider ~sequī~ family Spanish has ~seguir~, ~conseguir~ (“to obtain”), ~perseguir~ (“to pursue”), ~consecuencia~, ~secuencia~ and ~obsequio~ (“a gift,” originally a following-after in attendance).
en.ejercer:
From Latin ~exercēre~ (“to keep busy, train, drill, carry on”), a compound of ~ex-~ (“out”) and ~arcēre~ (“to keep off, shut in, confine”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂erk-~ (“to hold, contain, guard”) — the same root that gave Latin ~arca~ (“chest, box”). Cognate with Italian ~esercitare~, French ~exercer~ and Portuguese ~exercer~; English ~exercise~ was borrowed from the same verb through Old French.

The literal image is of driving animals or workers out of their enclosure to set them to work — hence “to keep busy, keep in motion, train.” In military Latin it meant to drill troops, and the past participle gave ~exercitus~, “a trained force,” the direct source of Spanish ~ejército~ (“army”). Spanish ~ejercer~ narrowed toward “to practice (a profession), exert (a right or authority),” while ~ejercitar~ kept the sense of training and physical exercise. From the same family come ~ejercicio~, ~ejercitar~ and ~ejército~.
en.elaborar:
From Latin ~ēlabōrāre~ (“to work out, produce by effort”), formed from ~ex-~ (“out, thoroughly”) and ~labōrāre~ (“to labor, toil”), from the noun ~labor~ (“labor, hardship”). It is cognate with French ~élaborer~, Italian ~elaborare~, and Portuguese ~elaborar~, and with the Latin-derived English ~elaborate~ and ~laborious~.

The origin of ~labor~ itself is uncertain: it has been proposed that it is related to ~labāre~ (“to totter, slip”), from the image of a body swaying under a heavy burden, but this is not established. The prefix ~ex-~ lent an intensive “thoroughly” force, so ~ēlabōrāre~ meant to work something out fully — hence the modern “to elaborate, produce.” The verb ~labōrāre~ left two Spanish descendants: the patrimonial ~labrar~ (“to till, work the land”) and the learned ~laborar~. The same family gave ~laboratorio~, ~colaborar~, ~laborioso~, and ~laborable~, all circling the ancient Roman sense of sustained, hard work.
en.elegir:
From Latin ~ēligere~ (“to pick out, to choose”), from ~ex-~ (“out of”) + ~legere~ (“to gather, to pick, to read”). ~legere~ comes from Proto-Italic *~legō~ and Proto-Indo-European *~leǵ-~ (“to gather, to collect”). The same root gave Ancient Greek ~légō~ (“I gather, I say”), the ancestor of ~-logy~ and ~logic~. Old Spanish inherited the verb as ~esleer~/~eslecher~ before the learned ~elegir~ reshaped it on the Latin model. Cognate with Italian ~eleggere~, French ~élire~, and Portuguese ~eleger~.

~legere~ began concretely — to gather up, as one gathers olives or firewood — and then specialized in two directions: to gather written signs with the eye (“to read”) and to gather out the best (“to choose,” with ~ex-~). Spanish ~elegir~ keeps only the choosing sense, and its past participle ~electo~ gave the political ~elección~ and ~electorado~. The gathering root *~leǵ-~ also seeded ~leer~ (“to read”), ~colegio~, ~coleccionar~, ~legión~, and ~inteligente~ (“one who chooses between,” ~inter-~ + ~legere~).
en.elevar:
From Latin ~elevāre~ (“to lift up, raise”), from ~ex-~ (“out, up”) and ~levāre~ (“to lighten, to raise”), a verb built on the adjective ~levis~ (“light, not heavy”); the root reaches back to Proto-Indo-European *~h₁lengʷʰ-~ (“lightweight”). It is cognate with Italian ~elevare~ and French ~élever~, and — through the same root — with English ~elevate~, ~lever~ and even ~light~ itself.

The striking fact is that Latin ~levāre~ left Spanish two verbs at once. ~Elevar~ is the learned borrowing, taken from books with its ~-l-~ intact and its “raise, lift” sense; but the same verb, inherited by mouth through the centuries, became the wholly ordinary ~llevar~, its ~l-~ palatalised to ~ll-~ and its meaning drifted from “to lift” to “to carry, to take.” The two are twins from one source.
