From Latin ~ligāre~ (“to bind, tie”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~leyǵ-~ (“to bind”). The Latin verb passed directly into Spanish as ~ligar~ and into its sisters as Italian ~legare~, Portuguese ~ligar~, and French ~lier~. Through ~ligāre~ and its derivatives, Spanish ~ligar~ is cognate with a surprising spread of English words — ~ligature~, ~ligament~, ~ally~, ~rely~, ~liable~, and ~league~ — all built on the idea of tying.

The core sense is simply “to bind,” and Spanish ~ligar~ still means to join, tie, or alloy. But it also picked up a lively colloquial sense, “to flirt” or “to hook up,” as though binding oneself to another for the evening. The prefixed ~obligāre~ (“to bind toward, oblige”) gave ~obligar~, and ~religāre~ (“to bind fast”) is one proposed source of ~religión~, though ancient writers debated whether ~religio~ came instead from ~relegere~ (“to reread, go over again”) — a genuinely disputed point. From the same root Spanish keeps ~liga~ (“league; garter”), ~ligadura~ (“ligature”), ~ligamento~, ~aliar~ (“to ally”), and ~ligazón~ (“bond”).
en.limitar:
From Latin ~limitare~ (“to mark off, set bounds”), formed from ~limes~ (genitive ~limitis~), “a boundary, a cross-path between fields, a frontier”. ~limes~ is usually derived from ~limus~ (“sidelong, transverse”) and set beside ~limen~ (“threshold”), though the exact relationship among these words is debated. It descends in Italian ~limitare~, French ~limiter~ and Portuguese ~limitar~.

The Roman ~limes~ began as the balk or path running crosswise between plots, then hardened into something grander: the fortified ~limes~ that marked the edge of the empire, from the German frontier to Hadrian's Wall. To ~limitare~ was to trace such a boundary, and Spanish ~limitar~ still means both “to set a limit” and “to border on” a neighbour. The family includes ~límite~, ~limítrofe~ (“bordering”) and ~limitación~, and English drew ~limit~ and ~limitation~ straight from the same Latin, while the neighbouring ~limen~ surfaces in English ~liminal~.
en.limpiar:
Spanish ~limpiar~ derives from the adjective ~limpio~ (“clean”), which comes from Latin ~limpidus~ (“clear, transparent, limpid”), especially of water. The verb continues a Late Latin ~limpidāre~ (“to make clear”). Through the Latin adjective ~limpiar~ is cognate with English ~limpid~ and French ~limpide~; Italian and Portuguese, however, reached the same idea by other words (~pulire~, ~limpar~).

The origin of ~limpidus~ is uncertain and debated. It has traditionally been linked to a Proto-Indo-European root *~leh₂p-~ (“to shine”) — which would make it kin to Ancient Greek ~lámpō~ (“to shine”) and Lithuanian ~liepsna~ (“flame”) — but another line ties it to Latin ~lympha~ (“clear water”), the water-nymph word, whose own spelling was reshaped by Greek ~νύμφη~ (~nýmphē~). Because the accounts diverge, the deep root is best left open. The sense-shift is easy to follow: what is “clear” becomes what is “clean.” From ~limpio~ Spanish built ~limpiar~, ~limpieza~ (“cleaning, cleanliness”), ~limpión~, and the adjective ~límpido~ (“limpid”).
en.llamar:
From Old Spanish ~clamar~, from Latin ~clāmāre~ (“to cry out, shout”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~kelh₁-~ (“to call, shout”). Cognate with Italian ~chiamare~, French ~clamer~, and Portuguese ~chamar~, and — through the same root — with Latin ~calāre~ (“to call out”) and the English borrowings ~claim~ and ~clamor~.

The initial Latin cluster ~cl-~ palatalized to the Spanish ~ll-~ (the same shift that turned ~clāvem~ into ~llave~ and ~plēnum~ into ~lleno~), so ~clāmāre~ yielded popular ~llamar~ while a learned ~clamar~ (“to clamor, cry out”) was later re-borrowed alongside it. The sense softened from the urgency of shouting to the everyday acts of calling, summoning, and — reflexively, in ~llamarse~ — being named: one no longer cries out a name but simply ~se llama~ it. The root also gave Spanish ~clamor~, ~reclamar~ (“to claim, demand”), and ~exclamar~, plus the derivatives ~llamada~ (“call”), ~llamamiento~ (“summons”), and ~llamativo~ (“eye-catching”).
en.llegar:
From Old Spanish ~llegar~, from Latin ~plicāre~ (“to fold”) — or, by a competing account, from its compound ~applicāre~ (“to bring to, to land a ship”), the initial ~a-~ later lost. Either way the ~pl-~ hardened into Spanish ~ll-~. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *~pleḱ-~ (“to plait, to fold”). Portuguese ~chegar~ came the same way; the folding sense stayed put in the learned doublet ~plegar~ and in Italian ~piegare~ and French ~plier~; English ~ply~ and ~apply~ are relatives.

How “to fold” became “to arrive” is debated. The usual explanation is nautical — a ship reaching harbor folds its sails, or is brought folded up against the shore — fitting for the seafaring peninsula, though it remains a proposal rather than a proven fact. Strikingly, the very same Latin verb went the opposite way in Romanian ~pleca~ (“to leave, to depart”), by one account from folding up a tent to move on — so a single root yielded both “arrive” and “leave.” Spanish derivatives include ~llegada~ (“arrival”) and the doublet family of ~plegar~, ~aplicar~, ~replicar~, and ~complicar~.
en.llenar:
From ~lleno~ (“full”), from Latin ~plēnus~ (“full”), from Proto-Indo-European *~pleh₁-~ (“to fill”); the Latin initial ~pl-~ regularly became Spanish ~ll-~. It is cognate with Italian ~pieno~, French ~plein~ and Portuguese ~cheio~, and, through the same root, with English ~full~ and ~plenty~ and German ~voll~.

The adjective ~plēnus~ gave the adjective ~lleno~, from which Spanish coined the verb ~llenar~, “to make full.” Beside the inherited ~ll-~ line, Spanish also borrowed the Latin ~pl-~ form learnedly, so the family runs double: popular ~lleno~, ~llenar~, ~rellenar~ alongside cultured ~pleno~, ~plenitud~ and ~pleamar~ (“high tide”). English ~fill~ itself is built on ~full~, from the very same PIE root *~pleh₁-~.
en.llevar:
From Old Spanish ~levar~, from Latin ~levāre~ (“to raise, to lift”), from the adjective ~levis~ (“light, not heavy”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₁lengʷʰ-~ (“light in weight”) — the same root that gave English its native ~light~. The Romance siblings are Italian ~levare~, French ~lever~, and Portuguese ~levar~; English also took the learned ~lever~, ~elevate~, ~alleviate~, and ~relieve~ from the same Latin stock.

The path from “to lift” to Spanish ~llevar~ (“to carry, to take, to wear”) runs through the natural chain of lifting a load, then bearing it, then bearing it away. Spanish split the work with a cousin: ~llevar~ carries something from here to there, while ~traer~ brings it toward the speaker. The plainer sense of “to raise” stayed with the doublet ~levantar~ (“to lift, to raise”), and the family also yields ~leve~ (“light, slight”), ~elevar~, ~aliviar~ (“to relieve”), ~relevar~ (“to relieve, to relay”), and ~sublevar~ (“to incite to revolt”).
en.llorar:
From Latin ~plōrāre~ (“to weep, wail, cry out”), of uncertain origin — possibly from Proto-Indo-European *~pleh₃(w)-~ (“to flow”), though the link is not secure. Latin ~pl-~ regularly became Spanish ~ll-~, as in ~plēnus~ → ~lleno~ (“full”) and ~pluvia~ → ~lluvia~ (“rain”). Cognate with Portuguese ~chorar~, Catalan ~plorar~ and French ~pleurer~.

In Latin ~plōrāre~ meant to cry out aloud, and only gradually narrowed toward weeping. Its Roman compounds still live in English through French: ~deplōrāre~ (“to lament”) gave ~deplore~ and ~implōrāre~ gave ~implore~; and — by one much-repeated but uncertain account — ~explōrāre~ was first a hunters' term, “to cry out” on sighting game, before it came to mean ~explore~. Spanish keeps ~plōrāre~'s core in ~llorar~ and built ~lloro~ (“weeping”), ~llorón~ (“crybaby”), ~lloroso~ (“tearful”) and ~lloriquear~ (“to whimper”).
en.localizar:
A modern verb formed on the adjective ~local~, from Latin ~locālis~ (“of a place”), from ~locus~ (“place, spot”). Older Latin had ~stlocus~, a word of uncertain origin; some link it to a Proto-Indo-European root *~stel-~ (“to set, place”), but that descent is debated. Cognate with Italian ~luogo~, French ~lieu~ and English ~locus~ and ~location~.

The learned ~locālis~ actually reached Spanish twice: inherited through popular speech it became ~lugar~ (“place”), while borrowed straight from Latin it gave the doublet ~local~ (“local; premises”). ~locus~ seeded a wide family — ~localidad~, ~colocar~, ~locomotora~, ~dislocar~ — and in the nineteenth century Spanish took ~localizar~ from French ~localiser~, meaning to fix a thing in its place. Fittingly for a word about location, ~locus~ still refuses to disclose its own origin.
en.lograr:
From Latin ~lucrārī~ (“to gain, to profit”), a deponent verb from the noun ~lucrum~ (“gain, profit, wealth”), from Proto-Indo-European *~leh₂w-~ (“to seize, to gain”). The same root surfaces in Germanic as Proto-Germanic *~launą~ (“reward”), giving German ~Lohn~ (“wage”) and Old English ~lēan~ (“reward”), and in Greek ~apolaúō~ (“to enjoy”). Within Romance, Spanish ~lograr~ stands beside the learned borrowing ~lucro~ and its Portuguese and Italian relatives.

The meaning traveled a satisfying road. Latin ~lucrārī~ was mercantile — to turn a profit — and Old Spanish ~lograr~ first meant “to enjoy or possess” something, to have the benefit of it. From “enjoying the gain” the verb slid to “obtaining the desired thing” and finally to today’s “to achieve, to manage to.” The word’s history is thus its own small success story: from raw profit, through enjoyment, to accomplishment. Alongside the popular ~lograr~ Spanish keeps the doublet ~logro~ (“achievement,” and formerly “usury, interest”), plus the learned ~lucro~ and ~lucrativo~, which stayed close to the original money-making sense.
en.luchar:
From Latin ~luctari~ (“to wrestle, to struggle”), attested since Plautus, from Proto-Indo-European *~lewg-~ (“to bend, to twist”). The Latin cluster ~-ct-~ palatalized to Spanish ~-ch-~, the same change that turned ~lacte~ into ~leche~ and ~pectus~ into ~pecho~. It is cognate with Italian ~lottare~, French ~lutter~ and Portuguese ~lutar~, and — through the deponent compound ~reluctari~ — with English ~reluctant~ (literally “struggling back”).

The image behind the root is a body twisting against an opponent, and ~luchar~ began as literal wrestling before broadening to any fight or striving — against an enemy, an illness, or oneself. By the traditional account the same *~lewg-~ root also yielded Latin ~luxus~ (“dislocated; excess”), whence Spanish ~lujo~ (“luxury”) and ~lujuria~ (“lust”) — the twist of a joint and the twist of indulgence sharing one ancestor. Closer to home the root gives ~lucha~, ~luchador~ and ~luchadora~.
en.lucir:
From Latin ~lūcēre~ (“to shine, be bright”), related to ~lux~ (“light”), from Proto-Indo-European *~lewk-~ (“to shine, be white”). Cognate with English ~light~, German ~Licht~, Greek ~leukós~ (“white”) and Sanskrit ~rócate~ (“shines”), and with the Latin kin ~lūna~ and ~lūmen~.

The root *~lewk-~ is a beacon across the family: Latin ~lūna~ (“moon”) is literally “the shining one,” from *~louksnā~. In Spanish it lit up ~luz~ (“light”), ~lucero~ (“bright star”), ~lúcido~ (“lucid”), ~alumbrar~ (“to illuminate”) and ~iluminar~. The verb ~lūcēre~ itself drifted from plain shining to display: to ~lucir~ is to shine in the sense of showing off — a new dress, a talent, a tan — while ~relucir~ keeps the older, literal glow.
en.mandar:
From Latin ~mandāre~ (“to entrust, to order”), a compound traditionally explained as ~manus~ (“hand”) + ~dāre~ (“to give”) — literally “to place in someone's hand.” ~dāre~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~deh₃-~ (“to give”). Cognate with Italian ~mandare~ (“to send”), French ~mander~, and Portuguese ~mandar~, and — through the compound — with English ~mandate~, ~command~, and ~demand~.

The literal picture — putting a task into someone's hand — explains the whole semantic spread. To hand someone a charge is to “entrust” it (the sense in English ~mandate~), and to entrust with authority shades into “to order,” which is why ~mandar~ means “to command.” But Spanish also took a second path: to put something in a messenger's hand is to “send” it, so ~mandar~ means “to send” as well — ~mandar una carta~ is to send a letter, ~mandar a alguien~ can be to order someone about. Few Spanish verbs carry so wide a range on one root. Related descendants include ~mando~ (“command, control”), ~mandato~ (“mandate”), ~mandamiento~ (“commandment”), ~comandar~ (“to command [troops]”), ~demandar~ (“to demand, to sue”), and ~encomendar~ (“to entrust”).
en.manejar:
From Italian ~maneggiare~ (“to handle, to manage, especially to handle a horse”), a denominative ultimately built on Latin ~manus~ (“hand”). Spanish borrowed it in the sixteenth century. The word is traditionally parsed as ~manus~ plus ~agere~ (“to drive by hand”), but that account is disputed: Corominas rejects it, treating ~maneggiare~ instead as a reinforced formation from ~mano~ / ~manus~, parallel to Italian ~maniglia~ (“handle”). Through the same Italian verb, Spanish ~manejar~ is cognate with English ~manage~ and French ~manège~ (“riding school”).

Its first home in Spanish was the riding school: to ~manejar~ a horse was to work it through its paces by hand and rein. From there it widened to handling tools, money, ideas and people — and in much of Latin America ~manejar~ became the ordinary verb for driving a car, where peninsular Spanish prefers ~conducir~. The Latin ~manus~ seeded a broad family, among them ~mano~, ~manejo~, ~manija~, ~maniobra~, ~manual~ and ~manuscrito~.
en.manifestar:
From Latin ~manifestare~ (“to make plain, reveal”), derived from the adjective ~manifestus~ (“caught in the act, flagrant, evident, palpable”). Its first element is clearly ~manus~ (“hand”); the second is disputed — it may descend from a Proto-Indo-European root *~dʰers-~ (“to be bold”), itself from *~dʰer-~ (“to hold”), but the analysis is uncertain and no confident sense can be assigned. Latin passed the verb to Italian ~manifestare~, French ~manifester~ and Portuguese ~manifestar~.

Whatever its build, ~manifestus~ evoked something so palpable it could almost be taken in the hand — a wrongdoer “caught red-handed”, a fact plain to all. Spanish ~manifestar~ accordingly means “to show, reveal, declare”, and reflexively ~manifestarse~ is “to demonstrate”, to make one's views public in the street. Hence the noun ~manifestación~ (“demonstration, manifestation”) and ~manifiesto~ (“manifesto”). The transparent first element ~manus~ anchors a huge Spanish family — ~mano~, ~manejar~, ~manual~ and ~mantener~ — and English borrowed the verb's own offspring in ~manifest~ and ~manifesto~.
en.mantener:
From Latin ~manū~ ~tenēre~, literally “to hold in the hand,” a phrase of ~manus~ (“hand”) and ~tenēre~ (“to hold, keep”) that fused into Vulgar Latin ~manutenēre~. The second element, shared with ~tener~, goes back to Proto-Italic *~tenēō~ and Proto-Indo-European *~ten-~ (“to stretch, extend”); the first, ~manus~, comes from Proto-Italic *~manus~ and *~man-~ (“hand”). Cognate Romance descendants include Italian ~mantenere~, Portuguese ~manter~ and French ~maintenir~; English ~maintain~ is the same compound, borrowed through Old French ~maintenir~.

The image is concrete: to “hold in the hand” became to keep, support, sustain and maintain — the range Spanish ~mantener~ still spans, from ~mantener~ una promesa to ~mantener~ a la familia. Its ~tenēre~ half anchors a huge family — ~tener~, ~contener~, ~detener~, ~obtener~, ~sostener~ and ~retener~ — while ~manus~ gives ~mano~, ~manejar~, ~manual~ and ~maniobra~ (“maneuver,” from ~manū~ ~operāre~, “to work by hand”). Through the root *~ten-~ (“to stretch”) ~mantener~ is even distantly kin to ~tender~, ~tienda~ (a stretched tent-shop) and English ~tenant~ and ~tension~.
en.maquinar:
From Latin ~māchinārī~ (“to contrive, devise, plot”), the verb of ~māchina~ (“machine, device, contrivance, trick”). Latin borrowed the noun from Doric Greek ~māchaná~ (Attic ~mēkhanḗ~, “device, means, contrivance”), from ~mêkhos~ (“means, expedient”), from Proto-Indo-European *~magʰ-~ (“to be able, to have power”). Through that root it is cognate with English ~machine~ and ~machination~, and — via Germanic — with English ~may~ and ~might~ and German ~Macht~ (“power”).

The Greek ~mēkhanḗ~ was the crane that lowered a god onto the stage — the original ~deus ex machina~ — and any clever contrivance; the metaphorical leap from “build a device” to “devise a plot” was already present in Latin ~māchinārī~. So Spanish ~maquinar~ means “to scheme, plot,” while its innocent doublet ~máquina~ kept the concrete “machine.” From the same source come ~maquinaria~, ~maquinación~, ~mecánico~ and ~mecanismo~ — the engineering and the intrigue springing from one Greek word for a device.
en.marcar:
Spanish ~marcar~ (“to mark”) has a debated immediate history: it is either a native formation from the noun ~marca~ (“mark, boundary”) plus the verb-ending ~-ar~, or a loan from Italian ~marcare~ (“to put a mark on”). Either way the deeper source is Germanic. The noun ~marca~ goes back, through Medieval Latin ~marca~, to Proto-Germanic *~markō~ (“boundary, borderland, region”), which entered Ibero-Romance from a Germanic tongue — Gothic or Frankish. So the root idea is not a scribble but a border. It is cognate with Italian ~marca~, German ~Mark~ and English ~mark~ and ~march~ (“borderland”).

The semantic path runs from the land inward. A ~marca~ was first a frontier district — the borderlands a ruler had to guard — which is exactly why medieval marches gave us titles like “marquis” (Spanish ~marqués~), the lord set over a ~marca~. From “boundary” the noun narrowed to the “mark” one sets to claim or delimit, and the verb ~marcar~ to the act of making such a mark — on cattle, on a page, on a scoreboard. Its Spanish kin spread across that whole span: ~marco~ (“frame”), ~marcador~ (“marker; scoreboard”), ~comarca~ (“district,” literally land within borders), ~demarcar~ (“to demarcate”) and ~marcapasos~ (“pacemaker”).
en.marchar:
Spanish ~marchar~ was borrowed from French ~marcher~ (“to walk, tread, march”), attested from the twelfth century. The ultimate origin is disputed. The favored account traces ~marcher~ to Frankish *~markōn~ (“to mark, to tread”), from Proto-Germanic *~markōną~, a verb on *~markō~ (“boundary, mark”); a rival proposal derives it instead from a Vulgar Latin *~marcāre~ (“to hammer,” from ~marcus~ “hammer”), but this is generally rejected, and the word’s confinement to French favors the Germanic source. English borrowed the French verb as ~march~; Italian has ~marciare~, Portuguese ~marchar~.

If the Germanic account is right, ~marchar~ shares a root with English ~mark~ and ~march~ (“borderland”) and with the Spanish loans ~marca~ (“mark, brand”), ~marcar~, ~comarca~ (“district”), and ~marqués~ (“marquis,” originally the warden of a border ~march~). The sense in Spanish widened from military marching to any purposeful going — a train ~marcha~, a person ~se marcha~ (“leaves”), and a machine ~marcha~ (“runs”) — plus the noun ~marcha~ (“march, pace, gear, nightlife”).
en.matar:
From Old Spanish ~matar~ (“to fell, subdue, kill”), a word shared by the Hispanic Romance languages whose ultimate origin is genuinely uncertain. The account favored by Corominas derives it from a Vulgar Latin *~mattāre~, from Latin ~mattus~ (“stunned, addled, sottish”) — the sense moving from “to daze, stun, fell” to “to kill.” ~mattus~ is itself of obscure origin; Corominas weighs, without endorsing, a link to Ancient Greek ~μάταιος~ (~mátaios~, “vain, foolish”), a connection that cannot be documented. By this account ~matar~ is related to Italian ~matto~ (“mad, crazy”) and French ~mat~ (“defeated,” as in checkmate); Portuguese also has ~matar~.

If the ~mattus~ etymology holds, the everyday Spanish verb for “to kill” is a cousin of the Italian word for “crazy” — a striking pairing, but one resting on a disputed root, so worth stating as hypothesis rather than fact. In Spanish the meaning settled firmly on killing and its figures: to ~matar~ time, thirst, or a light. From it grew a plain, grim family — ~matanza~ (“slaughter”), ~matador~ (“killer,” and the bullfighter who delivers the final blow) and ~rematar~ (“to finish off, to top off”).
en.mediar:
~Mediar~ comes from Latin ~mediāre~ (“to be in the middle, to halve”), from ~medius~ (“middle”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~medʰyo-~ (“middle”). It is cognate with English ~mediate~ and Italian ~mediare~, and — through the same root — with English ~middle~ and German ~Mitte~.

From “to be in the middle,” ~mediar~ came to mean “to intervene between two parties.” ~Medius~ seeded a broad family: ~medio~, ~mediano~, ~mediodía~ (“midday”), and ~medieval~ (from ~medium~ ~aevum~, “middle age”). Two are hidden in plain sight: ~meridiano~ (“meridian”) began as *~medīdiēs~, “midday,” whose first d dissimilated to r; and ~Mediterráneo~ is literally the sea “in the middle of the land.” To mediate, then, is simply to place oneself in the middle.
en.medir:
From Old Galician-Portuguese ~medir~, from Latin ~metiri~ (“to measure”), a deponent verb, from Proto-Indo-European *~meh₁-~ (“to measure”). The Latin ~-t-~ between vowels voiced and then vanished, giving ~metiri~ → ~medir~. It is cognate with Portuguese ~medir~ and, through the same root, with English ~measure~ (via Latin ~mensura~) and with Greek ~métron~ (“measure”).

The PIE root carried the idea of marking off a due amount, and one striking branch measured time: by the traditional account *~meh₁-~ also produced the word for the moon as the great measurer of the months, seen in English ~moon~ and ~month~. In Spanish the verb stayed close to its plain sense — to determine a size or extent — while spawning ~medida~, ~medición~, ~medidor~, ~mensura~, ~dimensión~ and ~inmenso~ (literally “unmeasurable”).
en.mejorar:
Spanish ~mejorar~ comes from Late Latin ~meliōrāre~ (“to make better”), a verb built on the Latin comparative ~melior~ (“better”). ~melior~ is generally traced to Proto-Indo-European *~mel-~ (“strong, great”), the same root credited with Latin ~multus~ (“much”) and Ancient Greek ~μάλα~ (mála, “very”). Its Romance reflexes are everywhere: the adjective survives as Spanish ~mejor~, Portuguese ~melhor~, French ~meilleur~, and Italian ~migliore~, and the verb as Portuguese ~melhorar~ and Italian ~migliorare~. English ~ameliorate~ borrowed the Latin verb through French.

There is a small surprise in ~mejor~: it serves as the comparative of ~bueno~ (“good”) yet shares no root with it. Latin ~bonus~ lacked a comparative of its own and borrowed ~melior~ from an unrelated word — the pattern called suppletion, the same quirk behind English “good/better.” So ~mejorar~ means, transparently, to make or become better. From the root Spanish keeps ~mejor~, ~mejora~ (“improvement”), ~mejoría~ (“recovery”), and ~mejoramiento~; through the cognate ~multus~ come ~mucho~, ~muy~, ~multitud~, and ~múltiple~.
en.mencionar:
From ~mención~ (“mention”), a learned noun taken from Latin ~mentiō~ (stem ~mentiōn-~, “a calling to mind, a naming”), which grows from the same root as ~meminī~ (“to remember”) and ~mēns~ (“mind”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *~men-~ (“to think”). The verb ~mencionar~ is cognate with French ~mentionner~, Italian ~menzionare~ and English ~mention~; through the shared root *~men-~ it is also kin to English ~mind~ and ~mental~.

Latin ~mentiō~ literally named the act of bringing something back to mind, and Spanish kept that thread: to ~mencionar~ is to summon a thing into speech, to call it to notice. Older and more colloquial is the inherited doublet ~mentar~ (“to name, to bring up”), alive in the blunt phrase ~mentar~ la madre. From the same root *~men-~ Spanish drew a broad cognitive vocabulary — ~mente~ (“mind”), ~mental~, ~memoria~, ~comentar~ (“to comment”) and ~mentor~ — and, by one account, even ~mentir~ (“to lie”), as though a falsehood were merely something thought up; but that last link is debated.
en.merecer:
From Latin ~merēscere~ (“to earn, deserve”), an inchoative form of ~merēre~ / ~mereō~ (“to earn, deserve, serve for pay”), traditionally traced to Proto-Indo-European *~(s)mer-~ (“to allot, assign, get a share”). Old Spanish had ~merecer~ already in the earliest texts. Cognate Romance forms include Portuguese ~merecer~ and Italian ~meritare~ (from the participle ~meritum~), while French kept the noun in ~mérite~. Through the participle ~meritum~ (“that which is earned”) English received the borrowings ~merit~ and ~meritorious~. The same PIE root surfaces in Ancient Greek ~μέρος~ (~méros~, “part, share”) and ~μοῖρα~ (~moîra~, “portion, fate”).

The semantic path is striking: from “to receive one's share” the verb slid to “to earn by service,” especially a soldier's pay (~stipendia merēre~ meant to serve a military campaign), and finally to “to be worthy of.” That is why the same root binds the ideas of a share, a wage, and desert. Modern Spanish ~merecer~ carries the moral weight — ~merecer la pena~ (“to be worth the trouble”) is an everyday phrase — and yields ~merecido~ (“deserved,” or as a noun “just deserts”), ~merecedor~ (“deserving”), ~mérito~, ~meritorio~ and ~emérito~ (“emeritus,” one who has earned release from duty). The Greek ~μοῖρα~, personified as the Fates, shows how deeply the notion of an allotted share ran.
en.meter:
From Old Spanish ~meter~, from Latin ~mittere~ (“to send, let go, release”). The deeper origin is uncertain; by one account ~mittere~ traces to Proto-Italic *~meitō~ and Proto-Indo-European *~meyth₂-~ (“to exchange, remove”), an extension of the root *~mey-~ (“to change”). It is cognate with Portuguese ~meter~, Italian ~mettere~, and French ~mettre~.

In Latin ~mittere~ meant “to send,” but already in Vulgar Latin the sense drifted toward “to put, place, insert,” which is what Spanish ~meter~ means today — you ~meter~ a key into a lock or a hand into a pocket. The learned family stayed closer to the original “send”: ~admitir~, ~remitir~, ~prometer~, and ~someter~ all preserve the Latin verb. From its participle ~missus~ came a cluster of everyday nouns: ~misión~ (“a sending”), ~mensaje~ (“message”), and ~remesa~ (“remittance, shipment”). Even ~misa~ (“Mass”) belongs here, from ~missa~ in the dismissal formula that once closed the service. English ~mission~ and ~message~ are cousins from the same Latin verb.
en.mezclar:
From Vulgar Latin *~misculāre~, a frequentative of Latin ~miscēre~ (“to mix”), from Proto-Italic *~miskēō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~meyǵ-~ (“to mix”). The root is widespread: cognates include Ancient Greek ~mísgō~, Sanskrit ~miśra~ (“mixed”), German ~mischen~, and English ~mix~ and ~mash~. From the same Vulgar Latin *~misculāre~ came French ~mêler~, Italian ~mescolare~, and Portuguese ~mesclar~, while Spanish also kept the learned ~miscēre~ line in ~miscelánea~.

Latin’s frequentative *~misculāre~ implied repeated, thorough mixing, and it is the popular ancestor of ~mezclar~, while the learned form ~miscēre~ fed a parallel bookish branch. The root ramifies richly in Spanish: ~mezcla~, the Italianate ~mezcolanza~ (“hodgepodge”), ~mestizo~ (“of mixed ancestry,” from Latin ~mixticius~), and the cultismos ~mixto~, ~mixtura~, and ~promiscuo~. A surprising outlier is English ~mustang~: it goes back through Spanish ~mesteño~ to ~mixta~, an animal of the mixed grazing commons — the same “mixing” idea, wearing a cowboy hat.
en.mirar:
From Latin ~mīrārī~ (“to wonder at, to marvel”), a deponent verb formed on the adjective ~mīrus~ (“wonderful, astonishing”). ~mīrus~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~smeiros~ and to Proto-Indo-European *~(s)mey-~ (“to smile, to be glad”) — so, remarkably, ~mirar~ is a blood relative of English ~smile~ and of Sanskrit ~sméra~ (“smiling”). Italian ~mirare~, French ~mirer~, and Portuguese ~mirar~ share the inheritance.

Here the surprise is a loss: Latin ~mīrārī~ was charged with astonishment, but everyday Spanish ~mirar~ drained the wonder away until it meant simply “to look at, to watch.” The amazement did not vanish, though — it took refuge in the learned offspring ~admirar~, ~milagro~ (from ~mīrāculum~), and ~maravilla~ (from ~mīrābilia~, “wonders”). English drew from the same well for ~admire~, ~miracle~, ~marvel~, and — through Vulgar Latin's “to look at” — ~mirror~, the glass you gaze into. Spanish adds ~mirada~, ~mirador~, and ~mira~.
en.moderar:
From Latin ~moderārī~ (“to keep within measure, restrain, regulate”), a verb built on ~modus~ (“measure, manner, limit”), from Proto-Indo-European *~med-~ (“to measure, take appropriate measures”). Cognate with Italian ~moderare~, French ~modérer~ and Portuguese ~moderar~; through the same root it is kin to English ~mete~ (“to mete out”) and, more distantly, to English ~medical~ and ~modest~.

The Latin verb already carried the idea of holding something to its proper ~modus~ — its due measure — so ~moderar~ has meant “to temper, soften, regulate” from the start, whether a speed, a tone, or a debate; the modern “to moderate” a forum or panel is a natural late extension of steering a discussion toward its right measure. From the same root ~modus~ Spanish inherited a rich family: ~modo~, ~moderno~, ~módulo~, ~cómodo~, ~modesto~ and ~modelo~, all turning on the notion of measure, manner, and fitting proportion.
en.modificar:
From Latin ~modificāre~ (“to limit, measure off, regulate”), a compound of ~modus~ (“measure, bound, manner”) and the combining form ~-ficāre~ (from ~facere~, “to make, do”) — literally “to make to measure.” ~modus~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~med-~ (“to measure, take appropriate measures”), while ~facere~ goes back to *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to put, place, set”). Cognates of *~med-~ include Latin ~moderārī~ (“to keep within measure”), ~medērī~ (“to heal”), and Ancient Greek ~mḗdomai~ (“to be mindful of, plan”). The Romance verbs align: Italian ~modificare~, French ~modifier~, Portuguese ~modificar~.

The word literally means “to make within measure,” and it kept the sense of adjusting something to fit — trimming, qualifying, tempering rather than remaking. That measuring instinct fans out across Spanish: from ~modus~ come ~modo~ (“manner, mode”), ~molde~ (“mold”), ~moderar~ (“to moderate”), ~cómodo~ (“comfortable, fitting”), ~modelo~ (“model”) and ~módulo~ (“module”). The “healing” side of the root *~med-~ — measured, prudent care — surfaces in ~médico~ (“doctor”), ~medicina~ (“medicine”) and ~remedio~ (“remedy”). And from ~facere~, the second half, Spanish keeps a vast crop of ~-ficar~ verbs (~verificar~, ~clarificar~, ~justificar~) all meaning “to make thus.”
en.molestar:
From Latin ~molestāre~ (“to trouble, to annoy”), a verb built on the adjective ~molestus~ (“troublesome, burdensome”), which Spanish took in as a learned word. By one widely cited account ~molestus~ is related to ~mōlēs~ (“mass, bulk, heavy burden”) — what molests being felt as a “weight” on the mind — but the sources hedge this link. Through that same disputed root, ~mōlēs~ has been tied to Greek ~μῶλος~ (“toil, effort”) and German ~mühen~ (“to tire oneself”). Cognate with Italian ~molestare~, Portuguese ~molestar~, and, by way of Old French ~molester~, English ~molest~.

The meaning stayed close to Latin: to disturb, bother, or pester. Spanish ~molestar~ is far milder than English ~molest~, which narrowed to a sexual sense the Spanish verb never took on. The adjective yielded ~molesto~ and the noun ~molestia~. Whether or not ~molestus~ truly springs from ~mōlēs~, that word for “burden” is securely the parent of a separate family: ~demoler~ and ~demolición~ (from ~dēmōlīrī~, “to pull a mass down”) and the modern coinage ~molécula~ (“a little mass”).
en.montar:
From Vulgar Latin *~montāre~ (“to climb a mountain”), a verb built on Latin ~mōns~ (genitive ~montis~, “mountain”), from Proto-Italic *~monts~, from Proto-Indo-European *~men-~ (“to project, jut out”) — the same root that yielded Latin ~ēminēre~ (“to stand out”) and ~prōminēre~ (“to project”). Cognate with Italian ~montare~, French ~monter~ and Portuguese ~montar~, and the source of English ~mount~ and ~amount~.

The image is a hill: to ~montar~ was first “to go up,” and from climbing a slope the verb spread to mounting a horse, then to assembling or “setting up” anything — a machine, a company, a play. English ~amount~ took the same path through Old French ~amonter~, “to go up (in total).” From ~mōns~ Spanish also keeps ~monte~, ~montaña~, ~montón~ and ~montura~.
en.morir:
From Vulgar Latin *~morīre~, a regularization of Classical Latin ~morī~ (“to die,” a deponent verb), from Proto-Indo-European *~mer-~ (“to die”). Cognate with Italian ~morire~, French ~mourir~ and Portuguese ~morrer~; through the root, with Sanskrit ~mṛtyú~ (“death”), Ancient Greek ~brotós~ (“mortal”) and — via Germanic — English ~murder~.

Classical ~morī~ was deponent (passive in form, active in meaning); Vulgar Latin recast it as an ordinary verb *~morīre~, the ancestor of every Romance form. From the participle ~mortuus~ and the noun ~mors~ (stem ~mort-~) came Spanish ~muerte~, ~muerto~, ~mortal~, ~moribundo~ and ~amortiguar~. A vivid relic survives in English ~mortgage~ — literally a “dead pledge” — while at the opposite pole Greek ~ambrosía~ (“the immortals’ food,” ~a-~ “not” + a form of *~mer-~) grows from the very same root.
en.mostrar:
From Latin ~mōnstrāre~ (“to show, point out”), a verb from the noun ~mōnstrum~ (“portent, omen, marvel”), itself derived from ~monēre~ (“to warn, remind, advise”), from Proto-Indo-European *~men-~ (“to think”). Cognate with Italian ~mostrare~, French ~montrer~, and Portuguese ~mostrar~; through the same Latin family come English ~muster~ (borrowed via Old French), ~monster~, and ~demonstrate~.

The chain hides a striking image: a ~mōnstrum~ was originally a divine sign — something shown by the gods to warn mortals — so “to show” and “to warn” were once the same gesture. Latin drained the ominous charge, leaving ~mōnstrāre~ as the neutral “to point out,” while the noun kept the dread and became English ~monster~. Old Spanish ~mostrar~ inherited the plain sense of displaying and indicating. From the same root Spanish keeps ~muestra~ (“sample, sign”), ~demostrar~ (“to prove”), ~amonestar~ (“to admonish,” preserving the older warning sense), and the noun ~monstruo~, which carries the ancient shiver the verb long ago shed.
en.motivar:
The verb ~motivar~ comes from Medieval Latin ~motīvus~ (“moving, causing motion”), from Latin ~movēre~ (“to move, set in motion”), whose supine stem is ~mōtus~. ~movēre~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~mewh₁-~ (“to push away, move”). Cognate — through the same Latin verb — with English ~move~, ~motion~, ~motive~, and ~motor~, with French ~mouvoir~ and ~motiver~, and with Italian ~muovere~.

The neuter noun ~motīvum~ meant “that which sets something moving,” and Spanish ~motivo~ still means the reason or ~motive~ that moves a person to act. To ~motivar~, then, is to supply that inner push — to move someone to do something, and, in modern usage, to motivate. The same root of “movement” runs surprisingly deep: an ~emoción~ (“emotion”) is by etymology a “moving out,” a stirring within; a ~motor~ is a “mover”; and to ~conmover~ is to move someone together, to touch them. Kindred Spanish words include ~motivo~, ~motivación~, ~mover~, ~movimiento~, ~móvil~, ~motor~, ~emoción~, and ~conmover~.
en.mover:
From Latin ~movēre~ (“to move, set in motion”), from Proto-Italic *~moweō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~mewh₁-~ (“to move, push away”). It is cognate with Italian ~muovere~, French ~mouvoir~ and Portuguese ~mover~, and — through the same root — with English ~move~, borrowed through Anglo-Norman, and ~motion~.

The core sense “to change position” stayed remarkably stable from Latin into Spanish, yet the verb grew figurative branches: one can ~mover~ a chess piece or ~mover~ an audience to tears. The Latin participle ~mōtus~ supplied a second, learned stem that seeded a broad family — ~movimiento~, ~móvil~, ~motor~, ~motivo~ and ~emoción~ (literally “a moving-out” of feeling) — beside the prefixed inheritances ~remover~, ~conmover~ and ~promover~. From the same source flow the everyday ~automóvil~ and ~mueble~ (“a piece of furniture,” that is, a movable good, opposed to ~inmueble~, “real estate”).
en.nacer:
From Old Spanish ~nascer~, from Vulgar Latin *~nāscere~ (a reshaping of the deponent), from Latin ~nāscī~ (“to be born”), earlier ~gnāscī~, from Proto-Italic *~gnāskōr~, from Proto-Indo-European *~ǵenh₁-~ (“to beget, give birth”). The initial ~gn-~ regularly simplified to ~n-~. Cognates run through Romance — Italian ~nascere~, French ~naître~, Portuguese ~nascer~ — and, through the root, Latin ~genus~ and ~gignō~ (“to beget”) and inherited English ~kin~.

The ~-sc-~ of ~nāscī~ is an inchoative suffix marking an action just beginning, so the verb frames birth as a coming-into-being in progress. From the same root *~ǵenh₁-~ Spanish drew a vast family: think of ~Navidad~, which descends from Latin ~nātīvitās~ (“birth” — the Nativity), and of ~nación~ (a people “born” together), ~naturaleza~, ~género~, and ~gente~. To be reborn is ~renacer~, the verb behind the very idea of a Renaissance.
en.narrar:
From Latin ~narrāre~ (“to relate, to tell”), from ~gnārus~ (“knowing, acquainted with”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ǵneh₃-~ (“to know”). The verb is, at heart, a derivative of the “know” root: to narrate is to make something known. Cognate with French ~narrer~, Italian ~narrare~ and Portuguese ~narrar~, and — through the same root — with English ~know~ and ~can~.

Latin ~narrāre~ meant to give an account, to report — the narrator being literally one who knows and passes that knowing on. From ~gnārus~ Latin also built ~ignārus~ (“not knowing”), the source of Spanish ~ignorar~ and ~ignorante~. The wider Indo-European family of *~ǵneh₃-~ is enormous, and Spanish drew on it repeatedly: ~conocer~, ~noticia~, ~nota~, ~notar~ and ~reconocer~ all trace to the same idea of knowing, as do the strictly literary ~narración~, ~narrador~ and ~narrativa~.
en.necesitar:
From Latin ~necessitās~ (accusative ~necessitātem~, “necessity, unavoidability”), an abstract noun built on ~necesse~ (“necessary, inevitable”). ~necesse~ is commonly analyzed as ~ne-~ (“not”) plus ~cessus~, the past participle of ~cēdere~ (“to yield, give way”) — so its literal sense is that from which there is no yielding, though the exact formation is debated. Spanish built the verb ~necesitar~ on the inherited noun ~necesidad~ (from ~necessitātem~). It is cognate with Italian ~necessitare~, and shares its root family with French ~nécessité~, Portuguese ~necessidade~, and English ~necessity~ and ~necessary~, all drawn from the same Latin source.

In classical Latin the idea lived mostly in the impersonal phrase ~necesse est~ (“it is necessary”), so need entered Romance first as a state of affairs rather than an action; Spanish only later shaped it into a plain transitive verb. If the ~ne-~ + ~cēdere~ etymology holds, “to need” is at bottom “to have no room to give way” — necessity as a door that will not open. From the same family Spanish keeps the noun ~necesidad~, the adjective ~necesario~, and the adverb ~necesariamente~, a tidy cluster all pointing back to what cannot be avoided.
en.negar:
From Latin ~negāre~ (“to say no, to deny, to refuse”). The first element is the ancient Proto-Indo-European negator *~ne~ (“not”), the same “no” that runs through half the languages of Europe; the second element is less certain, often connected to a root meaning “to say,” so that ~negāre~ would be, literally, “to say-not.” It gave Italian ~negare~, Portuguese ~negar~, and French ~nier~, and — through Latin ~dēnegāre~ and ~negāre~ — English ~deny~, ~negate~, and ~renege~.

The sense has held remarkably steady: ~negāre~ meant “to deny,” and so does ~negar~ two thousand years later. Its most delightful descendant hides its “no” in plain sight — Latin ~negōtium~ (“business”) is literally ~nec~ (“not”) plus ~ōtium~ (“leisure, rest”): business is the negation of leisure. From it came Spanish ~negocio~ (“business”) and English ~negotiate~. The rest of the family is more transparent: ~negativo~ (“negative”), ~negación~ (“denial”), ~denegar~ (“to refuse”), ~renegar~ (“to renounce”), ~renegado~ (“renegade”), and ~abnegación~ (“self-denial”), each carrying that primordial *~ne~ at its heart.
en.negociar:
From Latin ~negōtiārī~ (“to do business, to trade”), a verb from ~negōtium~ (“business, occupation”), which is transparently ~nec-~/~neg-~ (“not”) plus ~ōtium~ (“leisure, ease”) — literally “not-leisure.” English took ~negotiate~ from the same source, and the Romance cognates include French ~négocier~ and Italian ~negoziare~.

The word is a small philosophy: to a Roman, ~ōtium~ was cultivated leisure, the good life of study and rest, and its negation, ~negōtium~, was everything busy and worldly — trade, affairs, work. So business was defined, wryly, as the absence of leisure. Spanish preserves both halves of the opposition side by side: ~negocio~ (“business”), ~negociante~ (“trader”) and ~negociación~ descend from the ~negōtium~ side, while ~ocio~ (“leisure”) and ~ocioso~ (“idle”) descend from ~ōtium~ — the two words are exact etymological opposites.
en.nombrar:
From Latin ~nōmināre~ (“to name, to call by name”), a verb built on ~nōmen~ (“name”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₁nómn̥~ (“name”). The root is one of the best preserved in the family: it is cognate with English ~name~, German ~Name~, Ancient Greek ~ὄνομα~ (“name”), and Sanskrit ~nā́man~, as well as the Latin-derived English ~nominate~ and ~noun~.

Where Latin ~nōmināre~ meant simply “to utter the name of,” Spanish ~nombrar~ widened toward “to appoint” — to name someone to an office — a sense already latent in Roman administrative usage. The noun ~nombre~ descends directly from ~nōmen~. From the same root Spanish gathered a rich family: ~nómina~ (originally a “list of names,” now a payroll), ~nominar~, ~denominar~, ~renombre~ (“renown”), ~pronombre~, and ~nomenclatura~.
en.notar:
From Latin ~notāre~ (“to mark, jot down, observe”), from ~nota~ (“mark, sign, written note, letter or character”). The deeper origin of ~nota~ is debated: it is often linked to ~nōscere~ (“to come to know”), from earlier ~gnōscere~, from Proto-Indo-European *~ǵneh₃-~ (“to know”) — a ~nota~ being a means of recognition — but the connection is not certain and is best offered with caution. Cognate with Italian ~notare~, French ~noter~ and Portuguese ~notar~, and with English ~note~ and ~notice~.

In Rome ~nota~ covered the mark that identifies a thing, the shorthand signs of the clerk, and the musical note. Spanish ~notar~ kept the perceptual core — “to notice, observe, mark” — while the noun ~nota~ split into everyday senses: a written note, a grade at school, a musical note. The family is large and useful: ~notable~ (“notable”), ~notario~ (a “notary,” literally one who takes notes), ~anotar~ (“to jot down”) and ~notorio~ (“well-known”).
en.notificar:
From Latin ~notificāre~ (“to make known”), a compound of ~notus~ (“known”, past participle of ~noscere~, “to know”) and the combining form ~-ficāre~ (from ~facere~, “to make, do”). ~Noscere~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~ǵneh₃-~ (“to know”), one of the most widely reflected of all roots. Through it ~notificar~ is cognate with English ~know~, ~note~, and ~notice~, with Greek ~gignṓskō~ (“I know”), and with Italian ~notificare~ and French ~notifier~.

The literal force is “to make (something) known” — to render it ~notus~. The ~-ficāre~ half belongs to an enormous productive family (~verificar~, ~clarificar~, ~justificar~), all “making” something. From the same participle ~notus~ Spanish drew ~nota~, ~notar~, ~noticia~, ~notorio~, ~notable~, and ~notario~; and the wider PIE root *~ǵneh₃-~ surfaces in ~conocer~ (from ~cognoscere~), ~ignorar~ (from ~ignorāre~, “not to know”), and even ~noble~ (from ~gnōbilis~, “knowable, well-known”).
en.numerar:
From Latin ~numerāre~ (“to count, number, reckon”), the verb of ~numerus~ (“number”). ~numerus~ arose by rhotacism from Proto-Italic *~nomezos~, from Proto-Indo-European *~nem-~ (“to distribute, allot, take”). The root’s spread is striking: it gave Greek ~némein~ (“to distribute”) and ~nómos~ (“law, custom”), Germanic ~nehmen~ (German “to take”), and, via French ~nombre~, English ~number~.

The core idea is apportioning: to number a set is to deal it out one by one. Spanish ~numerar~ means “to number, to assign numbers,” as of pages or seats. From ~numerus~ Spanish drew ~número~, ~numeroso~, ~numeral~ and ~enumerar~; and from the Greek branch of the same root *~nem-~ — through ~nómos~ — came the international words ~autónomo~, ~economía~ and ~astronomía~, so counting and law-giving share one distant ancestor.
en.obligar:
From Latin ~obligāre~ (“to bind, to tie up, to bind by oath or duty”), a compound of ~ob-~ (“to, toward, against”) and ~ligāre~ (“to bind, to tie”). ~ligāre~ traces to the Proto-Indo-European root *~leyǵ-~ (“to bind”). The verb runs straight through Romance — Italian ~obbligare~, French ~obliger~, Portuguese ~obrigar~ — and through Latin loans it links to English ~oblige~, ~obligate~, ~ligament~, and ~ally~.

The idea is physical bondage made moral: to ~obligar~ is to “bind toward” a duty, to tie someone to an obligation as with a rope. Portuguese kept the image alive in everyday courtesy — ~obrigado~, the ordinary word for “thank you,” means literally “[I am] obliged.” From ~ligāre~ Spanish also draws ~ligar~ (“to tie, to bind”), ~ligamento~, ~liga~ (“league, garter”), ~aliar~ (“to ally”), and ~obligación~. And ~ligāre~ sits at the center of a famous etymological dispute: the origin of ~religión~. Lactantius derived it from ~religāre~ (“to bind fast” — religion as the bond between people and gods), while Cicero had derived it instead from ~relegere~ (“to read over again, to go through carefully”). The two accounts have never been settled, and the word's true origin remains genuinely uncertain.
en.observar:
From Latin ~observāre~ (“to watch over, attend to, heed”), formed from ~ob-~ (“towards, in front of”) and ~servāre~ (“to keep, guard, watch over”). ~Servāre~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~serwāō~ and to a Proto-Indo-European root *~ser-~ (“to protect, watch over”), also seen in Avestan ~haraiti~ (“heeds, protects”). Spanish ~observar~ is cognate with Italian ~osservare~, French ~observer~, Portuguese ~observar~ and English ~observe~. Note that ~servāre~ (“to guard”) is kept distinct by scholars from ~servīre~ (“to serve”), which springs instead from ~servus~ (“slave”).

The core image is guarding: to ~observar~ was first to keep something safe by watching it, and from that vigilant watching grew both meanings the verb carries today — to look attentively (to observe a phenomenon) and to comply, to keep (to observe a rule or a holiday). Latin ~servāre~ “to keep” seeded a productive Spanish family: ~conservar~ (“to conserve”), ~reservar~ (“to reserve”), ~preservar~ (“to preserve”) and the nouns ~observación~ and ~observatorio~. Each still turns on the idea of holding something in careful view — whether a law kept, a resource saved, or a star watched through the night.
en.obtener:
Spanish ~obtener~ comes from Latin ~obtinēre~ (“to hold onto, hold fast, possess”), formed from the prefix ~ob-~ (here “toward, against”) and ~tenēre~ (“to hold”). Because Spanish inherited ~tenēre~ as the everyday verb ~tener~, the compound was reshaped on that model rather than evolving purely by sound law. ~tenēre~ traces to Proto-Indo-European *~ten-~ (“to stretch”), which also lies, distantly, behind English ~thin~. Romance cognates include French ~obtenir~, Italian ~ottenere~ and Portuguese ~obter~.

The sense moved naturally from physically holding something to gaining and securing it — what you obtain is what you get a grip on. The root *~ten-~ (a hand stretched to hold) is one of the most productive in Spanish, giving the whole ~tener~ family: ~contener~ (“to contain”), ~mantener~ (“to maintain”), ~retener~ (“to retain”) and ~detener~ (“to stop, detain”), plus ~teniente~ (“lieutenant,” a place-holder) and the adjective ~tenaz~ (“tenacious”).
en.ocasionar:
Spanish ~ocasionar~ is built on the noun ~ocasión~, from Latin ~occāsiō~ (“opportunity, occasion,” literally “a falling”), from ~occidere~ (“to fall down, to set” — as the sun does), itself ~ob-~ (“down, toward”) plus ~cadere~ (“to fall”). The root is Proto-Indo-European *~ḱad-~ (“to fall”). Through ~cadere~ the family reaches Italian ~cadere~, Portuguese ~cair~, and French ~choir~, and, by borrowing, English ~cadence~, ~accident~, and ~occasion~ itself.

The imagery is of things falling into place: an ~occāsiō~ was the way circumstances came down around you — a chance, a juncture, an opening. Spanish kept that noun as “occasion, opportunity,” and coined ~ocasionar~ to mean making something happen — the occasion that brings a result about. From the same ~cadere~ Spanish inherited ~caer~ (“to fall”) and a rich crop of relatives: ~caso~ (“case, chance”), ~ocaso~ (“sunset, decline” — literally the sun’s falling), ~accidente~, ~cadencia~, ~decaer~, and ~recaer~ (“to relapse”).
en.ocultar:
From Latin ~occultāre~ (“to hide, to keep hidden”), the frequentative of ~occulere~ (“to cover over, conceal”), from ~ob-~ (here intensive) plus a verb akin to ~celāre~ (“to hide”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ḱel-~ (“to cover, to conceal”). This root is unusually productive across languages: through Latin it gives English ~occult~ and ~conceal~, and through Germanic it lies behind English ~hall~ and ~hell~ (both originally “a covered place”) and ~hull~.

Latin ~occultāre~ was the intensive, repeated form of “covering” — to hide something thoroughly, again and again — and Spanish inherited exactly that sense of deliberate concealment. The past participle gave the adjective and noun ~oculto~ (“hidden, occult”), from which ~ocultismo~ (“occultism”) was later coined for the study of hidden knowledge. From the neighbouring ~cella~ (“storeroom, chamber,” also from *~ḱel-~) Spanish draws ~celda~ (“cell”) and the learned ~célula~ — so a monk’s cell and the cell of biology share a root with the very act of hiding.
en.ocupar:
From Latin ~occupāre~ (“to seize, take possession of, occupy”), a compound of ~ob-~ (“over, towards”) and ~capere~ (“to take, seize, grasp”); within the compound ~capere~'s vowel weakened to the ~-cupāre~ seen here. The Proto-Indo-European root is *~keh₂p-~ (“to grasp, seize”). Spanish ~ocupar~ is cognate with Italian ~occupare~, French ~occuper~, Portuguese ~ocupar~ and English ~occupy~; through *~keh₂p-~ it also belongs with English ~capture~ and ~captive~ and the wider Latin ~capere~ family.

To ~ocupar~ was first to lay hold of something — a town, a post, a stretch of land — and from that grasping came the milder senses of filling a space and taking up time, so that a chair, a job, or an afternoon can all be “occupied.” A memorable surprise lurks in the family tree: by the standard account English ~have~ is not related to Latin ~habēre~ at all, but to ~capere~, both from *~keh₂p-~ — the two verbs merely look alike. From ~capere~ Spanish inherited ~caber~ (“to fit”), ~captar~, ~capturar~, ~cazar~ (“to hunt”) and, through its compounds, ~recibir~, ~concebir~ and ~ocupación~.
en.ocurrir:
From Latin ~occurrere~ (“to run to meet, to present itself”), an assimilated compound of ~ob-~ (“toward, to meet”) and ~currere~ (“to run”). ~currere~ comes from Proto-Italic *~korzō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~ḱers-~ (“to run”). The root surfaces in English ~car~ (through Latin ~carrus~) and, by a disputed account, in English ~horse~; the verb itself continues as Italian ~occorrere~ and Portuguese ~ocorrer~.

The picture is vivid: something “runs up to meet” you, and so it “happens” or “occurs.” Spanish keeps that liveliness in the reflexive ~ocurrírsele~ algo a alguien — an idea literally runs up to a person's mind, that is, “it occurs to them.” The event sense and the mental sense have coexisted since Latin. The running-root spread widely in Spanish: ~correr~, ~corriente~, ~carrera~, ~recorrer~, ~concurrir~, ~discurrir~, ~socorrer~, and the school word ~currículo~ (from ~currículum~, “a course, a running”).
en.ofrecer:
From Old Spanish ~ofrecer~ (also ~ofrir~), from a Vulgar Latin inchoative *~offerēscere~ reshaping Latin ~offerre~ (“to present, offer”), a compound of ~ob-~ (“toward, before”) and ~ferre~ (“to carry, bear”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~bʰer-~ (“to bear, carry”). Cognate with Italian ~offrire~, French ~offrir~, and Portuguese ~oferecer~, and — through ~ferre~ and its root — with English ~bear~ and the Latin borrowings ~offer~ and ~transfer~.

The extra syllable in ~ofrecer~ comes from the Latin inchoative suffix ~-ēscere~, which marked the beginning of an action and pulled the verb into the large Spanish ~-ecer~ class alongside ~parecer~, ~crecer~, and ~conocer~. Semantically the word kept ~offerre~'s literal image of “carrying something before” another — to present a gift, a price, resistance, or oneself. Its religious weight survives in ~ofrenda~ (“offering, oblation”) and the participle-noun ~oferta~ (“offer, bargain”), while the shared root ~ferre~ radiates through ~conferir~, ~preferir~, ~referir~, and ~transferir~, and ~ofrecer~ itself yields ~ofrecimiento~ (“offer, offering”).
en.olvidar:
From Vulgar Latin ~oblītāre~, a verb built on the participial stem of Latin ~oblīvīscī~ (“to forget”). The origin of ~oblīvīscī~ is uncertain; by one proposed account it is ~ob-~ plus the root of ~lēvis~ (“smooth”), which would make its literal sense something like “to smooth away” or “erase from the mind” — but this is speculation, not settled fact. Old Spanish had ~oblidar~ (used by Berceo) and ~olbidar~; the modern form is ~olvidar~. Cognate with French ~oublier~ and Catalan ~oblidar~.

Whatever its deepest root, the Latin verb clearly meant losing something from memory, and Spanish kept exactly that. From the same ~oblīvīscī~ English inherited ~oblivion~ and ~oblivious~, the state and the disposition of forgetting. Within Spanish the root yielded the noun ~olvido~ (“forgetting, oblivion”), the adjective ~olvidadizo~ (“forgetful”), and the prized ~inolvidable~ (“unforgettable”).
en.operar:
From Latin ~operārī~ (“to work, labor, be busy”), a deponent verb built on ~opus~ (genitive ~operis~, “work, labor, a work”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₃ep-~ (“to work, produce, to have abundance”). The same noun ~opus~ gave the plural ~opera~, which Spanish and English both borrowed as ~ópera~ / ~opera~ (musical “works”). Cognate Romance forms include Italian ~operare~, French ~opérer~ and Portuguese ~operar~; through the PIE root ~opus~ is kin to Latin ~ops~ (“wealth, resources”), whence Latin ~opulentus~ and Spanish ~opulento~, and to Sanskrit ~ápas~ (“work”).

Latin ~operārī~ meant simply to do work, and Spanish ~operar~ fans out from there: to operate a machine, to bring about an effect (~operar un cambio~), a bank or company that ~opera~ in a market, and — in medicine — to perform surgery, ~operar a un paciente~. That surgical sense, shared with English ~operate~, treats the surgeon's intervention as skilled labor upon the body. The hereditary, popular descendant of ~opera~ is Spanish ~obra~ (“work, deed, building site”), with its verb ~obrar~ (“to act, to work”); learned relatives include ~operación~, ~operario~ (“laborer”), ~opereta~, ~cooperar~ (“to work together”) and ~maniobra~ (“maneuver,” literally hand-work).
en.opinar:
From Latin ~opīnārī~ (also ~opīnor~, “to suppose, think, be of the opinion”). Its deeper origin is disputed: the old and tempting link to ~optāre~ (“to choose, wish”) is judged weak by modern etymologists, and de Vaan instead connects it to a Proto-Indo-European *~h₃ep-~ (“to take, grasp, choose”), seen in Hittite and Sanskrit — but the reconstruction is not secure and should be taken as one proposal, not settled fact. It is cognate with Italian ~opinare~ and French ~opiner~, and gave English ~opine~ and ~opinion~.

The verb kept its Latin job almost unchanged: to ~opinar~ is to hold and state a view, and the noun ~opinión~ is what results. Because the family stayed close to its abstract, mental core, its Spanish offshoots are few and transparent — ~opinable~ (“debatable, a matter of opinion”) and ~opinante~ (“one who opines”) — rather than a sprawling word-family. A Praenestine spelling ~opeinor~ from the third century BC shows the old diphthong that any correct etymology must explain.
en.oponer:
From Latin ~oppōnere~ (“to set against, place before, oppose”), a compound of ~ob-~ (“against, facing”) and ~pōnere~ (“to put, place”). ~pōnere~ is itself, by surface analysis, ~po-~ (“off, away”) plus ~sinere~ (“to let, leave”), and passes through Old Latin ~posnō~ to Proto-Italic; its ~po-~ element goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~h₂epó~ (“off, away”), the same particle behind English ~of~ and ~off~. From ~oppōnere~ descend Italian ~opporre~, Portuguese ~opor~, and French ~opposer~, while the whole ~pōnere~ clan gave the international -pose words: componer, exponer, depositar, proponer.

In Latin the participle was ~oppositus~, and the ~pōnere~/~positus~ split runs right through Spanish: the verb keeps the ~pon-~ stem (~oponer~, ~poner~, ~componer~, ~exponer~) while the nominal forms take ~posición~, ~oposición~, ~opuesto~. To oppose is literally to “place one thing over against another,” a spatial metaphor that hardened into the modern sense of resistance and rivalry. Cousins in the same family are legion: ~puesto~, ~posar~, ~apostar~, ~depósito~, ~propósito~, and the everyday ~oposición~ that names Spain’s competitive civil-service exams.
en.optar:
From Latin ~optāre~ (“to choose, to wish, to desire”), a verb whose deeper origin is uncertain. It appears to continue a Proto-Italic frequentative *~opetāō~ (from *~opeō~), otherwise preserved only in Umbrian ~upetu~, and no secure Proto-Indo-European root has been established for it. Alongside Spanish stand Italian ~optare~ and Portuguese ~optar~, together with the learned family that ~optāre~ generated within Latin itself.

Latin ~optāre~ carried both “to choose” and “to wish,” and Spanish ~optar~ keeps mainly the first — to opt for one path among several. The related noun ~optiō~ (“a choosing, a free choice”) gave Spanish ~opción~, while the compound ~adoptāre~ (“to choose to oneself”) gave ~adoptar~ — literally to choose a child into one’s family. Other members are the grammatical ~optativo~ (the “wishing” mood) and ~cooptar~ (to choose someone onto a body by the votes of its own members). Because the root itself is so obscure, here is a family whose branches are far clearer than its trunk.
en.optimizar:
Spanish ~optimizar~ is a modern derivative of ~óptimo~ (“optimal, best”) with the verb-forming suffix ~-izar~ (from Greek ~-ίζειν~ through Latin ~-izāre~). ~Óptimo~ descends from Latin ~optimus~ (“best”), which served as the suppletive superlative of ~bonus~ (“good”) — a paradigm that limped along on three unrelated stems, ~bonus~ / ~melior~ / ~optimus~. Italian ~ottimo~ and the English learned borrowings ~optimum~ and ~optimal~ share the same Latin source.

The deeper origin of ~optimus~ is disputed. By one account it is built on ~ops~ (“power, wealth, resources”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₃ep-~ (“to work, produce in abundance”), with a sense shift from “richest” to “most esteemed”; de Vaan instead reconstructs a superlative tied to ~ob~ (“in front of”). Either way, ~optimizar~ itself is a young, technical coinage — “to make optimal” — that spread with 19th- and 20th-century science alongside ~optimista~, ~optimismo~, and ~optimización~, the vocabulary of expecting, and engineering, the best.
en.ordenar:
From Latin ~ōrdināre~ (“to arrange, set in order, appoint”), a verb built on ~ōrdō~ (genitive ~ōrdinis~, “row, rank, order”), of uncertain deeper origin but perhaps connected with ~ōrdīrī~ (“to lay the warp, begin weaving”). Cognate with Italian ~ordinare~, French ~ordonner~, and Portuguese ~ordenar~; English took the same word through ~ordain~ and ~order~.

~ōrdō~ first named a concrete row — one traditional account traces it to the ordered threads of the warp on a loom — and from “row, rank” came “arrangement” and “command” (an order both organizes and instructs). Spanish ~ordenar~ carries all these: to put in order, to give an order, and to ordain a priest. The same ~ōrdō~ gave ~orden~ (“order”), ~ordenador~ (“computer,” in Spain), ~coordinar~, ~subordinar~, and ~ordinario~; through Latin ~ōrnāre~, a syncopated form of ~ōrdināre~, come ~adornar~ and ~ornamento~.
en.organizar:
From Medieval Latin ~organizāre~ (“to furnish with organs, to arrange into a working whole”), from Latin ~organum~ (“instrument, tool, organ”), borrowed from Ancient Greek ~órganon~ (ὄργανον, “tool, instrument”). ~órganon~ derives from ~érgon~ (“work, deed”) and the Proto-Indo-European *~werǵ-~ (“to do, to work”). That root is shared, remarkably, with English ~work~ and German ~Werk~. Spanish took ~organizar~ through learned channels. Cognate with Italian ~organizzare~ and French ~organiser~.

The chain of sense is elegant: an ~órganon~ was a tool for doing work, then a bodily “instrument” (an organ), and a body is many organs cooperating — so to ~organizar~ is to make separate parts function together like the organs of a living whole. The word lived in Spanish first in that biological and musical sense (the ~órgano~, the church instrument of many pipes) before it broadened to committees and revolutions. From the same *~werǵ-~ come ~órgano~, ~organismo~, ~orgía~ (Greek rites, literally “workings”), ~cirugía~ (“hand-work”), and ~energía~.
en.orientar:
From ~oriente~ (“the East”), from Latin ~oriēns~ (“rising”), the present participle of ~orīrī~ (“to rise, to come forth”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₃er-~ (“to rise, to move, to stir”). The East is simply where the sun rises. It is cognate, through that root, with Latin ~orīgō~ (“origin, source”) and Ancient Greek ~ὄρνυμι~ (“to rouse, to set in motion”); English ~origin~ and ~orient~ are Latin-borrowed kin.

To ~orientar~ meant first, quite literally, to align something toward the East — a habit visible in medieval churches built to face the sunrise and in old maps drawn with the East, ~oriente~, at the top; only later did it soften into “to guide, to position.” Its opposite, ~desorientar~ (“to disorient”), is the loss of that bearing. From the same rising-root come ~origen~, ~originar~, ~orto~ (“sunrise, the rising of a star”), and even ~aborto~ (“miscarriage”), from Latin ~aborīrī~ — to “rise away,” to fail to come forth.
en.originar:
From Latin ~orīginārī~ / ~orīgināre~, from ~orīgō~ (“a rising, source, beginning, lineage”), a noun built on ~orīrī~ (“to rise, arise, be born, appear above the horizon”). ~orīrī~ comes from Proto-Italic *~orjōr~ and Proto-Indo-European *~h₃er-~ (“to move, stir, rise”). Spanish ~originar~ is a learned borrowing; the noun ~origen~ (“origin”) came in the same way. Cognate with Italian ~originare~, French ~origine~, and — through ~orīgō~ — with English ~origin~ and ~original~.

~orīrī~ meant literally “to rise,” and its present participle ~oriēns~ (“rising”) named the direction of the rising sun — which is why the East is the ~Oriente~ and English says ~orient~. The same verb gave ~oriundo~ (“native, hailing from”) and ~aborigen~ (from ~ab orīgine~, “from the beginning”). Strikingly, its opposite lives in the same family: Latin ~aborīrī~ (“to miscarry, pass away,” literally “to rise away, fail to rise”) is the source of ~abortar~ — so ~originar~ and ~abortar~, beginning and failing-to-begin, spring from one root. To ~originar~ something is to make it rise into being; the metaphor is a sunrise.
en.otorgar:
From Vulgar Latin *~auctōricāre~ (“to authorize, vouch for, endorse”), from Latin ~auctor~ (“author, originator, one who vouches”), from ~augēre~ (“to increase, augment”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂ewg-~ (“to increase, grow”). The road to Spanish ran through monophthongization of ~au~, syncope, and the voicing of the inner consonant, turning *~auctōricāre~ into ~otorgar~. It is cognate with Old French ~otreier~ (Modern French ~octroyer~, “to grant”) and Occitan ~autrejar~; through ~augēre~ it is kin to English ~author~, ~augment~, and ~auction~, and to the Germanic ~wax~ (“to grow”).

An ~auctor~ was one who backs or guarantees, so *~auctōricāre~ meant to give one's backing — and Spanish ~otorgar~ still means to grant, bestow, or consent, keeping a legal flavor (one ~otorgar~ a will or a power of attorney). The patrimonial ~otorgar~ has a learned twin, ~autorizar~ (from Medieval Latin ~auctorizāre~), and shares the family with ~auge~, ~aumentar~, ~augusto~, and ~autoridad~ — all growing from the idea of increase.
en.oír:
From Latin ~audīre~ (“to hear”), from Proto-Italic *~awizdiō~, generally analyzed as a compound of a Proto-Indo-European element *~h₂ewis-~ (“clearly, manifestly”) and the verbal root *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to put, to render”) — literally “to render clear to the senses.” It is cognate with Ancient Greek ~αἰσθάνομαι~ (“to perceive”) and Sanskrit ~āvís~ (“manifestly”), and its Romance siblings include Italian ~udire~ and Portuguese ~ouvir~.

The intervocalic Latin d fell away as the word passed into Old Spanish, reducing four syllables to the terse modern ~oír~; the same erosion shaped French ~ouïr~, once the ordinary verb “to hear” and now archaic. A vivid relative is ~obedecer~ (“to obey”), from Latin ~oboedīre~ — ~ob-~ (“toward”) plus ~audīre~ — literally “to lend one's ear toward” someone. From the same Latin verb Spanish also draws ~audición~, ~auditorio~, ~audible~, ~oyente~, and the borrowing ~audio~.
en.padecer:
From Old Spanish ~padecer~ (also ~padescer~), from a Late/Vulgar Latin *~patēscere~, an inchoative built with the suffix ~-ēscere~ on the deponent verb ~patī~ (“to suffer, endure, undergo”), first person ~patior~. The Proto-Indo-European source is usually given as *~peh₁(i)-~ (“to hurt”), but it is uncertain, so it is offered here only tentatively. Cognate with Italian ~patire~ and Portuguese ~padecer~, with French ~pâtir~, and — through the participle ~passus~ — with English ~passion~ and ~passive~, and through ~patient~ (from ~patiēns~).

The Latin ~patī~ was morally neutral: it meant to undergo or experience whatever befalls one, good or ill. From its participle ~passus~ that idea fanned out remarkably, giving English ~passion~ (originally the enduring of suffering, as in the Passion of Christ), the grammatical ~passive~ (the voice whose subject undergoes the action rather than performing it), and ~patient~, literally “one who endures.” Spanish ~padecer~ narrowed the sense to bearing hardship or illness: one ~padece~ a disease, a hunger, a heartbreak. Kindred Spanish words abound: ~paciencia~, ~paciente~, ~pasión~, ~pasivo~, ~compasión~ (“a suffering-with”), and the noun ~padecimiento~ (“ailment, suffering”).
en.pagar:
Spanish ~pagar~ comes from Late Latin ~pācāre~ (“to pacify, appease, satisfy”), a verb on ~pāx~ (“peace”). ~pāx~ goes back, through Proto-Italic *~pāks~, to Proto-Indo-European *~peh₂ḱ-~ (“to fasten, join”) — peace conceived as the binding-together of parties — a root shared with Latin ~pangere~ (“to fix, fasten”) and ~pacīscī~ (“to make a pact”). Its Romance reflexes include French ~payer~, Portuguese ~pagar~, Italian ~pagare~, and Catalan ~pagar~; English ~pay~ was borrowed from Old French ~paiier~.

The meaning traveled a very human road: to ~pācāre~ a creditor was to “appease” him, and appeasing a creditor means handing over money — so “pacify” slid into “pay.” The old sense still peeks through: someone ~pagado de sí mismo~ is “pleased with himself,” satisfied rather than paid. From ~pāx~ Spanish gathered ~paz~ (“peace”), ~pago~ (“payment”), ~pagador~, ~pacífico~, ~pacto~, and ~apaciguar~ (“to appease”). Most striking is ~apagar~ (“to switch off, extinguish”), from Vulgar Latin *~appācāre~: to quiet a flame is, quite literally, to make peace with it.
en.paginar:
A modern, learned formation from the noun ~página~ (“page”), which Spanish took from Latin ~pāgina~ (“page, column of writing, leaf of papyrus”). ~pāgina~ derives from ~pangere~ (“to fix, fasten, drive in”), from Proto-Italic *~pangō~ and Proto-Indo-European *~peh₂ǵ-~ (“to attach, fasten”). ~paginar~ itself is not an inherited word but was coined on the Latin stem to mean “to number the pages.” Cognate with French ~paginer~ and Italian ~paginare~; through the root, ~página~ is kin to English ~page~ and — via Latin ~pāx~ (“peace, a binding agreement”) — to English ~pact~ and Spanish ~paz~.

How a word for “fastening” came to mean “page” is debated. The usual account runs through the making of a book: separate sheets were fastened together, so a ~pāgina~ was a fixed-in leaf. Ayto and Watkins propose a more agricultural image, offered as an alternative rather than settled fact: a ~pāgina~ was first a trellis of vines fastened to stakes, whose orderly rows suggested the columns of writing on a scroll. Either way the root idea is “things fixed in ordered ranks.” From the same ~pangere~ Spanish holds ~compaginar~ (“to collate, make consistent”), and from the wider root *~peh₂ǵ-~ come ~pacto~ (“pact”) and ~paz~ (“peace”). To ~paginar~ a document is, at bottom, to fasten an order onto its pages.
en.parar:
From Latin ~parāre~ (“to prepare, make ready”), from Proto-Italic *~parō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~perh₃-~ (“to grant, provide”). Cognate with Italian ~parare~, Portuguese ~parar~, and French ~parer~ (“to adorn, parry”); from the same Latin verb English drew ~prepare~ and ~apparatus~.

The Latin verb meant “to prepare, arrange,” and in Ibero-Romance it drifted from readying something toward halting and coming to rest — perhaps by way of “to set in position, hold in place.” The sources record the shift but do not fully explain it, so the intermediate step is best offered as a plausible bridge rather than a settled fact. That is why modern Spanish uses the verb for stopping a bus, warding off a blow, and ending up somewhere. The noun ~paro~ carries this to its conclusion — a work stoppage, unemployment, even a cardiac arrest — and ~parada~ names a bus stop or a military parade. From the same Latin verb Spanish also built ~preparar~, ~reparar~, ~amparar~ (“to shelter”), and the noun ~aparato~ (“apparatus, device”).
en.parecer:
From Old Spanish ~pareçer~, from Vulgar Latin *~parēscere~, an inchoative formed on Latin ~pārēre~ (“to appear, become visible, show oneself”). The inchoative suffix ~-ēscere~ marked a coming-into-view, which the ~-ecer~ ending of Spanish still carries. Cognate with Italian ~parere~, French ~paraître~, Portuguese ~parecer~, and Catalan ~parèixer~; through Latin ~appārēre~ English is kin by way of ~appear~ and ~apparent~.

Latin ~pārēre~ meant “to come into sight”; the inchoative *~parēscere~ stressed the moment of appearing, and from “to appear” Spanish ~parecer~ slid naturally into “to seem” — for what appears is not always what is. Reflexive ~parecerse~ took the further step to “to resemble,” and the noun use in ~el parecer~ means an “opinion,” literally how a thing appears to someone. The prefixed ~aparecer~ (“to appear”) and ~desaparecer~ (“to disappear”) stayed closer to the root sense, while ~comparecer~ (“to appear in court”) narrowed it to legal presence. From the same base come ~aparición~, ~apariencia~, ~parecido~, and ~aparente~.
en.parir:
From Latin ~parere~ (also ~parĕre~, “to give birth, to bring forth, to produce”), from Proto-Italic *~parjō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~perh₃-~ (“to bring forth, to grant, to allot”). The root shows up in Ancient Greek ~époron~ (“I gave, granted”), Sanskrit ~pṛṇā́ti~ (“grants, bestows”), and — through the Latin agent noun ~parēns~ — in English ~parent~. Sisters of ~parere~ are Italian ~parire~ and Portuguese ~parir~.

The Latin verb meant productive bringing-forth of every kind, but Spanish narrowed ~parir~ almost entirely to animal and human birth, giving it a blunt, earthy register beside the polite ~dar a luz~ (“to give to the light”). A vivid relative hides in ~víbora~ (“viper”): Latin ~vīpera~ was understood as ~vīvus~ + ~parere~, “the one that bears its young alive” — an ancient (if not strictly accurate) belief about the snake. Other kin include ~parto~ (“childbirth”), ~parturienta~, ~posparto~, and the -parous words ~vivíparo~ and ~ovíparo~. Note that ~parere~ (“give birth”) is a different verb from ~parāre~ (“prepare”), which fathered ~preparar~ and ~reparar~.
en.participar:
From Latin ~participāre~ (“to share, to partake”), from the adjective ~particeps~ (“sharing, partaking”), a compound of ~pars~ (“part”) and ~capere~ (“to take, to seize”) — literally “taking a part.” ~capere~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~keh₂p-~ (“to grasp”). Cognate with French ~participer~, Italian ~partecipare~, and English ~participate~ and ~participle~.

The image behind the word is delightfully literal: to participate is to take your portion of something shared. Latin ~particeps~ was originally an everyday adjective for anyone who had a share in an affair. From ~pars~ Spanish drew a large family — ~parte~, ~partícipe~, ~participio~ (the grammatical “participle,” which likewise “shares” properties of verb and adjective), and ~partido~ (“party, match”). The other half, ~capere~, is even more prolific, giving ~caber~ (“to fit”), ~captar~, and even ~cazar~ (“to hunt,” i.e., to catch). To take part, in short, is to seize your slice.
en.partir:
Spanish ~partir~ descends from Latin ~partīre~ (also deponent ~partīrī~, “to divide, to share out”), a verb built on the noun ~pars~ (stem ~partis~, “a part, a share”). The deeper prehistory of ~pars~ is debated: it is usually linked with Latin ~pār~ (“equal”), ~portiō~ (“portion”) and ~parāre~ (“to make ready”), but the Proto-Indo-European root behind them is disputed and no single reconstruction is secure. Romance cognates are plentiful — French ~partir~, Italian ~partire~, Portuguese ~partir~ — and English ~part~ was borrowed from the same Latin stock.

~partir~ still means both “to split” and “to share,” but it also took on the sense “to depart” — to part from company, to set out (~partir de viaje~, “to leave on a trip”); French carried that branch all the way, so its ~partir~ means simply “to leave.” The noun ~pars~ underlies a broad Spanish family: ~parte~ (“part”), ~partido~ (“party; match”), ~partícula~ (“particle”), ~repartir~ (“to distribute”), ~compartir~ (“to share”) and the musical ~partitura~ (“score”).
en.pasar:
From Late Latin ~passāre~, a frequentative of Latin ~passus~ (“a step, a pace”), originally the past participle of ~pandere~ (“to spread out, to stretch”), from Proto-Indo-European *~peth₂-~ (“to spread”). Cognate with Italian ~passare~, French ~passer~, and Portuguese ~passar~; English ~pass~ entered through Old French rather than directly from Latin.

The image at the root is bodily: a ~passus~ was the stretch of the legs in a single stride, and by extension the Roman unit of distance measured by that stride. From “to take a step” the verb widened to “to move past, to cross, to go through,” and then to the whole sweep of senses Spanish now gives it — to happen (« ¿qué pasa? »), to spend time, to pass an exam, to hand something over. The same family seeded ~paso~ (“step”), ~pasaje~ (“passage, fare”), ~pasaporte~ (literally a warrant to ~pasar~ a port or gate), ~paseo~ (“a stroll”), and the ubiquitous ~pasado~ (“the past; passed”).
en.pasear:
A derivative of ~paso~ (“step, pace”) with the frequentative-flavored suffix ~-ear~, giving the sense of stepping about at leisure. ~paso~ comes from Latin ~passus~ (“a step, pace”), originally the past participle of ~pandere~ (“to spread, stretch out”) — a pace being the stretch opened between the feet. ~passus~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~patstus~ and Proto-Indo-European *~peth₂-~ (“to spread”). Through French it gave English ~pace~ and ~pass~, and Italian has ~passeggiare~ (“to stroll”).

The suffix ~-ear~ often adds a sense of repeated, unhurried action, and that is exactly the difference between ~pasar~ (“to pass, go by”) and ~pasear~ (“to stroll, take a walk”) — not to cross a distance but to step along it for pleasure. Its noun is ~paseo~ (“a walk; a promenade”). From the same ~passus~ Spanish also has ~paso~, ~pasar~, ~pasaje~, ~pasillo~ (“corridor”) and ~compás~ (“a pair of compasses; a beat”), while ~pandere~ itself surfaces in ~expandir~ (“to expand”).
en.pedir:
From Latin ~petere~ (“to make for, to seek, to ask, to aim at, even to attack”), from Proto-Indo-European *~peth₂-~ (“to fly, to rush”). The root’s flight-sense shows plainly in its cognates: Greek ~pétomai~ (“I fly”) and ~píptō~ (“I fall”), Sanskrit ~pátati~ (“flies, falls”), and — through Germanic — English ~feather~, literally “the flying thing.” In Romance, Portuguese ~pedir~ is the direct sibling; Italian and French chose other verbs for “to ask.”

The semantic heart is motion toward a target: ~petere~ first meant to rush at or make for something, which is why the one verb could mean both “to attack” and “to request” — to ask is to launch yourself at what you want. Spanish wore the sound down to the humble ~pedir~, but the vigorous original survives in a crowd of learned relatives: ~petición~ (“petition, request”), ~competir~ (“to compete,” to seek alongside), ~apetito~ (“appetite,” a seeking-toward), ~ímpetu~ (“impetus, a rushing upon”), ~repetir~ (“to seek again”), and ~perpetuo~ (“continually rushing onward”). English shares the set through ~petition~, ~compete~, ~appetite~, and ~impetus~.
en.pegar:
From Latin ~picāre~ (“to coat with pitch”), from ~pix~, genitive ~picis~ (“pitch, tar”), from Proto-Indo-European *~pik-~. A genuine cognate is Greek ~πίσσα~ (~píssa~, “pitch”); English ~pitch~ comes from the very same Latin ~pix~, borrowed into Old English. Romance kept the verb as Portuguese ~pegar~ (“to stick; to catch”) and Italian ~appiccare~.

The first meaning was concrete: pitch is glue, so ~picāre~ meant to join, stick, or fasten one thing to another — and ~pegar~ still means “to glue, to stick.” The sense “to hit,” the everyday modern one, came later; by Corominas's account it grew out of “to press close up against” → “to set upon” → “to land blows,” and the blow-dealing ~pegar~ is well attested by the age of the Quixote. The adhesive root lives on in ~pegamento~ (“glue”), ~pegajoso~ (“sticky”), ~pez~ (“pitch” itself), and — best of all — ~despegar~, “to unstick,” which is also the Spanish word for an airplane's takeoff.
en.pelear:
A Spanish derivative of ~pelo~ (“hair”) plus the verbal suffix ~-ear~. ~pelo~ descends from Latin ~pilus~ (“a hair”), of disputed deeper origin but often linked to a Proto-Indo-European base *~pilo-~ (“hair”). Cognate through ~pilus~ with Italian ~pelo~ and French ~poil~, and with the borrowed English ~pile~ (the raised nap of a fabric) and ~plush~.

This is the famous etymology where fighting begins with hair: the traditional account, given in the standard dictionaries, derives ~pelear~ from ~pelo~ on the image of two combatants grabbing and pulling each other's hair — literally “to come to hairs.” From that vivid picture the verb generalized to fighting and quarreling of every kind, physical or verbal, and reflexive ~pelearse~ covers falling out with a friend. The same ~pelo~ gave Spanish ~peludo~ (“hairy”), ~pelaje~ (“coat, fur”), ~peluca~ (“wig”), ~pelusa~, and ~peluquero~ (“barber, hairdresser”).
en.pensar:
From Old Spanish ~pensar~, from Latin ~pēnsāre~ (“to weigh, ponder”), the frequentative of ~pendere~ (“to weigh, to hang”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~(s)pend-~ (“to pull, stretch”).
