Spanish ~plaza~ descends from Latin ~platea~ (“broad street, courtyard”), borrowed from Ancient Greek ~πλατεῖα~ (plateîa, “broad”), the feminine of ~πλατύς~ (platýs, “broad, flat”), from Proto-Indo-European *~pleth₂-~ (“flat, to spread”). The very same elements built French ~remplacer~ and, through Old French, English ~place~; Italian has the parallel ~rimpiazzare~.

To ~reemplazar~ is literally to put one thing “in the place” of another, again — the noun ~plaza~ (a town’s open place) and the verb of substitution grow from one image of open, level ground. The broad-and-flat root spread widely in Spanish: ~plaza~, ~plato~ (“plate,” a flat dish, also from ~πλατύς~), ~chato~ (“flat-nosed”), and ~aplastar~ (“to flatten, squash”) all descend from it, as does — in English — the everyday word ~place~ itself.
en.referir:
Directly from Latin ~referre~ (“to carry back, to bring back word, to report”), a compound of ~re-~ (“back, again”) and ~ferre~ (“to carry, to bear”). ~ferre~ traces to Proto-Italic *~ferō~ and to Proto-Indo-European *~bʰer-~ (“to carry, to bear”), the same immensely productive root that gives Ancient Greek ~phérō~, Sanskrit ~bhárati~, and English ~bear~. The verb lives on in Italian ~riferire~, French ~référer~, and Portuguese ~referir~.

The core image is concrete — to carry something back to a source or a listener — which is why ~referir~ spans “to recount,” “to report,” and, reflexively as ~referirse~, “to allude to.” A fossil of Roman grammar rides along in ~referéndum~: it is a gerundive, literally “matters that must be carried back” to the people for a vote. English borrowed the same stem for ~referee~ and ~reference~. Within Spanish the compound sits beside its siblings ~conferir~, ~inferir~, ~proferir~, and ~transferir~, and beside the noun family ~referencia~ and ~relación~.
en.reflejar:
From Latin ~reflexus~ (“bent back, reflected”), the past participle of ~reflectere~ (“to bend back”), a compound of ~re-~ (“back”) and ~flectere~ (“to bend”), a verb of uncertain deeper origin. Spanish did not inherit its verb straight from ~reflectere~; instead Romance rebuilt it on the noun ~reflejo~, itself descended from ~reflexus~, and from that noun derived ~reflejar~. It is cognate with English ~reflect~ and ~reflex~, with Italian ~riflettere~, French ~réfléchir~, and Portuguese ~reflectir~.

The Latin verb described a physical bending-back — of a road, an arm, and above all of light — and that optical sense still dominates: a mirror ~refleja~ an image. From there grew the figure of thought, so that a face may reflect an emotion or a novel reflect its age. The same root fed a large learned family in Spanish, including ~reflexión~, ~reflexivo~, ~reflector~ and the doublet verb ~reflectar~; and beyond the ~re-~ prefix, ~flectere~ itself gave ~flexible~ and ~flexión~.
en.reflexionar:
~reflexionar~ is a denominal verb, built in Spanish on the noun ~reflexión~, which comes from Latin ~reflexiō~ (“a bending back”), the action noun of ~reflectere~ (“to bend back”). That verb joins the prefix ~re-~ (“back”) to ~flectere~ (“to bend, curve”), a Latin verb whose deeper origin is uncertain and has no secure Indo-European pedigree. Through ~flectere~ and its participle ~flexus~, ~reflexionar~ is kin to English ~reflect~, ~flexible~ and ~inflection~, to French ~réfléchir~, and to Spanish ~reflejar~ — a doublet that took the popular route while ~reflexionar~ kept the learned Latin ~-x-~.

The metaphor is optical: light ~reflectere~ “bends back” from a surface, and Latin already used the verb for turning the mind back upon itself. Spanish split the inheritance into two words: ~reflejar~ for the physical bouncing of light or images, and ~reflexionar~ for the mental act of bending thought back — pondering. So a mirror ~refleja~ your face, but you ~reflexionas~ over a decision. The ~flectere~ family fans out across Spanish in ~flexible~, ~reflejo~, ~inflexión~, ~circunflejo~, ~deflexión~ and ~flexionar~, every one preserving the ancient idea of a bend or curve.
en.reforzar:
From ~re-~ (“again, intensively”) plus ~forzar~ (“to force”), the latter from Vulgar Latin *~fortiāre~, from Late Latin ~fortia~ (“strength, force” — a neuter plural of ~fortis~ reinterpreted as a feminine singular), ultimately from Latin ~fortis~ (“strong”). It thus shares its root with ~fortalecer~. Cognate with Italian ~rinforzare~, French ~renforcer~, and English ~reinforce~ and ~force~ itself.

The pivot of the word is ~fortia~. Classical Latin had no such feminine noun; speakers took the neuter plural of ~fortis~ — “strong things” — and re-heard it as a single feminine “strength,” which became Spanish ~fuerza~. From ~fuerza~ came the verb ~forzar~, and ~reforzar~ simply adds ~re-~ to give “to strengthen again, to reinforce.” The prefix here is intensive as much as repetitive: to ~reforzar~ a wall or an argument is to pile more strength onto it. Close kin sit all around it — ~fuerza~, ~forzar~, ~esforzarse~ (“to exert oneself”), ~fuerte~ (“strong”), and its near-synonym ~fortalecer~.
en.regalar:
The origin of ~regalar~ is debated. The account favored by Corominas and the DLE takes it from French ~régaler~ (“to entertain lavishly, to feast”), a derivative of Old French ~gale~ (“merriment, pleasure”) — the same root that gave ~galante~ and ~gala~ — and probably of Germanic origin. A rival, popular account instead derives it from Latin ~regalis~ (“royal, kingly,” from ~rēx~, “king”), so that to ~regalar~ someone would be to treat them like a king. The forms are close enough to have long been confused, but the Romance philologists lean toward the French ~gale~, not the Latin ~rēx~.

Whichever etymology is right, the modern sense is young: for centuries ~regalar~ meant to entertain, delight or treat sumptuously — to ~regalar~ a guest was to lavish food, comfort and honor on them — and the everyday meaning “to give a gift” is only clearly attested in the eighteenth century. From it Spanish formed ~regalo~ (“gift”) and the adjective ~regalado~ (“given freely; dirt-cheap; luxurious”). The seductive image of “treating someone like a king” is memorable, but it belongs to the contested ~regalis~ derivation; on the account most philologists prefer, ~regalar~ is instead cousin to ~gala~ and ~galante~, words of festivity and courtly display rather than royalty.
en.regir:
From Latin ~regere~ (“to rule, guide, direct, keep straight”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₃reǵ-~ (“to straighten, to rule”). Cognate with Italian ~reggere~ and French ~régir~, and — through the same root — with English ~right~ and ~regent~, Latin ~rēx~ (“king”), and Sanskrit ~rāj-~.

The root’s core image is the straight line: to rule was to keep a people, a course, or a rule literally straight, and ~regir~ still carries that steering sense — a law that ~rige~, a principle that governs conduct. Latin ~regere~ came into Spanish twice: learnedly as ~regir~, and by popular descent — through the ~-igere~ shift — in verbs like ~erguir~ (“to raise upright”). The same root *~h₃reǵ-~ seeded one of Spanish’s largest families: ~rey~ (“king”), ~reino~, ~regla~ and ~reja~ (both from ~rēgula~), ~régimen~, ~región~, ~recto~, ~regir~’s compounds ~corregir~ and ~dirigir~, and the borrowed ~real~ and ~regalía~.
en.registrar:
From ~registro~ (“register, record”), borrowed from Medieval Latin ~registrum~, an alteration of Late Latin ~regesta~ (“a list, things recorded”) — the neuter plural of ~regestus~, past participle of ~regerere~ (“to carry back, record, enter”). That verb is ~re-~ (“back”) plus ~gerere~ (“to carry, bear, conduct”), from Proto-Italic *~gezō~. The word travelled across Europe: English ~register~, French ~registre~, Italian ~registro~, all from the same medieval Latin source.

The literal notion was that of “carrying things back” into a record — entering them where they can be retrieved — and Spanish ~registrar~ still spans the whole range: to record, to enter in a register, and (perhaps surprisingly) to search or frisk, as customs officers ~registran~ luggage. From ~gerere~, “to carry, manage,” Spanish inherited a rich crop: ~gesto~ (“gesture,” a thing carried out), ~gestión~, ~gerente~, ~digerir~, ~sugerir~ and ~congerie~.
en.regresar:
From Latin ~regressus~, the past participle of ~regredī~ (“to go back, return”), from ~re-~ (“back”) plus ~gradī~ (“to step, walk”), itself from ~gradus~ (“step, pace, degree”). The ultimate source is Proto-Indo-European *~gʰredʰ-~ (“to walk, go”). Spanish built ~regresar~ on the participial stem rather than inheriting the old verb directly. The base ~gradī~ is also the well of Italian and Portuguese ~gradual~, French ~degré~ (“degree”), and — through Latin compounds — the English borrowings ~progress~, ~congress~, ~aggression~ and ~degree~, all of them literally about stepping forward, together, or against.

In Latin ~regredī~ was a plain verb of motion — to step back the way one came. Spanish ~regresar~ keeps that concrete core (“to return, come back”), and in much of Latin America it is the ordinary word for going home, alongside ~volver~. The same participial pattern gave the noun ~regreso~ (“return”) and the adjective ~regresivo~ (“regressive”). The ~gradī~ family is enormous in Spanish: ~grado~ (“degree, grade”), ~gradual~, ~grada~ (“tier, step”), ~progreso~, ~ingresar~ (“to enter, deposit”), ~egresar~ (“to graduate,” American Spanish), ~agredir~ (“to attack,” literally to step toward) and ~transgredir~ (“to transgress,” to step across). Every one hides a footstep inside it.
en.regular:
From Late Latin ~rēgulāre~ (“to control by rule”), from Latin ~rēgula~ (“a straight stick, a ruler, hence a rule”), from ~regere~ (“to keep straight, to direct, to rule”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₃reǵ-~ (“to straighten, to direct, to make right”). This is one of the great PIE roots: cognate with English ~right~ and ~rule~, German ~recht~ (“right”), and — through the Latin ~rēx~ (“king”) — with Spanish ~rey~.

The ~rēgula~ was first a carpenter's straightedge — the physical bar against which things were made true — and ~regular~ still carries that image of bringing something into measure. A homely cousin is ~arreglar~ (“to fix, arrange, tidy”), from Vulgar Latin ~adregulāre~ — literally to bring back to the rule. From the same directing-root Spanish holds ~regla~ (“rule, ruler”), ~regir~ (“to govern”), ~régimen~, ~dirigir~ (“to direct”), and ~corregir~ (“to correct,” to straighten alongside).
en.reiterar:
From Latin ~reiterāre~ (“to repeat, say again”), built from the prefix ~re-~ (“again”) and ~iterāre~ (“to do a second time”), which comes from the adverb ~iterum~ (“again, anew”). ~iterum~ itself was formed on the Proto-Indo-European pronominal root *~i-~ (the source also of Latin ~is~, “he, that one”); an alternative analysis routes it through *~h₁íteros~ (“other”). Spanish ~reiterar~ has close relatives in Italian ~reiterare~, French ~réitérer~ and English ~reiterate~ and ~iterate~.

The meaning has held remarkably steady — to reiterate is simply to say a thing again — which is fitting for a word literally meaning “to other-times it.” The same pronominal stem underlies Latin ~item~ (“likewise, also”), borrowed whole into English as the noun ~item~, once a word that introduced each new entry on a list (“item, …; item, …”). From the Latin verb Spanish draws ~reiteración~, ~iterar~, ~iteración~ and ~iterativo~, the last now at home in mathematics and computing.
en.relacionar:
A modern denominal verb: Spanish ~relación~ (“relation”) plus the verb-forming ~-ar~. ~relación~ comes from Latin ~relātiōnem~ (accusative of ~relātiō~, “a carrying back, a report”), built on ~relātus~, the participle of ~referre~ (“to carry back, to report”), from ~re-~ (“back”) and ~ferre~ (“to carry, to bear”). ~ferre~ rests on Proto-Italic *~ferō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~bʰer-~ (“to carry, to bear”) — one of the most widespread of all roots, cognate with Ancient Greek ~phérō~, Sanskrit ~bhárati~, and English ~bear~. Portuguese matches it as ~relacionar~.

Notably, where English took ~relate~ straight from the Latin participle, Spanish assembled ~relacionar~ later and from the noun, so it literally means “to put into relation.” A quirk of ~ferre~ is that its own past participle ~lātus~ is suppletive, borrowed from an unrelated root — which is why the “-lation” words look nothing like “fer-.” The vast *~bʰer-~ family in Spanish includes ~referir~, ~preferir~, ~transferir~, ~conferir~, ~diferir~, and — through ~offerre~ and ~sufferre~ — ~ofrecer~ and ~sufrir~.
en.relajar:
From Latin ~relaxāre~ (“to loosen, stretch out, ease”), formed with ~re-~ over ~laxāre~ (“to loosen, slacken”), itself derived from the adjective ~laxus~ (“loose, slack, wide”), from Proto-Indo-European *~sleg-~ (“to be slack, languid”). Through ~laxus~ the family reaches Spanish ~laxo~ and ~laxante~, and through the sibling verb ~languēre~ (“to be faint”) from the same root, Spanish ~lánguido~ and English ~languid~. Spanish ~relajar~ is cognate with French ~relâcher~, and with English ~relax~ and ~lax~ — and, by way of Old French ~relaissier~, with English ~release~ itself.

The sense stayed physical — “to loosen” a muscle, a rope, a rule — before broadening to mental ease. The memorable twist is a doublet: ~laxāre~ came down two roads at once. The learned road gave ~relajar~; the popular, spoken road wore the same verb down through ~lexar~ and ~dexar~ into everyday ~dejar~ (“to leave, let go”). So ~relajar~ and ~dejar~ are Spanish twins from one Latin parent. The adverb ~lejos~ (“far”), from Latin ~laxius~, belongs to the family too — distance as a kind of loosening.
en.relatar:
From Latin ~relātus~, the past participle of ~referre~ (“to carry back, report, relate”), which joins ~re-~ (“back”) to ~ferre~ (“to carry, bear”); Spanish formed ~relatar~ on the noun ~relato~ (“a report, tale”). A curious suppletion lies inside it: ~ferre~ did not build its participle from its own stem but borrowed one from a different verb — ~lātus~, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *~telh₂-~ (“to bear, lift up”), the same root as ~tollere~ (“to raise”). ~ferre~ itself descends from PIE *~bʰer-~ (“to carry”), cognate with English ~bear~ and ~bring~. The Spanish verb is cognate with French ~relater~ and English ~relate~ and ~relation~.

The sense traveled from the literal “to carry back” to “to report, narrate, tell.” From the ~ferre~/~lātus~ family Spanish keeps ~referir~, ~referencia~, ~relación~ and ~relativo~; from the root *~telh₂-~ come ~tolerar~ and ~trasladar~. The most memorable heir of that root is a proper name: the Titan ~Atlas~, literally “the bearer,” who in myth holds up the sky — the same idea of carrying a heavy load that sits at the heart of ~relatar~, where the teller “carries back” an account of events.
en.remitir:
From Latin ~remittere~ (“to send back, let go”), which is ~re-~ (“back”) plus ~mittere~ (“to send, release”), a verb of genuinely uncertain deeper origin; by one account (de Vaan) it traces to Proto-Indo-European *~meit(H)-~ (“to exchange”), whose sense drifted from “exchange” to “give, let go, send”, but other reconstructions compete and the matter is unsettled. It is cognate with French ~remettre~ and English ~remit~ and ~submit~.

In Latin ~remittere~ ran from “send back” to “slacken, forgive, relax”, and the Spanish verb still means both to forward something and to subside, as when a fever eases. The everyday descendant of ~mittere~ is ~meter~ (“to put in”), while the learned line yields ~remisión~, ~remesa~ (“a remittance, a shipment”), ~misión~, and — through the same participial stem — ~mensaje~ and ~prometer~.
en.rendir:
From Old Spanish ~rendir~, from Vulgar Latin *~rendere~, a reshaping of Latin ~reddere~ (“to give back, return”) under the pull of ~prendere~ (“to take”) and ~vendere~ (“to sell”). ~reddere~ is ~re-~ (“back”) + ~dare~ (“to give”), from Proto-Indo-European *~deh₃-~ (“to give”). Cognate with Italian ~rendere~, French ~rendre~, and Portuguese ~render~; English borrowed the French verb as ~render~.

Latin ~reddere~ meant simply to hand back what was owed. Spanish stretched that core into a remarkable fan of senses: to ~rendir~ can mean to surrender (~rendirse~, to give oneself back to a victor), to produce or yield (a field that ~rinde~, an investment that returns a profit), and to render in the sense of paying what is due — hence the phrase ~rendir homenaje~, to pay homage. The thread running through all of them is “giving back what is owed,” whether that is a fortress, a harvest, or an honor. The past participle ~rendido~ came to mean “worn out, spent,” the state of one who has given everything back. From the same verb Spanish drew ~rendición~ (“surrender”), ~rendimiento~ (“performance, yield”), ~rédito~ (“interest, return”), and, through the participle ~reddita~ (“things paid back”), the everyday noun ~renta~ (“income, rent”).
en.renovar:
From Latin ~renovāre~ (“to renew, restore”), from ~re-~ (“again”) plus ~novāre~ (“to make new”), a verb on ~novus~ (“new”), from Proto-Indo-European *~néwos~ (“new”). Cognate with Italian ~rinnovare~ and Portuguese ~renovar~, and — through ~novus~ — with English ~new~, German ~neu~, Sanskrit ~náva~ and Greek ~néos~.

The kernel is simply ~novus~, and its offspring in Spanish spread far past the idea of renewal: ~nuevo~ (“new”), ~novato~ (“novice, rookie”), ~novedad~ (“novelty, news”) and even ~novela~ (“novel”) — a story that was, once, a piece of news. ~renovāre~ meant to make new again, whether vows, a lease, or a city wall; Spanish keeps that in ~renovar~ and its learned sibling ~innovar~ (“to innovate”). English borrowed the same stem twice, as ~renew~ and ~renovate~.
en.renunciar:
From Latin ~renūntiāre~ (“to bring back word, report; to retract, renounce”), from ~re-~ (“back”) plus ~nūntiāre~ (“to announce”), a verb built on ~nūntius~ (“messenger, message”). Old Spanish took it as ~renunciar~; the Romance siblings match it closely — Portuguese ~renunciar~, Italian ~rinunciare~, French ~renoncer~, and, borrowed through French, English ~renounce~. The base ~nūntius~ also gave English ~announce~, ~denounce~, and ~pronounce~. The deeper origin of ~nūntius~ itself is uncertain, so etymologists leave its Indo-European root unsettled.

The Latin verb first meant to carry a message back to whoever sent you — to report. From there it slid toward the negative: to send back word that you decline something, to disclaim or retract it, and finally to give up a right, office, or claim. That is the modern Spanish sense, whether one ~renuncia~ a job, an inheritance, or a habit. The same ~nūntius~ seeded a whole Spanish family: ~anunciar~ (“to announce”), ~denunciar~ (“to denounce, report”), ~pronunciar~, ~enunciar~, and the noun ~nuncio~ (“envoy,” especially the papal one).
en.reparar:
Spanish ~reparar~ (“to repair; to notice”) comes straight from Latin ~reparāre~, from ~re-~ (“again”) + ~parāre~ (“to prepare, make ready, procure”), from Proto-Indo-European *~perh₃-~ (“to bring forth, produce, procure”). The Romance siblings are transparent — Italian ~riparare~, French ~réparer~, Portuguese ~reparar~ — and English ~repair~ came through Old French from the same verb, alongside ~prepare~ and ~apparatus~.

Latin ~reparāre~ meant “to make ready again, restore,” and that is the everyday Spanish sense: to fix what is broken, ~reparar~ un coche. But Spanish grew a second, quieter meaning from the idea of stopping to set oneself right — ~reparar en algo~, “to notice, to take note of something,” as if the mind pauses and readies itself on it. The base ~parāre~ scattered widely across Spanish: ~parar~ (“to stop”), ~preparar~ (“to prepare”), ~separar~ (“to separate”), ~comparar~ (“to compare”) and ~aparato~ (“device, apparatus”), all turning on the old sense of making ready.
en.repartir:
From ~re-~ (“again, back”) plus ~partir~ (“to divide, share”), which comes from Latin ~partīrī~ (“to share, distribute”), a verb built on ~pars~ (genitive ~partis~, “a part, portion”). The noun descends from Proto-Indo-European *~per-~ (“to grant, allot, distribute”). This verb is mirrored by French ~répartir~, Italian ~ripartire~, and Portuguese ~repartir~.

Latin ~partīrī~ already carried both senses that Spanish preserves — “to split into parts” and “to share out” — so a single act of ~repartir~ both divides a thing and hands its pieces around. The noun ~reparto~ names a distribution or, in theater and film, a cast. From the same family come ~parte~, ~partido~, ~partición~, and, through the sister noun ~portiō~, the word ~porción~.
en.repetir:
From Latin ~repetere~ (“to seek again, to fetch back, to demand anew”), a compound of ~re-~ (“again, back”) and ~petere~ (“to seek, aim at, make for, attack”). ~petere~ descends from the Proto-Indo-European root *~peth₂-~ (“to fly, to fall”) — the notion of darting toward something. It is cognate with Ancient Greek ~pétomai~ (“I fly”) and Sanskrit ~pátati~ (“flies, falls”); through Latin it gave Italian ~ripetere~, French ~répéter~, and English ~repeat~.

In Latin ~petere~ carried the double charge of “to head for” and “to go at,” which is why it could mean both to request and to assault; ~repetere~ added “again,” giving “to fetch back” and then plain “to do over.” Spanish ~repetir~ inherited the “do again” sense, and colloquially even means to take a second helping of food. The flying root sprays through the vocabulary: ~repetición~ (“repetition”), ~petición~ (“request”), ~apetito~ (“appetite,” a reaching toward), ~competir~ (“to compete,” to seek together), ~ímpetu~ (“impetus”), and ~perpetuo~ (“perpetual”). Even the ~-peto~ hidden in ~apetecer~ still carries that ancient sense of flying toward what one wants.
en.reportar:
From Latin ~reportāre~ (“to carry back, bring back, report”), a compound of ~re-~ (“back”) and ~portāre~ (“to carry”), from Proto-Italic *~portāō~ and the Proto-Indo-European root *~per-~ (“to carry across, pass over”) — the same ~portāre~ that underlies ~soportar~, ~transportar~, and ~exportar~. The compound spread across the Romance languages as Italian ~riportare~ and French ~reporter~, and English took it, through Old French, as ~report~.

The literal core is “to carry back” — and a report is exactly that, an account carried back to those who sent you. Classical and older Spanish ~reportar~ leaned on other branches of the image: “to bring, to yield (a benefit),” as when an investment yields returns, and reflexively ~reportarse~, “to restrain oneself, calm down,” as if carrying one’s temper back under control. The now-common sense “to report (news, an incident)” is a modern borrowing, reinforced by English ~report~; it is especially frequent in Latin American Spanish, where peninsular usage would often prefer ~informar~. Related nouns include ~reporte~ (“report”), ~reportaje~ (“news feature,” from French ~reportage~), and ~reportero~ (“reporter”).
en.representar:
From Latin ~repraesentāre~ (“to make present, to bring before one, to display”), from ~re-~ + ~praesentāre~ (“to present”), from the adjective ~praesens~ (“present, at hand”). ~praesens~ is itself ~prae-~ (“before, in front”) plus a participle of ~esse~ (“to be”) — literally, “being before” one's eyes. Spanish took the learned ~representar~ from Latin, alongside the noun ~representación~. Cognate with Italian ~rappresentare~, French ~représenter~, Portuguese ~representar~, and, through Old French, English ~represent~.

The core image is theatrical and literal at once: to ~representar~ is to make something ~praesens~ — present again, brought back before the eyes — whether a lawyer standing in for a client, an actor embodying a role, or a sign standing for a thing. Latin ~repraesentāre~ also meant “to pay on the spot, in cash,” the immediacy of ready money. From ~praesens~ and ~esse~ Spanish gathered ~presente~, ~presencia~, ~representante~, and ~ausente~ (“absent,” from ~ab-~ + the same participle), the mirror image of being there.
en.reproducir:
From ~re-~ (“again”) plus ~producir~ (“to produce”), which descends from Latin ~producere~ (“to lead forth, bring forth”), a compound of ~pro-~ (“forth”) and ~ducere~ (“to lead, draw”), from Proto-Indo-European *~dewk-~ (“to lead, draw”). Cognate with Italian ~riprodurre~, French ~reproduire~ and Portuguese ~reproduzir~, and — through ~ducere~ — with English ~produce~, ~conduct~ and ~duke~, and with German ~ziehen~ (“to pull”).

The literal core is “to lead forth again.” From ~producere~'s sense of drawing something out into the open, ~reproducir~ came to mean making a fresh copy of what already exists — first of texts and images, then of sounds, and biologically of living things that ~se reproducen~. The ~ducere~ family is one of Spanish's most productive: ~producir~, ~producto~, ~producción~, ~reproductor~, ~conducir~, ~deducir~, ~introducir~ and ~educar~ all pull, lead or draw on the same root.
en.requerir:
From Latin ~requīrere~ (“to seek again, to ask for, to need”), from ~re-~ (“again, back”) + ~quaerere~ (“to seek, to ask”). The Old Spanish form was ~requerir~, remodeled on the many ~-quirere~ compounds. The origin of ~quaerere~ itself is uncertain: it is usually traced to Proto-Italic *~kʷaizō~ and a Proto-Indo-European *~kʷeh₂-~ (“to acquire”), though older proposals connected it instead to roots meaning “to seek” or “to see.” Cognate compounds gave English ~require~, ~acquire~, and ~inquire~, and the base survives in Spanish ~querer~ and French ~quérir~.

~quaerere~ meant “to seek,” and its ~re-~ intensified that into “to seek insistently, to demand” — the sense modern ~requerir~ keeps when a law or a task “requires” something of us. The plain verb took a startling turn on Spanish soil: it became ~querer~, “to want, to love,” so the Latin idea of seeking softened into Spanish desiring. From the same family come ~cuestión~ (“question”), ~pesquisa~ (“inquiry”), ~encuesta~ (“survey”), ~adquirir~, and ~conquistar~.
en.resaltar:
From ~re-~ (“back, again”) plus ~saltar~ (“to jump”), from Latin ~saltāre~ (“to leap, to dance”), the frequentative of ~salīre~ (“to jump, to leap”), from Proto-Indo-European *~sel-~ (“to jump”). Cognate with Italian ~saltare~ and French ~sauter~, and, through the same root, with English ~salient~ and ~somersault~.

The Latin frequentative is already a small story: to leap over and over, ~saltāre~, was “to dance.” ~resaltar~ began as “to leap back, to rebound,” then named a piece of architecture that juts out — a moulding that “jumps” from the wall — and from that projecting it became figurative: “to stand out, to be conspicuous,” and so “to highlight” (hacer ~resaltar~). From ~salīre~ Spanish keeps ~salir~, ~salida~, ~saliente~ and ~sobresalir~; from ~saltāre~, ~salto~, ~asaltar~ and ~sobresaltar~; and the cousin ~resultar~ (“to result”) is one more leap outward.
en.rescatar:
From Vulgar Latin *~reexcaptāre~, a triple compound of ~re-~ (“back, again”), ~ex-~ (“out”), and ~captāre~ (“to try to seize,” the frequentative of ~capere~, “to take”). ~capere~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~keh₂p-~ (“to grasp, seize”). Corominas held that ~rescatar~ did not reach Castilian directly from Latin but arrived late, borrowed from Catalan ~rescatar~ or Italian ~riscattare~ — the ~ex-~ layer points to that Italian route. Cognate with French ~racheter~ (“to buy back”) and Portuguese ~resgatar~, and — through ~capere~ — with English ~capture~ and ~receive~.

The literal sense is a chain of undoings — to grasp back out — and the oldest Spanish meaning was commercial and grim: to ~rescatar~ was to ransom a captive, to buy back a person seized in war or piracy, a live transaction on the frontier between Christian and Muslim Iberia. From that came the noun ~rescate~ (“ransom, rescue”). Only later did the word broaden to the modern “to rescue, recover, save,” pulling someone or something from danger with no payment implied. The base ~captāre~ seeded a wide Spanish family: ~captar~, ~cazar~ (“to hunt,” from the same frequentative), ~caza~, and the learned ~captura~; while its parent ~capere~ underlies ~caber~, ~capaz~, and ~recibir~. Today one can ~rescatar~ a drowning swimmer, a failing bank, or a forgotten song from oblivion.
en.reservar:
From Latin ~reservāre~ (“to keep back, save up”), from ~re-~ (“back”) plus ~servāre~ (“to keep, guard, watch over, preserve”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ser-~ (“to protect”). It came into Spanish and its Romance neighbors alike — French ~réserver~, Portuguese ~reservar~ — and belongs to a busy Latin family that also gave ~conservar~, ~observar~, and ~preservar~.

A useful warning: despite appearances, ~servāre~ (“to guard”) is not the source of ~servir~ (“to serve”), which comes from ~servus~ (“slave”); whether ~servus~ itself belongs to the same root *~ser-~ is debated. The guarding sense is the key to ~reservar~: to keep something back, safe, held in store for later — a table, a seat, a right, a judgment. From it Spanish draws the noun ~reserva~ (a stock, a nature reserve, a soldier in the reserves, and the discretion of someone who acts “con reserva”). To reserve a room is, at root, to guard it against all other comers until you arrive.
en.residir:
From Latin ~residēre~ (“to remain sitting, stay behind”), a compound of ~re-~ (“back, again”) and ~sedēre~ (“to sit”), from Proto-Indo-European *~sed-~ (“to sit”). Cognate through that root with Italian ~sedere~ and, in the Germanic branch, with English ~sit~ and ~seat~.

The literal image is of someone who keeps their seat while others move on — who “settles” in a place — and from that came the modern sense of dwelling or residing. The same root sat deep in everyday Spanish: ~sede~ (“seat, headquarters”), ~sesión~, ~residencia~, and ~presidir~ (“to sit before,” to preside) all belong to it, as does the humble ~silla~ (“chair”), from Latin ~sella~. So the word for where you live and the word for what you sit on trace back to a single Indo-European idea of sitting.
en.resistir:
From Latin ~resistere~ (“to stand back, withstand”), from ~re-~ (“back, against”) plus ~sistere~ (“to take a stand, halt”), a reduplicated verb built on the root of ~stāre~ (“to stand”) and ultimately on Proto-Indo-European *~steh₂-~ (“to stand”). Cognate — all through ~sistere~ — with English ~resist~, ~assist~, and ~consist~, and with Italian ~resistere~.

The image is bodily and stubborn: to resist is to plant oneself and not be moved, to “stand against.” Latin ~sistere~ was a factory of prefixed verbs, and Spanish inherited nearly the whole set — ~asistir~ (“to attend, assist”), ~insistir~, ~persistir~, ~desistir~, ~consistir~, and ~existir~ (“to stand forth,” to exist). All of them hide the same standing figure inside a different prefix. And because ~sistere~ sprang from the same *~steh₂-~ that gave ~estar~, the Spanish verbs of standing, staying, and resisting are, at root, one gesture: holding one’s ground.
en.resolver:
From Latin ~resolvere~ (“to loosen, untie, dissolve, break up”), a compound of ~re-~ (“un-, back”) and ~solvere~ (“to loosen, release, dissolve”). ~solvere~ itself is contracted from *~se-luere~ — ~se-~ (“apart”) plus the verb ~luere~ (“to loosen, release”) — going back to Proto-Indo-European *~leu-~ (“to loosen, divide, cut apart”). The same root gave Greek ~lýein~ (“to loosen, untie”), the source of the ~-lysis~ in analysis, and, through Germanic, English ~loose~ and ~lose~; the learned Latin branch gave English ~solve~. Beside the learned ~resolver~, Spanish also kept a fully popular descendant of ~solvere~: the everyday ~soltar~ (“to let go, release”).

The metaphor beneath ~resolver~ is physical: to un-loosen a knot. From untying a literal tangle the verb moved to dissolving a substance, then to clearing up a difficulty and finally to reaching a firm decision — the modern senses “to solve,” “to resolve,” and “to decide.” Spanish spread the ~solvere~ family widely: ~solución~ (“solution,” originally a loosening or dissolving), ~disolver~ (“to dissolve”), ~absolver~ (“to absolve,” to loosen someone from guilt), ~resolución~, and the popular ~soltar~ with its past participle ~suelto~ (“loose, free”). A ~resolución~ and a knot ~suelto~ are, etymologically, the same act: something once bound has been let go.
en.respaldar:
Spanish ~respaldar~ is built on ~respaldo~ (“back of a seat; backrest; backing”), itself ~re-~ plus ~espalda~ (“back, of the body”). ~Espalda~ descends by metathesis from Vulgar Latin *~spatla~, from Latin ~spatula~ (“a small flat blade”), the diminutive of ~spatha~ (“broad blade, sword”), a borrowing of Ancient Greek ~σπάθη~ (~spáthē~, “broad blade”). Cognate with Italian ~spalla~ and French ~épaule~ (both “shoulder”), and with English ~spatula~, ~spade~, and ~epaulette~; the sword-word itself lives on as Spanish ~espada~.

The surprise is anatomical: the ~spatula~, a “little blade,” named the flat of the shoulder and then the whole back — the same image gives French ~épaule~. From ~espalda~ Spanish formed ~respaldo~, first the physical back of a chair, then, figuratively, the ~respaldo~ one lends a person or plan; and ~respaldar~ followed, meaning literally “to furnish with a back” and then “to back, support, endorse” — the same metaphor English reaches for in the verb ~back~. Kin include ~espaldar~, ~espalda~, and the learned ~espátula~.
en.respetar:
From Latin ~respectare~ (“to look back at, to regard”), a frequentative of ~respicere~ (“to look back, to consider”), from ~re-~ (“back”) and ~specere~ (“to look at”), from Proto-Indo-European *~spek-~ (“to observe”). Spanish ~respetar~ is a semi-learned form; the fully learned doublet ~respectar~ (“to concern, to regard”) survives mainly in the phrase ~respecto a~. It is cognate with English ~respect~, Italian ~rispettare~ and Portuguese ~respeitar~.

The literal core is to look again, to turn one’s gaze back toward something worth a second look — and from that repeated regard grew the moral sense of holding a person or thing in esteem. The two Spanish doublets split the labor: ~respetar~ took the ethical meaning, ~respectar~ the neutral “to concern.” The same root *~spek-~ is enormously productive, giving ~espectáculo~, ~aspecto~, ~inspeccionar~, ~espejo~ (from ~speculum~) and even ~espía~.
en.responder:
From Latin ~respondēre~ (“to answer; to promise in return”), from ~re-~ (“back”) and ~spondēre~ (“to pledge, promise solemnly”), from Proto-Italic *~spondeō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~spend-~ (“to make an offering, perform a rite”). Cognates fill Romance — Italian ~rispondere~, French ~répondre~, Portuguese ~responder~ — and reach English ~respond~; Ancient Greek ~σπένδω~ (“to pour a libation”) shares the root, as, through the participle, does English ~spouse~.

The buried image is ritual: ~spondēre~ was to make a solemn pledge, first sworn over a libation poured to the gods — exactly the sense of Greek ~σπένδω~ — so to respond is to pledge back, to meet a promise with a promise. From the participle ~sponsus~/~sponsa~ (“the betrothed, the promised one”) Spanish drew ~esposo~ and ~esposa~ (“husband, wife”). Strikingly, ~esposas~ also means “handcuffs,” the binding ones — the same notion of being bound by a pledge. Kin include ~respuesta~, ~responsable~, and ~corresponder~.
en.resultar:
From Latin ~resultāre~ (“to spring back, to rebound”), the frequentative of ~resilīre~ (“to leap back”), from ~re-~ (“back”) plus ~salīre~ (“to leap, to jump”), from Proto-Indo-European *~sel-~ (“to jump”). Cognate with French ~résulter~, Italian ~risultare~, and English ~result~ and ~resilient~ — the latter still carrying the sense of springing back.

The metaphor is athletic: a result is what leaps out or rebounds from a set of circumstances, the way a ball bounces off a wall. Classical Latin ~resultāre~ could even mean “to echo,” sound rebounding from a surface. From the same ~salīre~ Spanish inherited a whole leaping family: ~saltar~ (“to jump”), ~salir~ (“to go out,” originally to leap forth), ~resaltar~ (“to stand out”), ~asaltar~ (“to assault,” to leap upon), and ~sobresalir~ (“to excel,” to leap above). Every outcome, etymologically, is a little rebound.
en.resumir:
From Latin ~resūmere~ (“to take up again, resume”), from ~re-~ (“again”) plus ~sūmere~ (“to take”), itself ~sub-~ (“up from under”) plus ~emere~ (“to take, to buy”), from a Proto-Indo-European root *~h₁em-~ (“to take, distribute”). English drew from the same verb ~resume~, ~assume~, ~consume~ and ~presume~; the Romance cognates include French ~résumer~ and Italian ~riassumere~.

To ~resūmere~ was to “take back up” what had been set down — a thread of argument, a task — and from “taking up again” grew the idea of gathering a matter into its essentials, “to summarize.” English preserves the split neatly: to ~resume~ is to continue, while a ~résumé~ is a summary. Spanish keeps the noun ~resumen~ (“summary”) and, from ~sūmere~ and ~emere~, a wide kin: ~asumir~, ~consumir~, ~presumir~, ~ejemplo~ and ~redimir~.
en.retirar:
From ~re-~ (“back, again”) + ~tirar~ (“to pull, throw”), reinforced by French ~retirer~, from which English ~retire~ also descends. The base ~tirar~ is common to the western Romance languages — Italian ~tirare~, French ~tirer~, Portuguese ~tirar~ — yet its ultimate origin is one of the most stubborn puzzles in Romance etymology. Corominas calls it deeply obscure and declines to settle it: no Latin etymon accounts for the whole family cleanly. Among the proposals he weighs are a Germanic ~teran~ (“to tear, rend”), championed by Diez, and a formation in Roman military slang from an Iranian word for “arrow” (~tir~), used by the Parthian archers who harried the legions. Both remain speculative.

In Spanish the prefixed ~retirar~ layered the notion of “back” onto “pull,” yielding “to pull back, withdraw” — a hand, a troop, an offer, or oneself into solitude. From that grew the reflexive ~retirarse~ (“to withdraw, go to bed, retire from work”) and the nouns ~retiro~ (“retreat, seclusion, retirement pension”) and ~retirada~ (“a military retreat”). The same restless base ~tirar~ radiated across the language into ~tiro~ (“a shot”), ~tirón~ (“a yank”), ~tirador~ (“shooter; handle”), and ~estirar~ (“to stretch”). It is a fitting irony that a verb all about pulling things definitively into place should have an origin no etymologist has ever managed to pin down.
en.retomar:
A transparent compound of ~re-~ (“again”) and ~tomar~ (“to take”) — so “to take up again, resume.” The interest lies in ~tomar~ itself, a verb found only in Castilian and Portuguese and of genuinely uncertain origin. The account most often cited, first proposed by Pio Rajna and treated as plausible by Corominas, derives it from Latin ~autumāre~ (“to affirm, assert”), which in Hispanic Latin would have been clipped to *~tumāre~ — much as ~auferre~ stood beside ~ferre~. This is disputed, not settled; Corominas presents it as the strongest candidate while noting it remains unproven, and he argues against a rival onomatopoeic guess.

If the ~autumāre~ etymology is right, the thread is legal: “to assert a claim to something” shades into “to take possession of it,” and indeed in medieval texts ~tomar~ predominates precisely in the sense of seizing or claiming — which is the fact that first suggested the etymology. From it Spanish forms ~retomar~, ~toma~ (“a taking; a shot, a take”), and ~retoma~; Portuguese matches with ~tomar~ and ~retomar~.
en.reunir:
From the prefix ~re-~ (“again”) and ~unir~ (“to unite”), itself from Latin ~ūnīre~ (“to make one, join together”), from ~ūnus~ (“one”), from Proto-Indo-European *~óynos~ (“one, single”). Cognate with French ~réunir~ and Italian ~riunire~; through ~ūnus~ it is kin to English ~unite~ and, from the same root, the humble ~one~.

The composition is transparent: to ~reunir~ is literally to “one again” — to make separate things one once more, hence to gather or bring together. The Latin ~ūnus~ was extraordinarily productive, and Spanish reaps the harvest: ~unión~ (“union”), ~unidad~ (“unity”), ~uno~ (“one”), ~único~ (“only, unique”), and even ~universo~ (“universe”), from ~ūniversus~, literally “turned into one.” The reflexive ~reunirse~ (“to meet, get together”) and the noun ~reunión~ (“meeting”) are the verb’s everyday faces.
en.revelar:
From Latin ~revēlāre~ (“to unveil, uncover”), a compound of ~re-~ (here “un-, reversal”) and ~vēlāre~ (“to veil, cover”), from ~vēlum~ (“a veil, cloth, sail”). The deep root of ~vēlum~ is disputed: it goes back to a Proto-Italic *~wekslom~, which some derive from Proto-Indo-European *~weg-~ (“to weave”) — making it kin to English ~wick~ (“candle wick”) — while others trace it instead to *~weǵʰ-~ (“to convey, ride”), i.e. “that which drives (a ship),” a hypothesis that would tie it to Proto-Slavic ~veslo~ (“oar”). The sources do not settle the question, so the veil-versus-sail ancestry is best left open. Spanish inherited the word learnedly; its Romance siblings include French ~révéler~ and Italian ~rivelare~, and, from the same ~vēlum~, French ~voile~ and English ~veil~.

Semantically ~revelar~ is transparent: to pull the ~vēlum~ off something so it can be seen — hence “to reveal, disclose.” Religion supplied its loftiest use: divine ~revelación~ is truth unveiled, and the last book of the New Testament, the Apocalypse, is literally an “un-covering.” Spanish then handed the verb a strikingly modern job: in photography, ~revelar~ is “to develop” film — to coax the latent, hidden image out from behind its chemical veil into the light. Two cautions for learners. First, ~revelar~ (“reveal”) is a near-homophone of ~rebelar~ (“to rebel”), spelled with a b and wholly unrelated. Second, its own family is easy to see: ~velo~ (“veil”), ~velar~ (“to veil; to keep vigil”), ~desvelar~ (“to unveil; to keep awake”), and ~revelación~.
en.revisar:
A learned formation from Latin ~revīsus~, participle of ~revīsere~ (“to look back at, to visit again”), or equally analyzable as Spanish ~re-~ (“again”) + ~visar~. Either way it rests on Latin ~vidēre~ (“to see”), through its frequentative ~vīsere~ / ~vīsāre~. ~vidēre~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~weyd-~ (“to see, to know”). Cognate with French ~réviser~ and English ~revise~, and — through ~vidēre~ — with English ~vision~, ~view~, and ~evident~.

The prefix ~re-~ carries the whole meaning: to ~revisar~ is to “see again” — to look a second time in order to check, correct, or update. Spanish uses it for everything from proofreading a text to a mechanic servicing a car to a doctor giving a check-up. The PIE root *~weyd-~ was famously double-sided, meaning both “to see” and, in the perfect, “to have seen” hence “to know” — the same pairing that links Latin ~vidēre~ (“to see”) to Greek ~oîda~ (“I know”) and English ~wit~ and ~wise~. From ~vidēre~ Spanish drew ~ver~ (“to see”), ~vista~ (“sight, view”), ~visión~, ~revista~ (“magazine,” something looked over again and again), ~aviso~, and ~evidente~.
en.reír:
From Old Spanish ~reír~ (also ~riír~), from Latin ~rīdēre~ (“to laugh, smile, mock”). The deeper origin is genuinely uncertain: de Vaan finds no secure Indo-European source for ~rīdēre~ and rejects the once-proposed link to Sanskrit ~vrīḍate~ (“to be ashamed”), so no confident Proto-Indo-European root can be given here. Within Romance the descent is clear and regular: cognate with Italian ~ridere~, French ~rire~, Portuguese ~rir~, and Catalan ~riure~, all from the same Latin verb. English borrowed learned relatives — ~risible~ and ~deride~ — directly from Latin rather than inheriting them.

The chain from Latin to Spanish is a small phonetic drama: intervocalic ~-d-~ in ~rīdēre~ fell away, the two vowels collided, and Old Spanish ~riír~ contracted to modern ~reír~ — a verb whose hiatus still forces the written accent: ~reír~, ~río~, ~rieron~. The prefixed ~subrīdēre~ (“to smile,” literally “to laugh a little under”) gave ~sonreír~, with ~son-~ softening the sense. From the same root Spanish holds ~risa~ (“laughter”), ~risueño~ (“smiling, cheerful”), ~ridículo~, and ~irrisión~. The meaning has stayed remarkably stable across two thousand years — whatever ~rīdēre~ once sprang from, Romans and Spanish speakers alike have simply laughed with it.
en.robar:
From Old Spanish ~robar~, from Vulgar Latin *~raubāre~, borrowed from a Germanic (West Germanic / Frankish) verb *~raubōn~ (“to rob, plunder”), from Proto-Germanic *~raubōną~, from Proto-Indo-European *~Hrewp-~ (“to tear, break off”). Cognate with English ~rob~ and ~reave~ (as in ~bereave~), German ~rauben~ and the noun ~Raub~ (“robbery”), Italian ~rubare~, and Portuguese ~roubar~.

Like much of the vocabulary of war, ~robar~ entered Latin from the Germanic peoples who moved through the late Empire. That same Germanic “spoils” root left a surprising civilian trace: Spanish ~ropa~ (“clothing”) goes back to a Germanic word for booty — Gothic *~rauba~ (“spoils, stripped garments”) — because clothing was among the first things taken from a defeated enemy. English preserves the identical pairing in ~rob~ beside ~robe~, a garment whose name once meant plunder. In Spanish the family clusters around the noun ~robo~ (“theft”), the booty-born ~ropa~, and the compound ~guardarropa~ (“wardrobe”).
en.rodar:
Spanish ~rodar~ comes from Latin ~rotāre~ (“to turn, whirl”), a verb formed from the noun ~rota~ (“wheel”). ~rota~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~Hroth₂o-~, from the root *~ret-~ (“to run, roll”). It has cognates far outside Latin: German ~Rad~ (“wheel”), Sanskrit ~ratha~ (“chariot”), Old Irish ~roth~ and Welsh ~rhod~. Within Romance the verb is echoed by Italian ~rotare~ and Portuguese ~rodar~.

~rodar~ kept the physical sense of turning like a wheel — a stone, a car, an actor rolling through a film shoot (~rodar una película~, “to shoot a film”). The old noun ~rota~ left an unusually rich Spanish family. Beyond obvious relatives like ~rueda~ (“wheel”) and ~rotar~ (“to rotate”), it hides inside ~redondo~ (“round,” from ~rotundus~), ~rodear~ (“to surround”) and ~alrededor~ (“around”). The most charming descendant is ~rodilla~ (“knee”), from Vulgar Latin ~rotella~ (“little wheel”) — the joint named for the way the leg pivots on it.
en.rodear:
A Spanish formation from the noun ~rueda~ (“wheel”) plus the verbal suffix ~-ear~, so at root “to wheel around” something. ~rueda~ itself comes from Latin ~rota~ (“wheel”), from Proto-Indo-European *~Hroth₂o-~ (“wheel”), a derivative of *~ret-~ (“to run, to roll”). The word is widespread: cognate with German ~Rad~ (“wheel”) and Sanskrit ~rátha~ (“chariot”), while Latin ~rotundus~ yielded Spanish ~redondo~ (“round”) and English ~rotate~.

To ~rodear~ is to trace a circle about a thing — to surround, or to take the long way round. The noun ~rodeo~ names exactly that “going around”: a roundabout route, an evasion, or the cattle roundup in which riders circle the herd — the sense English borrowed wholesale as ~rodeo~. The wheel-root spun off a wide Spanish family besides: ~rodar~ (“to roll”), ~rotar~, ~rodillo~ (“roller”), and ~rótula~ (“kneecap”).
en.romper:
Spanish ~romper~ descends directly from Latin ~rumpere~ (“to break, burst”), inherited through Vulgar Latin with regular loss of the nasal before the plosive. The Latin verb goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~Hrewp-~ (“to break”), its present formed with a nasal infix. It is cognate with Italian ~rompere~, French ~rompre~, and Portuguese ~romper~, and — through the same root — with Sanskrit ~lumpáti~ (“breaks”) and, more distantly, with the English words below.

Latin ~rumpere~ was extraordinarily productive in prefixed compounds, and English borrowed the lot from its participle ~ruptus~: ~rupture~, ~erupt~, ~corrupt~, ~interrupt~, ~abrupt~, and ~disrupt~. Spanish kept a parallel learned family beside the everyday ~romper~: ~ruptura~ (“rupture”), ~corromper~ (“to corrupt”), ~interrumpir~ (“to interrupt”), and ~irrumpir~ (“to burst in”). A pleasant survival is ~rompeolas~ (“breakwater”), literally “it breaks waves,” preserving the raw physical force of the original verb.
en.saber:
From Vulgar Latin *~sapēre~, a reshaping of Latin ~sapere~ (“to taste; to have good sense, to be wise”), from Proto-Italic *~sapjō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~seh₁p-~ (“to taste, to perceive”). The verb runs straight across Romance as Italian ~sapere~, French ~savoir~, and Portuguese ~saber~; English carries the same root in the borrowings ~sapient~, ~savor~, ~insipid~ (“without taste”), and ~sage~ (“wise”).

The metaphor inside the word is that of the palate: to know is to have tasted, to have discernment — the tongue standing in for the mind. Latin already ran both senses side by side, and Spanish kept the double life, since ~saber~ still means both “to know” and “to taste” (« esta sopa sabe a ajo », “this soup tastes of garlic”). From the same root grew ~sabio~ (“wise; a sage”), ~sabor~ (“flavor”), ~sabroso~ (“tasty”), ~sabiduría~ (“wisdom”), and the adjective ~sabihondo~ (“know-it-all”). Spanish neatly distinguishes ~saber~ (to know a fact) from ~conocer~ (to be acquainted with).
en.sacar:
Modern Spanish ~sacar~ descends from Old Spanish ~sacar~, but its ultimate origin is genuinely disputed. By the account Corominas favors, it comes from Gothic ~sakan~ (“to quarrel, dispute, accuse at law”), a Germanic legal term: to ~sacar~ would first have meant to obtain something by winning a lawsuit, and only later to extract or take out in general. A competing account instead links it to Medieval Latin ~saccāre~ and to ~saccus~ (“sack”) — from Greek ~sákkos~, itself a Semitic loan — imagining the act of pulling goods out of a bag. The earliest Castilian traces are Latinized forms like ~saccāre~ in tenth-century documents. Portuguese ~sacar~ (“to draw out; to draw a weapon or withdraw money”) matches the Spanish form closely, and the two languages share the ambiguity of the source.

Because the origin is unsettled, the vivid legal image — winning by litigation — should be taken as a hypothesis, not a fact. What is clear is the semantic breadth Spanish gave the verb: to take out, extract, withdraw, obtain, and figuratively to deduce (~sacar en claro~) or to snap a photo (~sacar una foto~). From it Spanish built ~sacacorchos~ (“corkscrew”), ~sacapuntas~ (“pencil sharpener”), the noun ~saca~ (“large sack; withdrawal”), and the compound ~entresacar~ (“to pick out, thin out”). The related ~sonsacar~ (“to draw information out of someone, to wheedle”) preserves almost perfectly the notion of extracting something someone would rather keep — whichever of the two etymologies proves right.
en.salir:
From Latin ~salīre~ (“to jump, leap, spring”), from Proto-Italic *~saljō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~sel-~ (“to spring, jump”). The same root gave Ancient Greek ~hállomai~ (“to leap”) and, most likely, Sanskrit ~sárati~ (“flows, runs”). Through Latin and French, ~salīre~ furnished English ~salient~ and ~sally~, while its frequentative ~saltāre~ (“to leap repeatedly, dance”) gave Spanish ~saltar~ and Italian ~saltare~.

The leap became a departure. In Vulgar Latin ~salīre~ drifted from “to jump” toward “to jump out, spring forth,” and Old Spanish ~salir~ settled into the everyday “to go out, leave, exit” it has today — a spring of water still ~sale~ from the ground, keeping the old image alive. Its relatives cluster around leaping and springing: ~salto~ (“a jump”), ~saltar~, ~sobresalir~ (“to stand out,” literally to “leap above”), ~salida~ (“exit, departure”) and ~asaltar~ (“to assault,” to leap upon). English ~assault~ and ~somersault~ leap from the very same Latin verb.
en.saltar:
From Latin ~saltāre~ (“to dance, leap”), the frequentative of ~salīre~ (“to jump, spring”), from Proto-Italic *~saliō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~sel-~ (“to jump”). Cognate with Italian ~saltare~, French ~sauter~ and Portuguese ~saltar~, and — through ~salīre~ — with English ~salient~, ~sally~ and the ~-sault~ of ~assault~ and ~somersault~.

Because ~saltāre~ was the “leap again and again” of a dancer, Latin used it for dancing as well as jumping; Spanish took the leaping sense and let the noun ~baile~ carry dancing. A ~somersault~ hides the etymology neatly: it is “a leap over,” from ~suprā~ (“over”) + ~saltus~ (“a jump”). From the same root Spanish gathers ~salto~, ~saltamontes~ (literally “leap-hills”), ~sobresaltar~ and ~resaltar~.
en.salvar:
From Late Latin ~salvāre~ (“to save, make safe”), a verb built on Latin ~salvus~ (“safe, whole, unharmed”), from Proto-Indo-European *~solh₂-~ (“whole, every”). Cognate with Italian ~salvare~, French ~sauver~, and Portuguese ~salvar~. English ~save~ and ~safe~ both descend, through Old French, from ~salvus~, as does ~salvage~; and through the same PIE root the Latin adjective is cognate with Ancient Greek ~hólos~ (“whole”), source of the ~holo-~ in “holograph.”

The root idea is wholeness: to save is to keep something entire and unharmed. Latin ~salvus~ gave the greeting ~salvē~ (“be well, hail”), and the interjection survives in Spanish ~salve~. Christianity gave ~salvar~ its theological weight — ~salvación~ (“salvation”), ~Salvador~ (“Savior”) — beside the everyday senses of rescuing and the computing sense of saving a file. The family is wide: ~salvo~ (“safe; except”), ~a salvo~ (“in safety”), ~salvavidas~ (“lifeguard, life preserver”), ~salvoconducto~ (“safe-conduct”), and ~salvaguardar~ (“to safeguard”). The noun ~salud~ (“health”), from the related ~salūs~, springs from the same idea of being whole and sound.
en.sancionar:
Spanish ~sancionar~ derives from the noun ~sanción~ plus ~-ar~. ~sanción~ comes from Latin ~sanctiō~ (“a making binding, ordinance”), from the verb ~sancīre~ (“to make sacred, ratify, decree”), which is built on ~sanctus~ (“holy, sacred”) and belongs with ~sacer~ (“consecrated, holy”). All trace to Proto-Indo-European *~seh₂k-~ (“to sanctify, make a treaty”). The same root gives English ~saint~, ~sacred~ and ~sanction~, Italian ~sanzionare~ and French ~sanctionner~.

The original idea was religious: to ~sancīre~ a law was to make it sacred and therefore inviolable, hedged by divine penalty. That double edge survives as a striking quirk — ~sancionar~ is an auto-antonym, meaning both “to approve, ratify” (a law is sanctioned) and “to penalize” (an offender is sanctioned), exactly like English ~sanction~. The penalty half preserves the old sense that breaking a sacred rule invites punishment. From the same *~seh₂k-~ Spanish keeps a visibly religious cluster — ~santo~ (“saint, holy”), ~sagrado~ (“sacred”), ~santificar~ (“to sanctify”) and ~sagrar~ (“to consecrate”).
en.satisfacer:
From Latin ~satisfacere~ (“to do enough, satisfy”), a compound of ~satis~ (“enough”) and ~facere~ (“to do, make”). ~satis~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~seh₂-~ (“to satiate, be full”) and ~facere~ to *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to put, place, do”). Cognate with Italian ~soddisfare~, French ~satisfaire~, and Portuguese ~satisfazer~; English took ~satisfy~ through Old French. Surprisingly, English ~sad~ belongs to the same *~seh₂-~ family — its original sense was “sated, full” — while ~facere~ shares its root with English ~do~.

The compound is transparent: to satisfy a debt, a creditor, or a hunger is to do (~facere~) enough (~satis~) to meet it. Roman law used ~satisfacere~ for discharging an obligation, and that legal weight survives in the modern range of ~satisfacer~ — to satisfy a person, a requirement, or a curiosity. Like ~hacer~, it conjugates irregularly (~satisfago~, ~satisfizo~, ~satisfaré~). Its family includes ~satisfacción~, ~satisfactorio~, and the past participle ~satisfecho~ (“satisfied, content”). From ~satis~ alone Spanish also drew ~saciar~ (“to sate”) and ~saturar~ (“to saturate”), and the archaic ~asaz~ (“enough”), from ~ad~ ~satis~.
en.seguir:
From Vulgar Latin *~sequēre~, a reshaping of the Latin deponent ~sequī~ (“to follow”), from Proto-Italic *~sekʷōr~, from Proto-Indo-European *~sekʷ-~ (“to follow”). The root is deep and wide: cognate with Sanskrit ~sácate~, Ancient Greek ~hépomai~ (“I follow”), and, in the Romance line, Italian ~seguire~, French ~suivre~, and Portuguese ~seguir~. English draws on the same root through Latin borrowings like ~sequence~, ~sequel~, ~second~, and ~pursue~.

Beyond plain “to follow,” Spanish ~seguir~ took on “to continue, to keep on” — « sigo esperando », “I’m still waiting” — so the verb tracks both a person and an action through time. The prefixed compounds are especially productive: ~conseguir~ (“to obtain,” literally to follow through to the end), ~perseguir~ (“to pursue, to persecute”), ~proseguir~ (“to carry on”), and ~subsiguiente~ (“subsequent”). From the same PIE root, through other Latin stems, Spanish also inherited ~secuencia~, ~consecuencia~, ~séquito~ (“retinue”), and ~ejecutar~ (“to execute”).
en.seleccionar:
From the noun ~selección~ (“selection”), a learned borrowing of Latin ~sēlēctiō~ (“a picking out, choice”), the action noun of ~sēligere~ (“to pick out, select”). ~sēligere~ is itself a compound of ~sē-~ (“apart, aside”) and ~legere~ (“to gather, collect,” later “to read”). ~legere~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~leǵ-~ (“to gather, collect”). The root’s most famous cognate is Ancient Greek ~légō~ (“I gather; I say”) and its offspring ~lógos~ (“word, reason”). The verb ~seleccionar~ itself is a modern denominal — Spanish built it from ~selección~ rather than inheriting it whole — paralleled by Italian ~selezionare~, French ~sélectionner~ and Portuguese ~selecionar~.

The heart of the word is ~legere~’s gathering: to select is to gather items apart from the rest, picking out the chosen few. That gathering-and-choosing sense radiates widely. From ~legere~ Spanish holds ~leer~ (“to read,” gathering letters with the eye), ~elegir~ (“to choose”), ~colegir~ (“to infer, gather”), ~colección~ (“collection”), ~elección~ (“election”), ~lector~ (“reader”) and ~legible~ (“legible”). The same root, through Latin ~intellegere~ (“to discern, gather between”) and ~dīligere~ (“to single out, esteem”), gave ~inteligente~ and ~diligente~. And through Greek ~lógos~ it seeded the whole family of ~-logía~ sciences. To ~seleccionar~ a team, then, is to do in the stadium what a reader does on the page: gather the best and set them apart.
en.sentar:
From Vulgar Latin *~sedentāre~, a verb built on ~sedēns~ (genitive ~sedentis~), the present participle of Latin ~sedēre~ (“to sit”), from Proto-Indo-European *~sed-~ (“to sit”). That root is one of the most widespread in the family: it gave English ~sit~ and ~seat~ (via Old English ~sittan~), German ~sitzen~, and the Latin ~sedēre~ that also partly underlies Spanish ~ser~. Portuguese ~sentar~ and Italian ~sedere~ are Romance kin.

Spanish turned the participle into a fresh verb: *~sedentāre~ meant “to cause to be sitting,” which is exactly what ~sentar~ does — you ~sientas~ a guest at the table. The same “sit” root produced a large and varied family: ~sede~ (“seat, see”), ~sesión~ (“a sitting”), ~sedimento~ (what settles), ~sedentario~, ~asentar~, ~presidir~ (“to sit in front of”) and ~residir~. Even ~silla~ (“chair”) descends, through ~sella~, from this root.
en.sentir:
From Latin ~sentīre~ (“to feel, perceive, be of an opinion”), from Proto-Indo-European *~sent-~, reconstructed with the sense “to head for, go, find one’s way.” It is cognate with Italian ~sentire~, Portuguese ~sentir~ and French ~sentir~, and — through the same Latin verb — with English ~sense~, ~sentiment~ and ~scent~; through Germanic the root also gives English ~send~ and German ~Sinn~ (“sense, mind”) and ~senden~ (“to send”).

The semantic leap from “to go” to “to feel” is striking: to perceive was, on this reconstruction, to “find one’s way” mentally toward a thing — to discern it. Latin ~sentīre~ already spanned bodily sensation, emotion and judgment, a breadth Spanish ~sentir~ keeps (“to feel” and “to be sorry”). From the same stem come ~sentido~ (“sense, meaning”), ~sentimiento~ (“feeling”), ~sensación~ (via ~sēnsus~), ~consentir~ (“to consent”), ~presentir~ (“to have a foreboding”) and ~sensato~ (“sensible”).
en.separar:
Spanish ~separar~ comes from Latin ~sēparāre~ (“to pull apart, divide”), a compound of ~sē-~ (“apart, aside”) and ~parāre~ (“to make ready, prepare”), the latter from Proto-Indo-European *~perh₃-~ (“to produce, procure”). Cognates include Italian ~separare~, French ~séparer~, and Portuguese ~separar~; and from ~parāre~ alone come Spanish ~parar~ and ~preparar~ and English ~prepare~.

The image behind ~sēparāre~ is homely: to “make ready apart,” to arrange things each on its own side. From Latin, French produced a second, popularized descendant, ~sevrer~ (“to wean”), and English borrowed its Frenchified doublet ~sever~ (“to cut off”), so ~separate~ and ~sever~ are ultimately the same word wearing different clothes. English ~several~ (“distinct,” then “more than one”) belongs to the family too. Spanish descendants cluster thickly: ~separación~ (“separation”), ~inseparable~ (“inseparable”), ~separata~ (“offprint”), and the noun ~separo~ used in Mexico for a holding cell.
en.ser:
Spanish ~ser~ descends, in its commonest forms, from Latin ~esse~ (“to be”), which reaches back to Proto-Indo-European *~h₁es-~ (“to be”). That root also gave Italian ~essere~, French ~être~, and the English verb itself — ~is~ and ~am~ — as well as German ~ist~. From the Latin present ~esse~ Spanish keeps ~soy~, ~es~, and ~son~; but the paradigm is famously stitched together, and several of its everyday forms descend not from ~esse~ at all.

The present indicative (~soy~, ~eres~, ~es~, ~somos~, ~sois~, ~son~) and the imperfect (~era~, from Latin ~eram~) continue ~esse~ — though ~eres~ is a curiosity, descending from the Latin future ~eris~ (“you will be”), pressed into a present to keep it distinct from ~es~. A second donor, ~sedēre~ (“to sit”), from *~sed-~, supplied the infinitive ~ser~ itself (through Old Spanish ~seer~), the future and conditional (~seré~, ~sería~), the present subjunctive (~sea~), and the imperative (~sé~) — so the very name of the verb means, etymologically, “to sit.” A third donor, the Latin perfect ~fuī~, from *~bʰuH-~ (“to become, grow”), gave the preterite (~fui~, ~fuiste~, ~fue~) — forms shared identically with ~ir~ (“to go”), so that ~fui~ means both “I was” and “I went,” context alone deciding.

From the ~esse~ / *~h₁es-~ side comes a wide family of learned words: ~ente~, ~esencia~, ~presente~, ~ausente~, and ~interés~. From ~sedēre~ (“to sit”) comes another cluster built on the idea of sitting or settling: ~sede~ (“seat, see”), ~sentar~, ~sesión~, and ~residir~. The suppletion that looks so chaotic in the paradigm is, in the vocabulary, two tidy word-families braided into one verb.
en.servir:
From Latin ~servīre~ (“to be a slave, to serve”), derived from ~servus~ (“slave, servant”). There the trail grows faint: the origin of ~servus~ is uncertain. It is usually traced to Proto-Italic *~serwos~ and compared with Umbrian ~seritu~, and it has sometimes been proposed as an Etruscan borrowing, but no account is secure, so the deeper root is best left open. The verb passed intact into Italian ~servire~, French ~servir~, and Portuguese ~servir~.

In Rome ~servīre~ meant literally to live in bondage; as that social reality faded, the word softened into today's neutral senses of waiting on someone, serving food, and — in ~servir~ para algo — simply being useful. A caution for the curious: Latin ~servāre~ (“to keep, to guard”), the source of ~conservar~ and ~observar~, springs from a different root and is not a relative, despite the resemblance. The genuine family of ~servus~ includes ~siervo~, ~servicio~, ~servil~, ~servidumbre~, and ~servidor~; its present participle ~servientem~ gave both Spanish ~sirviente~ and, by a long detour through French, English ~sergeant~.
en.señalar:
A denominative from ~señal~ (“sign, mark, signal”), which comes from Late Latin ~signālis~ (“of a sign”), from Latin ~signum~ (“mark, sign, military standard”). The root of ~signum~ is genuinely disputed: one account derives it from Proto-Indo-European *~sek-~ (“to cut”), making a sign “something cut or carved”; another from *~sekʷ-~ (“to follow,” as in Latin ~sequī~), making it “the standard the troops follow.” The forms are cognate with Italian ~segnalare~, French ~signaler~ and English ~signal~ and ~sign~.

From ~signālis~ Spanish built the noun ~señal~ and then the verb ~señalar~, “to mark” and hence “to point out, indicate.” Because the deeper origin is unsettled, the vivid “a sign is something carved” reading should be offered only as one contested hypothesis, not as fact. The same ~signum~ radiates through Spanish: ~seña~ (“gesture, sign”), ~signo~, ~diseñar~ (“to design,” via Italian) and, most surprisingly, ~enseñar~ (“to teach”), from Latin ~īnsignāre~, literally “to mark in, imprint.”
en.significar:
Spanish ~significar~ was borrowed from Latin ~significāre~ (“to make a sign, to indicate”), a transparent compound of ~signum~ (“sign, mark, token”) and ~-ficāre~, the combining form of ~facere~ (“to make, do,” from Proto-Indo-European *~dʰeh₁-~, “to put, place”). So the word means, literally, “to make a sign.” The deeper root of ~signum~ itself is disputed: it is traced to Proto-Italic *~seknom~ and thence either to Proto-Indo-European *~sek-~ (“to cut”) or to *~sekʷ-~ (“to follow”), and the sources do not settle between them. It is cognate with Italian ~significare~, French ~signifier~ and English ~signify~.

If ~signum~ began as a “cut” mark or a “follow” token, both readings suit a sign — a notch scored into a surface, or the trail one follows. From “to make a sign” the verb moved naturally to “to be a sign of,” that is “to mean”; a word ~significa~ something the way a symptom signifies a disease. The ~signum~ family is one of the richest in Spanish. Popular descent gave ~seña~ (“sign”), ~señal~ (“signal”) and ~señalar~ (“to point out”); learned borrowing gave ~signo~, ~significado~ (“meaning”), ~insignia~, and — through ~dēsignāre~ — ~diseñar~ (“to design”). All of them are still, at heart, about setting down a mark that stands for something else.
en.situar:
From Late Latin ~situāre~ (“to place, locate, set in position”), formed on Latin ~situs~ (“site, position, situation”), which is the past participle of the verb ~sinere~ (“to let, allow; to set down, lay”). De Vaan traces ~sinere~ to a Proto-Indo-European root *~tḱey-~ (“to settle, build”), the same root behind Sanskrit ~kṣéti~ (“he dwells”). Because ~situs~ passed into the Romance languages and into learned Latin borrowings alike, its offspring are widespread: English ~site~ and ~situate~, French ~site~, Italian ~sito~, and Portuguese ~sítio~ all stand beside Spanish ~sitio~.

The chain hides a quiet irony: ~sinere~ meant “to let be, leave alone,” so a ~situs~ was first a place where something had simply been left — and one old sense of Latin ~situs~ was precisely the “neglect, mold, decay” that settles on a thing left untouched. Medieval clerks turned the noun back into the verb ~situāre~, “to give a thing its place,” and Spanish inherited it as ~situar~. From the same noun Spanish keeps ~sitio~ (“place; also a military siege,” a spot one occupies and holds) and ~situación~ (“situation”), while the reflexive ~situarse~ means to find or position oneself. What began as land left to itself became the vocabulary of putting things deliberately in their place.
en.sobrevivir:
From ~sobre-~ (“over, beyond,” from Latin ~super~) plus ~vivir~ (“to live,” from Latin ~vīvere~), a calque of Latin ~supervivere~ (“to outlive”). ~vīvere~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~gʷeyh₃-~ (“to live”). Cognate with Portuguese ~sobreviver~, French ~survivre~ and Italian ~sopravvivere~, and — through ~vīvere~ — with English ~vital~, ~vivid~ and ~revive~; the same PIE root gave Ancient Greek ~bíos~ (“life”) and, in Germanic, the archaic English ~quick~ (“living, alive”).

The literal sense is spatial-turned-temporal: to live beyond a limit — beyond a disaster, an era, or another person — hence “to outlive, survive, endure.” The prefix ~super~ (“over”) itself descends from PIE *~uper~, kin to English ~over~ and Greek ~hyper~. Spanish draws deeply on the ~vīvere~ branch: ~vida~, ~vívido~, ~vital~, ~convivir~, ~revivir~ and ~víveres~ (“provisions”), while ~sobrevivir~ yields ~superviviente~ and ~supervivencia~ — all circling the plain fact of staying alive.
en.soler:
Spanish ~soler~ was inherited through Old Spanish ~soler~ from Latin ~solēre~ (“to be accustomed, to be wont”). Its deeper origin is disputed. One tradition (Walde-Hoffmann, Pokorny) reconstructs Proto-Italic *~sweðēō~ and a Proto-Indo-European *~swé-dʰh₁-~, literally “to set as one's own,” from *~swé~ (“self”) plus *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to put, place”); on this account ~solēre~ would be close kin to ~sodālis~ (“companion”) and ~suēscō~ (“to grow accustomed”). De Vaan rejects that derivation on sound grounds — a following ~ē~ should have blocked the shift *~swe-~ > ~so-~ — and looks instead toward *~sel-~ / ~solum~ (“ground, base”). The safe statement is that ~solēre~ is old and its ultimate root unsettled. It is cognate with Italian ~solere~ and Catalan ~soler~, and with the now-archaic Portuguese ~soer~.

In Spanish ~soler~ became a pure habit-marker, an auxiliary that adds “usually” to whatever verb follows: ~suele~ llover (“it usually rains”), ~solíamos~ caminar (“we used to walk”). Fittingly for a verb about the customary, it is itself defective, living almost entirely in the present and the imperfect — one rarely meets it in the future or the preterite, because a one-off habit is a contradiction. The “custom” sense is preserved beautifully in a common relative: ~insólito~ (“unusual, extraordinary”), from Latin ~insolitus~, literally “un-accustomed” — what does not usually happen. Beside it stand the rarer ~sólito~ (“customary”) and ~desueto~ / ~desuetud~ (“disused, desuetude”). Thus a single Latin verb of habit gave Spanish both its everyday word for “to usually do” and its bookish word for what breaks all habit.
en.solicitar:
Spanish ~solicitar~ comes from Latin ~sollicitāre~ (“to disturb, stir up, agitate”), a verb built on the adjective ~sollicitus~ (“thoroughly moved, anxious, worried”). That adjective is transparent: ~sollus~ (“whole, entire”) plus ~citus~ (“set in motion, roused”), the past participle of ~ciēre~ (“to move, stir”). ~sollus~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~solh₂-~ (“whole”), the root behind Greek ~hólos~ (“whole,” as in ~holo-~) and Latin ~salvus~ (“safe”); ~ciēre~ reflects *~keyh₁-~ (“to set in motion”). English borrowed the family directly: ~solicit~, ~solicitous~, and ~solicitude~ all sit beside the Spanish verb.

The literal Latin sense was physical agitation — to shake something thoroughly, to trouble it entirely. From “to disturb, importune” the meaning softened into “to entreat, petition,” and Spanish ~solicitar~ now spans a polite request (~solicitar una beca~, “to apply for a scholarship”), a formal application, and the still-charged ~solicitar a alguien~ (“to court or proposition someone”), where the old sense of stirring another person up survives. The past participle gave ~solícito~ (“attentive, obliging”) and the noun ~solicitud~ (“request; application; solicitude”). Through the same root *~solh₂-~ Spanish also holds ~sólido~, ~salvo~, ~salud~, and ~católico~ (from Greek ~katholikós~, “universal, on the whole”).
en.soltar:
From Vulgar Latin *~soltāre~, a verb built on ~suelto~ (“loose, released”), which descends from ~solŭtus~, a Vulgar Latin variant of Classical ~solūtus~ (“loosened, freed”), the past participle of ~solvere~ (“to loosen, release, dissolve”). ~solvere~ joins the separative prefix ~se-~ to ~luere~ (“to loosen”), from Proto-Indo-European *~lewH-~ (“to cut apart, loosen”). It is cognate with Portuguese ~soltar~; through ~solvere~ it is kin to English ~solve~, ~dissolve~ and ~solution~; and through the PIE root, to Ancient Greek ~λύω~ (“I loosen”) and ~λύσις~ (“a loosening”), the ancestor of analysis and dialysis.

Latin had no simple verb *soltāre; Spanish minted its own from the participle-turned-adjective ~suelto~, so the sense stayed close to “to let loose”: to release, untie, set free, and figuratively to blurt out (soltar una carcajada, to burst out laughing). From the same ~solvere~ family come ~absolver~, ~disolver~, ~resolver~, ~soltura~ and ~solución~. The adjective ~soltero~ (“unmarried, single”) is traditionally attached to this family — the single person as one who is “unbound” — but it may instead descend from Latin ~solitarius~ (“solitary, alone”); the two forms clearly influenced each other, and the sources do not fully settle the matter.
en.solucionar:
A modern verb built on the noun ~solución~ (“solution”), from Latin ~solutio~ (“a loosening, dissolving”), from ~solvere~ (“to loosen, release, dissolve”), itself ~se-~ (“apart”) plus ~luere~ (“to loosen, wash”), from Proto-Indo-European *~lewh₃-~ (“to wash, loosen”). Cognate through Latin with English ~solve~, ~dissolve~ and ~absolute~, and with French ~solution~.

Latin ~solvere~ combined the separative ~se-~ with ~luere~, so to solve was literally to loosen or untie a bind. Its past participle ~solutus~ gave Spanish ~suelto~ (“loose”) and a learned family: ~soluble~, ~solvente~, ~absolver~, ~disolver~ and ~resolver~. The noun ~solución~ held both senses at once — a substance dissolved in liquid, and a knotty problem untied — and only in the modern era did Spanish coin the everyday verb ~solucionar~ from it, beside the older ~resolver~.
en.someter:
From Latin ~submittere~ (“to place under, lower, let down; to subject”), a compound of ~sub-~ (“under”) and ~mittere~ (“to send, let go”). It is thus a close sibling of ~committere~ above, built on the same ~mittere~, which traces through Proto-Italic *~meitō~ to the Proto-Indo-European root *~meyth₂-~ (“to exchange”), an extension of *~mey-~ (“to change”). Spanish ~someter~ is the inherited reflex; alongside it the language kept learned forms from the participle ~submissus~. Romance cognates include French ~soumettre~ and Italian ~sottomettere~ / ~sommettere~, and English ~submit~ comes from the same ~submittere~.

The literal picture is spatial: to “send under” is to bring beneath one’s power — hence ~someter~ “to subdue, subject, put down (a revolt),” and reflexively ~someterse~ “to submit, yield, give in.” The verb keeps a useful ambiguity English splits between “subdue” (imposing from above) and “submit” (yielding from below), the difference lying only in who does the sending-under. From the participle ~submissus~ came the learned pair ~sumiso~ (“submissive, meek”) and ~sumisión~ (“submission, obedience”), which sit beside ~sometimiento~ (“subjection”) built on the verb. It is a nice symmetry of Latin word-building that ~sub-~ + ~mittere~ (“send under”) and ~com-~ + ~mittere~ (“send together”) should have travelled into Spanish as the near-rhyming ~someter~ and ~cometer~, two prefixes turning one humble verb of “sending” to opposite ends.
en.sonar:
~sonar~ descends from Latin ~sonāre~ (“to make a sound, resound”), a verb from the noun ~sonus~ (“sound, noise”). ~sonus~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~swonos~ and the Proto-Indo-European root *~swenh₂-~ (“to sound, resound”). The most charming cognate is English ~swan~: from Proto-Germanic *~swanaz~, literally “the sounding one, the singing bird.” Sanskrit ~svan~ (“to sound”) and Russian ~zvon~ (“chime, ring”) belong to the same family, and English ~sound~ itself is a borrowing of ~sonus~ through Old French.

Spanish kept the plain sense — bells, instruments, and phones all ~sonar~ — plus idiomatic branches: a name that ~suena~ is one that “rings a bell,” and ~sonarse~ (“to blow one's nose”) trades on the noise. From ~sonus~ and ~sonāre~ spring a large family: ~sonido~ (“sound”), ~sonoro~, ~son~ (“tune,” as in the Cuban dance), ~sonata~ (via Italian), ~resonar~, ~consonante~, and ~sonajero~ (“baby's rattle”).
en.sonreír:
From Latin ~subrīdēre~, from ~sub-~ (“under, slightly”) plus ~rīdēre~ (“to laugh”), whose own origin the sources leave uncertain. The prefix ~sub-~ regularly surfaced in Spanish as ~son-~ before r, giving ~sonreír~ beside plain ~reír~ (“to laugh”). It is cognate with Italian ~sorridere~, French ~sourire~ and Portuguese ~sorrir~; through ~rīdēre~ English shares ~risible~, ~ridicule~ and ~deride~.

The compound is quietly literal: a smile is an “under-laugh,” mirth kept below the full voice of laughter. Because ~rīdēre~ is of unknown origin — some have proposed it is imitative, but the sources do not settle the matter — no confident Indo-European root can be attached here. Within Spanish the same stem yielded the noun ~sonrisa~ (“smile”) beside ~risa~ (“laughter”), plus ~ridículo~, ~irrisorio~ and the participial adjective ~sonriente~ (“smiling”).
en.soportar:
From Latin ~supportāre~ (“to carry up, convey, bring”), a compound of ~sub-~ (“up from under”) and ~portāre~ (“to carry”), from Proto-Italic *~portāō~ and ultimately the Proto-Indo-European root *~per-~ (“to carry across, pass over”). The same verb reached the other Romance languages as French ~supporter~, Italian ~sopportare~, and Portuguese ~suportar~, and English borrowed it, through Old French, as ~support~.

The literal Latin sense was to shoulder a load and carry it upward; from bearing physical weight the verb slid to bearing hardship, and Spanish ~soportar~ now means chiefly “to endure, put up with, tolerate.” This makes it a classic false friend of English ~support~: « no lo puedo ~soportar~ » means “I can’t stand it,” not “I can’t support it.” Spanish keeps the load-bearing sense too — a beam can ~soportar~ a roof — and the noun ~soporte~ means a “stand, bracket, support.” From the same ~portāre~ come a whole convoy of verbs: ~aportar~, ~transportar~, ~importar~, ~exportar~, and ~deportar~.
en.sorprender:
Spanish ~sorprender~ came in from French ~surprendre~ (“to overtake, catch unawares”), a compound of ~sur-~ (“over, upon,” from Latin ~super~) and ~prendre~ (“to take”). ~prendre~ continues Latin ~prehendere~ (“to seize, grasp, catch”), itself ~prae-~ (“before”) plus a verbal element ~-hendere~. That ~-hendere~ rests on the Proto-Indo-European root *~ǵʰend-~ (“to seize, take”), whose scattered kin include Greek ~khandánein~ (“to hold, contain”), Old Norse ~geta~ (“to get, obtain”), and, through Germanic, English ~get~ itself. Because Spanish reshaped the French word on the pattern of its own inherited ~prender~ (“to seize, catch; to catch fire”), the family is doubly present in the language — one branch borrowed, one branch inherited.

The metaphor is vivid and physical: to surprise someone is to “take” them from “over” or “above,” catching them before they can react — the same military image that lets ~sorprender~ mean “to take by surprise, ambush.” From the astonishment sense grew the noun ~sorpresa~ (“a surprise”) and the adjective ~sorprendente~ (“surprising, astonishing”). The inherited ~prender~ side of the family is one of the richest in Spanish: ~prisión~ (“prison”) and ~preso~/~presa~ (“prisoner; prey”) for the “seizing,” ~aprender~ (“to learn,” to “grasp” knowledge), ~comprender~ (“to understand,” to grasp fully), ~emprender~ (“to undertake”), and ~prenda~ (“a garment; a pledge”). English ~prehensile~ and ~comprehend~ preserve the fuller Latin ~-hendere~ that French and Spanish wore away.
en.sostener:
From Latin ~sustinēre~ (“to hold up, support, endure”), from ~sus-~ (a form of ~sub-~, “under, up from under”) plus ~tenēre~ (“to hold”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ten-~ (“to stretch”). Cognate with Italian ~sostenere~, French ~soutenir~, and — through Old French — English ~sustain~.

The image is physical: to hold a thing up from below, and from there to support, maintain, and endure. Spanish ~sostener~ still spans all of these — the same ~sostener~ holds a weight, an argument, or a conversation.
